questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

MITSINA THE HERMIT

This is a tale told by the Zuni Indians of America’s southwest.

Long ago, before men and women lived on Earth, gods and goddesses lived in Heaven.

But not all the gods and goddesses were good. Sharp-sighted Mitsina was an evil god. Lying and cheating were his favourite tricks.

Awonawilona, the ever-burning sun god, cast Mitsina from Heaven down to Earth. There, in the dense Canyon of the Pines, Mitsina settled and did his building. After his house was finished, Mitsina passed his time by playing cane-cards: a game like dice, a game of gambling. But there were neither men nor women with whom to gamble. So he played alone.

After a thousand years, men and women began to live on earth.

Sometimes it happened that a warrior went hunting for deer, and came upon Mitsina’s lodgings. From within, the warrior heard a strange sound — rr — like wind whistling through the pine trees. Curious, the warrior came closer and placed his ear against the wall. He heard the windy sound again, louder still.

Then he climbed the ladder leading to the roof and looked down through the sky-hole, through which the smoke rose. There he saw old Mitsina playing at cane-cards. As Mitsina rolled the cane-cards on his buffalo blanket, he shouted ‘Rrrrrr!’ — like an icy north wind blowing.

Mitsina was old, but he had good eyes. He caught sight of the warrior.

‘I was just playing a game of cane-cards’, Mitsina said. ‘Won’t you come down and join me?’

The warrior climbed down the ladder and entered Mitsina’s house.

Source: David Shapiro, Mitsina the Hermit, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

parts.stem: What can be said about this passage?
options: It is a parable from the Zuni Indians.
It is a folktale of the Zuni Indians.
It is an epic of the southwest Indians.
It is a biography of Mitsina.
parts.hint: Read how the passage begins. It tells you what kind of text it is and who tells it.

steps.explain: Read the first sentence.
steps.work: “This is a tale told by the Zuni Indians of America’s southwest.”

steps.explain: What kind of story is this?
steps.work: It has gods, a made-up long-ago time, and no named writer: a story handed down by a people is a folktale.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A parable is a short story that teaches a lesson with everyday people. An epic is a long poem about a hero. A biography tells the real life story of a person.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: What can be said about this passage
keyPoints.note: Look at the first sentence: it tells you what kind of story this is.

questions.stem: AEROPLANE is to FLIGHT PATH as MOTOR VEHICLE is to ?
questions.hint: A flight path is the way an aeroplane travels from one place to another. What do we call the way a car travels from one place to another?

steps.explain: Find the link in the first pair.
steps.work: An AEROPLANE follows a FLIGHT PATH: the line it travels along from where it starts to where it lands. (vehicle → the path it follows)

steps.explain: Use the same link for MOTOR VEHICLE. What path does a car follow from start to finish?

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A highway and a road are the physical things a car drives on. A flight path is not a physical thing in the sky, it is the chosen way to travel, just like a route.

A map only shows places, it is not a path a car follows.

steps.explain: AEROPLANE : FLIGHT PATH matches MOTOR VEHICLE : ROUTE.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A flight path is a way of travelling, not a thing on the ground. Find the matching word for a car.

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

THE PARABLE OF THE TEN GIRLS

Once there were ten girls who took their oil lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and the other five were wise. The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take any extra oil with them, while the wise ones took containers full of oil for their lamps. The bridegroom was late in coming, so the girls began to nod and fall asleep.

It was already midnight when the cry rang out, ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come and meet him!’ The ten girls woke up and trimmed their lamps. Then the foolish ones said to the wise ones, ‘Let us have some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’ ‘No indeed,’ the wise ones answered, ‘there is not enough for you and for us. Go to the shop and buy some for yourselves.’ So the foolish girls went off to buy some oil; and while they were gone, the bridegroom arrived. The five girls who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was closed.

Later the other girls arrived. ‘Sir, sir! Let us in!’ they cried out. ‘Certainly not! I don’t know you,’ the bridegroom answered.

Source: Matthew, Chapter 25, verses 1–12, Today’s English Version, New York, American Bible Society, 1976

parts.stem: Why is this called a parable?
options: it is a story that uses an example to teach a lesson
it is a story from ancient life and times
it is a religious story and fable
it is a true story that teaches a lesson
parts.hint: A parable is a special kind of story. Look at how this story uses ten girls and their lamps to make a point.

steps.explain: Look at what happens in the story.
steps.work: Five girls are foolish and do not bring extra oil. Five girls are wise and do bring it. Only the wise girls are let in.

steps.explain: Ask what the story is really teaching.
steps.work: It is not really about lamps and oil. It uses the girls as an EXAMPLE to teach a lesson: be ready and prepared.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B — many old stories come from ancient times, but that does not make them parables.

C — it is religious, but “fable” is a story with talking animals.

D — a parable is not a true event, it is a made-up story.

steps.explain: A parable is a story that uses an example to teach a lesson.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Why is this called a parable
keyPoints.note: A parable uses a simple made-up story as an example to teach a lesson.

parts.stem: How do we know that this parable is not from modern times?

the oil was carried around in containers
the parable was used only in ancient times
parts.hint: Look for something in the story that people do not use any more today.

steps.explain: Read the story for things that belong to the past.
steps.work:
“Once there were ten girls who took their oil lamps…”

Today we use electric lights and torches. Oil lamps point to old times.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — people wait for others today too.

C — we still carry oil and liquids in containers today.

D — this is not something the story tells us, and parables are still told today.

steps.explain: The oil lamps show that the story is from the past.
steps.work: The answer is B.

parts.stem: What does the parable say about the bridegroom?

he expected to be met by the ten girls

steps.explain: Find what the bridegroom says.
steps.work:
“‘Certainly not! I don’t know you,’ the bridegroom answered.”

He says this to the foolish girls who arrive late.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — the story does not talk about respect.

B — the bridegroom was late, not early (“The bridegroom was late in coming”).

D — he was expected by the ten girls, but the parable does not say what he expected.

parts.stem: What does the parable say about the wise girls?
options: they expected the bridegroom to be late
they were just thinking of themselves
they were able to get their lamps going in time
they were allowed into the wedding feast
parts.hint: Find what happens to the five wise girls when the bridegroom arrives.

steps.explain: Find the sentence about the wise girls going in.
steps.work:
“The five girls who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was closed.”

The five who were ready are the wise girls.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — the story says they brought extra oil, but it does not say why.

B — the story does not say they were selfish, only that there was not enough oil to share.

C — the story does not say they got their lamps going; it says they “trimmed their lamps”.

steps.explain: The wise girls were allowed into the wedding feast.
steps.work: The answer is D.

parts.stem: What do you think is the main point of this parable?
options: this is a story about the problems of not being punctual
this is a story that shows being ready for everything is rewarded
this is a story about being prepared
this is a story about five wise and five foolish girls
parts.hint: The main point is the lesson of the story. Which option says that being ready is rewarded, including what happened to the ones who were ready and the ones who were not?

steps.explain: Think about what happened to each group.
steps.work: The wise girls were prepared (they had extra oil) and were let in. The foolish girls were not prepared and were shut out.

steps.explain: The lesson must say what is rewarded, not only what the story is about.
steps.work:
A — it is about the bridegroom being late, not about being punctual.

C — “being prepared” is true, but it does not say what the story shows about being prepared.

D — this only says who is in the story.

B — being ready for everything is rewarded. ✓

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The main point is the lesson the story teaches, not just what happens in it.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

THE STORY OF ARTHUR STACE

Eternity

A short, grey-haired and lightly built man, who looked quite frail, would often be seen in the early mornings around Wynyard Station. They say that he was always dressed the same, with a grey felt hat, tie and double-breasted navy blue suit.

He began early, usually before dawn, and he wandered through many of the inner Sydney suburbs. As he walked every so often he would stop, pull out a chalk, bend down and write on the footpath in large, neat running-writing — ETERNITY. He would walk a further hundred metres then write it again, ETERNITY, nothing else, only one word. For 37 years he chalked this one-word message to the whole of Sydney and he wrote it more than half a million times.

For many years the writer of these ‘Eternity’ signs was anonymous. It mystified Sydney. He did not like publicity and the mystery of the unknown writer of ETERNITY only became clear in 1956. One day Rev. Lisle Thompson, who knew Stace as a church cleaner, saw him take out his chalk and write the well-known ‘Eternity’ sign on the footpath. He did it without realising that he had been spotted. Arthur Stace died of a stroke in a nursing home on July 30, 1967. He was 83.

Sources: Reverend Lisle M. Thompson, The Crooked Made Straight, St Barnabas web site; transcript of a book by Keith Dunstan, Ratbags

parts.stem: What is the main idea of the article?
options: how the writer of ‘Eternity’ was discovered
the lifetime work of a man
some publicity for the writer of ‘Eternity’
parts.hint: The main idea covers the whole article. The article is about a man and what he did for most of his life.

steps.explain: Say what each paragraph is about.
steps.work:
Paragraph 1: what Arthur Stace looked like.

Paragraph 2: what he did every morning — wrote ETERNITY on the footpaths for 37 years.

Paragraph 3: the mystery of who the writer was, and how he was found.

steps.explain: Find the idea that covers all three paragraphs.
steps.work: The article tells the story of a man and the one-word message he chalked for 37 years — his lifetime work.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A — only paragraph 3 is about being discovered.

C — religion is only mentioned briefly.

D — Stace did not like publicity.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The main idea must cover the whole article, not just one paragraph.

parts.stem: What can we judge about the man who wrote ‘Eternity’?
options: he was a minister of religion
parts.hint: Judge him from what the article says he did and did not like. Did he want to be famous?

steps.explain: Find the clues about how he behaved.
steps.work: “He did not like publicity…” and “…without realising that he had been spotted.” He wrote for 37 years without asking for any credit.

steps.explain: What kind of person does not want credit for work he does?
steps.work: A humble person — someone who is not boastful and does not need to be praised.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B — nothing says he was poor.

C — he was unknown for many years, but this is a fact, not a judgement about him as a person.

D — he was a church cleaner, not a minister.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: To judge means to work out what kind of person he was from clues in the article.

parts.stem: Why did Arthur Stace write ‘Eternity’ on the footpaths of Sydney?

parts.hint: Find the sentence that says what the word ETERNITY was meant to be.

steps.explain: So what was he doing when he wrote the word?

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A, B and D are guesses about why he did it. The article only states that it was a message to the whole of Sydney.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The reason is stated in the article. Find the word “message”.

questions.stem:
Here is a phrase from the start of a famous poem. The letters are coded. Which new word might have the code 5 3 3 1 7 1?

Earth has not anything to show...
12345 678 901 23456789 01 2345...
questions.hint: Write the code number under every letter of the phrase. A number can stand for more than one letter. Then test each option letter by letter.

steps.explain: Write the number under each letter of the phrase, the way the question does.
steps.work:
Earth: E1 a2 r3 t4 h5

has: h6 a7 s8

not: n9 o0 t1

anything: a2 n3 y4 t5 h6 i7 n8 g9

to: t0 o1

show: s2 h3 o4 w5

steps.explain: Make a list of the letters that each digit can stand for. A digit can stand for more than one letter.
Use the list to decode 5 3 3 1 7 1 one digit at a time.
steps.work:
5 → h, t or w

3 → r, n or h

3 → r, n or h

1 → E, t or o

7 → a or i

1 → E, t or o

steps.explain: Test each option: every letter must be in the list for its digit.
steps.work:
THREAT: T(5) ✓ H(3) ✓ R(3) ✓ E(1) ✓ A(7) ✓ T(1) ✓ — all six letters fit.

THREAD: the last letter D is not in the phrase at all. ✗

THE SON: T(5) ✓ H(3) ✓ E(3)? E is only 1. ✗

TRYING: T(5) ✓ R(3) ✓ Y(3)? Y is 4. ✗

steps.explain: Only one option can be made from the code.
steps.work: The word is THREAT. The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Write each digit with every letter it can stand for, then test the options.

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

THE GREAT DEPRESSION

The Great Depression of the 1930s was a worldwide financial disaster. It all began in the United States, with the Wall Street Crash of 1929.

America was prosperous in the 1920s. People invested in the stock market, and many made a fortune. They borrowed money from the banks on the strength of their shares. But in 1929 those share prices started falling. People started selling off their shares. The more shares were sold, the more prices fell. Investors began to panic and tried to sell their shares before they became worthless. Prices fell even further and finally the stock market collapsed. People couldn’t repay their bank loans because their stocks and shares were worthless. They went broke and so did the banks. The crash destroyed the American economy and soon the effects were felt throughout the world.

Factories and businesses closed down or dismissed many workers. Millions of people could not find work, and many families were hungry. The worst years of the Depression were 1929–1934, but for many people, life was difficult for ten years or more afterwards. The Second World War (1939–1945) was a time of hunger, too. So the years 1929–1950 were a time of hunger and poverty for millions of people around the world.

In Australia, the 1920s had been fairly prosperous. Wool and wheat were our strongest primary industries. We sent these products overseas, and our exports earned a great deal of money. By 1929, however, prices paid for Australia’s wool and wheat overseas had dropped when countries like the United States reduced their imports.

As well, secondary industries, such as shoe making, were unable to compete for markets overseas. Wage rates were lowered and more and more people were dismissed from their jobs. Thousands of men walked the city streets looking for work so that they could pay their rents and feed and clothe their families. But work was scarce. Soon they left home to look for work in the country. Few were successful.

Source: Edel Wignell, Battlers of the Great Depression, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990, pp. 6–7

parts.stem: What was the Great Depression?
options: the ruin of the American economy
parts.hint: Look at the very first sentence of the passage. It says what the Great Depression was.

steps.explain: Find the first sentence.
steps.work: “The Great Depression of the 1930s was a worldwide financial disaster.”

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
B — the Wall Street Crash was how it began, not what it was.

C — the ruin of the American economy was one effect of it.

D — hunger from 1929–1950 was one result, not the definition.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: The very first sentence defines it. The other options are causes or results.

meta.source: Excel Practice Opportunity Class Tests · Year 4

parts.stem: What was one cause of the Great Depression?
options: the price of shares fell in 1929
parts.hint: A cause is something that happened BEFORE the Depression and made it happen. Some options are results that came afterwards.

steps.explain: Find the sentences that explain how it began.
steps.work: “They borrowed money from the banks on the strength of their shares. But in 1929 those share prices started falling… People couldn’t repay their bank loans.”

steps.explain: Sort the options into causes and results.
steps.work: Factories closing down and millions losing work came AFTER the crash: they are results. The share prices falling is part of the crash itself. People borrowing money from the banks was the thing that set up the trouble.

steps.explain: Choose the cause.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: A cause comes before the Depression. A result comes after it. Do not mix them up.

steps.work: 1929–1950 includes the hungry years afterwards. 1929 is only the year of the crash. 1939–1945 is the Second World War.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

questions.stem:
Here is a phrase written in a secret code. Each number can stand for more than one letter. To help you, part of the phrase has been decoded.

5 6 3 4 6 1 0 7 7
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ A N D
5 6 3 4 2 9 6
_ _ _ _ _ _ _

Which sentence could stand for this code?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 600 180" width="95%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q19.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="600" height="180"/></svg>

questions.hint: The decoded letters A, N and D in “and” give you three code numbers: 0 = A, 7 = N, 7 = D. Wait: look at the digits 1, 0, 7, 7 under “and”. Use the repeated digits to test each option.

steps.explain: Read the code. The two words in the code have the digits 5 6 3 4 6 1 (6 letters, first word) and 5 6 3 4 2 9 6 (7 letters, last word).
steps.work: Both words start with the same four digits: 5 6 3 4. The same digits stand for the same letters.

steps.explain: So the first four letters of the two words are the same, the first word has 6 letters and the last word has 7. Look at the options for this.
steps.work:
Native (6) / natural (7): NATI ≠ NATU ✗

People (6) / parties (7): PEOP ≠ PART ✗

Master (6) / mistress (8): wrong length and MAST ≠ MIST ✗

Forget (6) / forgive (7): FORG = FORG ✓

steps.explain: Check the other repeated digits. In the first word the digit 6 is the 2nd and 5th digit; in the last word 6 is the 2nd and 7th digit.
steps.work: FORGET: the 2nd letter is O and the 5th letter is E. The digit 6 is shown for both. The code says it can stand for more than one letter, so this is allowed. FORGIVE: the 2nd letter O and the 7th letter E.

steps.explain: Only “Forget and forgive” fits the code.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.text: Each number can stand for more than one letter
keyPoints.note: Compare the two words in the code: their first four digits are the same, so their first four letters must be the same.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

ORIENTEERING

Orienteering is a sport which began in Europe in 1918. It is very popular in Scandinavia. In Sweden, an annual five-day orienteering event attracts over 15 000 participants.

To ‘orient’ yourself means to work out where you are. In orienteering, people run or walk around a course, using a compass and a map to find their way.

Orienteering is known as the ‘O sport’. Sometimes it is called ‘thought sport’, because orienteers need to think about where the controls might be and when they should run.

Another name for orienteering is ‘cunning running’, because you must think about the best way to go. Which route should you choose? Should you run down the long track or climb over the big hill?

Runners use a compass and map to find red and white markers in the bush. The markers are called controls.

Each runner chooses a course. There are easy, or novice, courses for beginners. There are harder courses for runners or walkers who have done orienteering before. And there are very hard, or elite, courses for the best runners.

Orienteering is popular with people of all ages in many parts of the world.

Orienteering began in Australia in 1969. In 1985, the world championships were held in this country.

Source: Hazel Edwards, Cunning Running, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

parts.stem: How could orienteering be described best of all?
options: an activity for those who are good runners
as an activity that requires thinking
as an activity that involves teamwork
as an activity that requires fitness and strength
parts.hint: Look at the names the passage gives to orienteering. What do those names say about it?

steps.explain: Find the other names for orienteering.
steps.work: It is called a “thought sport” and “cunning running”. Both names are about thinking.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A — the courses are for all levels, not only good runners. C — the passage never mentions teamwork. D — fitness helps, but the passage stresses thinking.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The passage gives two names that describe the sport. What do they have in common?

‘Defeated in battle and trapped in a cave, the mighty Japanese warrior and his supporters prepare to die by their own swords. In that cave is a bee trapped in a spider’s web. questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

NOT ZACKLY

Leigh and Julie were fed up with the weather, and so was Bandit. For the first precious week of the school holidays it had rained without stopping. There was water everywhere… pouring from the cloud-filled sky, running in rivulets down the face of the windowpanes, lying in muddy pools in the garden, cascading along the gutters in the street outside. There had been nothing else to do except stay dry indoors, reading and watching television.

Julie sat slumped in the beanbag with the book she was reading. She looked up in surprise as a sudden shaft of sunlight beamed through the window.

‘I don’t believe it!’ she said, scrambling to her feet. ‘Leigh! It’s stopped raining. There’s blue sky outside. Enough to make a sailor a pair of trousers.’

Leigh, who had been trying to fix the propeller on to his model aeroplane, came up beside her. ‘Let’s get out and go for a walk’, he said, ‘before it starts raining all over again.’

‘Walk?’ Bandit leapt to his feet. With a joyful yelp, he rushed to the door and waited anxiously for it to be opened.

‘We’d better tell Mum where we’re going’, said Julie. ‘Mum!’ she shouted back into the house. ‘We’re going to the paddock to look at the creek.’

‘Then be careful’, called Jean.

‘We will!’

Leigh grabbed parkas from the hook in the passageway and Julie brought boots. Leigh opened the door and Bandit, pushing past, skedaddled down the steps. He sprang around, bounding and barking.

‘Shut up, Bandit!’ said Leigh.

They hurried off down the street with Bandit, intent on adventure, loping ahead of them. Steam rose from the wet bitumen.

Zachary, standing at the living-room window of his home, saw them go. He had stood there every day that week, staring out at the empty street, at the rain and the storm-clouds, waiting for something to happen. Like Leigh and Julie, he was bored. He hurried outside.

Source: Mary Small, Not Zackly, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990, pp. 2–4

parts.stem: Whom, does the story say, was fed up with the weather?
parts.hint: Find everyone who is described as fed up, bored or tired of the rain, not only in the first sentence. Do not forget the dog, and check the last paragraph.

steps.explain: Read the first sentence.
steps.work: “Leigh and Julie were fed up with the weather, and so was Bandit.”

steps.explain: Check the last paragraph for anyone else who is unhappy about the weather.
steps.work: “Zachary… had stood there every day that week, staring out at the empty street, at the rain and the storm-clouds… Like Leigh and Julie, he was bored.”

steps.explain: Count everyone: Leigh, Julie, Bandit and Zachary. Jean (the mother) is never said to be fed up.
steps.work: We are not told whether Jean was bored with the weather.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Check the whole passage, not just the first sentence. Zachary also had a hard time with the rain.

parts.stem: What are the RIVULETS mentioned in the first paragraph?

steps.work: A window is small, so the water running down it makes thin, narrow streams.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: rivers of water are far too big for a window. Large drops would not “run”. “Bolts of water” is not a real meaning.

steps.explain: A rivulet is a small stream.
steps.work: The answer is B.

parts.stem: What does this phrase — ‘Enough to make a sailor a pair of trousers’ — mean?

steps.work: A says the sun was shining, but she only says there is blue sky. B is about the colour of the sky. D is silly: she is not talking about the shape of the clouds.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

1232  45  567.  567  45  6  768.

Which sentence could stand for this code?
options: Take it Sam. Sam is a man.
Come in Joe. Joe is a man.
Here is Pat. Pat is a dog.
Here is Sam. Sam is a man.
questions.hint: Count the letters in each code word: 1232 has 4, 45 has 2, 567 has 3, 6 has 1 and 768 has 3. Then see which option has words of exactly these lengths and repeats words in the same places.

steps.explain: Write down the length of each code word.
steps.work: The code has 7 words: 4, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3 letters. The 3rd and 4th words use the same digits (567) and the 2nd and 5th words use the same digits (45), so those words are the same.

steps.explain: Check the word lengths and repeats in each option.
steps.work:
Take it Sam. Sam is a man: 4, 2, 3 | 3, 2, 1, 3 but “it” and “is” are different 2-letter words, while the code repeats 45. ✗

Come in Joe. Joe is a man: “in” and “is” are different words. ✗

Here is Pat. Pat is a dog: the lengths match, but the code 567 has a 7 that also appears in 768, and PAT and DOG do not share any letter. ✗

Here is Sam. Sam is a man: “is” repeats, “Sam” repeats, and SAM and MAN share the letters M and A. ✓

steps.explain: Write the digits under the letters of option D.
steps.work: HERE = 1232 (H1 E2 R3 E2), IS = 45 (I4 S5), SAM = 567 (S5 A6 M7), SAM = 567, IS = 45, A = 6, MAN = 768 (M7 A6 N8). Every digit is the same letter each time. ✓

steps.explain: Only option D fits the code.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Compare the pattern of repeated code numbers with the repeated words in each option. Also count the letters in each word.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following passage.

DECOY GANNETS

In January 1988 there were six gannets (sea birds) on Cat Island, an islet east of Flinders Island in Bass Strait. Eighty years ago a huge colony of 10 000 gannets nested there. In 1950 there were only 200 left. The numbers decreased until, in 1984, a bushfire killed most of the remaining few birds.

Humans were the gannets’ main enemies. Some fishermen killed them to use as bait in crayfish pots. Other people used them as targets for shooting.

The Australasian gannet is a large bird with a white and black body and golden feathers on its head. In flight its wings stretch almost two metres across.

For ten years officers of the Department of Lands, Parks and Wildlife had been trying to get gannets to come back to their old breeding ground. In 1987 and 1988 fake gannets were used as decoys. The decoy gannets were moulded from polyurethane and wire, and weighted with bricks. They were painted by school children on Flinders Island, who took care with all the details, such as eye and beak markings. The decoys are very lifelike. From a distance it is difficult to tell which is a fake and which is a real bird.

When the fake birds were put on Cat Island in 1987, gannets landed immediately. They started tapping beaks with the decoys. In that first year, one started nesting among the decoys. In 1988 six gannets arrived, nested and hatched three chicks.

Other birds have been fooled by the decoys. A pair of sea eagles (enemies of the gannet) swooped and attacked. They damaged some of the decoys by ripping at them with their talons, tearing their heads off and smashing their beaks.

Everyone, including the children who painted the decoys, hopes that the gannets have returned permanently, and that their numbers will rise every year.

Source: Edel Wignell, Saving Wildlife, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990, pp. 6–7

parts.stem: Where is Cat Island? It is an island:
options: off the east coast of Australia
parts.hint: Find where the passage puts Cat Island. It names a piece of water near another island.

steps.explain: Find the sentence.
steps.work: “…six gannets on Cat Island, an islet east of Flinders Island in Bass Strait.”

steps.explain: Use what you know: Bass Strait is the sea between Tasmania and the south coast of Victoria.
steps.work: So Cat Island, which is in Bass Strait, is between Tasmania and Victoria.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Torres Strait is in the far north of Australia. South Australia is on the other side of Victoria. The island is not off the east coast.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: The passage gives a clue: the name of the strait.

questions.stem:
Questions 5 to 9 refer to the following passage.

AUTUMN LEAVES

The changing colours of the leaves is an indication of the coming of autumn. Trees have a built-in process that brings about the autumn landscape of red, yellow, orange and brown colours. The process starts with changes in the length of the day and temperature.

Leaves usually appear to be green because they do not absorb green light. They absorb red and blue and this is involved in photosynthesis. The green appearance comes from chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the tree’s ‘food’; it is a pigment that transfers energy from the light to chemicals.

Once the autumn begins, the trees are sensitive to changes in the air temperature and the amount of daylight. This brings about a response to use the resources stored in chlorophyll. The chlorophyll is then broken down causing the green appearance of the leaves to disappear.

When the chlorophyll is removed other molecules appear. These appear as the yellow and orange colours of the leaves in autumn. These molecules always exist in leaves but they do not appear until the chlorophyll is removed from the leaves.

Source: Julie Novak, Daily Illini, 30 October 1998, ‘Colourful, falling leaves mark beginning of fall’

parts.stem: What is the main topic of this passage?
parts.hint: The main topic covers the whole passage. What is the passage explaining from beginning to end?

steps.explain: Say what each paragraph is about.
steps.work:
Paragraph 1: the leaves change colour in autumn.

Paragraph 2: why leaves look green (chlorophyll).

Paragraph 3: chlorophyll breaks down when autumn begins.

Paragraph 4: other colours then appear.

steps.explain: Find the idea that covers all four.
steps.work: All four paragraphs explain why the leaves change colour.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: B and C are only the setting. D — photosynthesis is mentioned but it is only one detail.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: The main topic must cover all four paragraphs.

parts.stem:
In which order does the process of changing colours occur?

II. When chlorophyll disappears then the orange colours present in the leaf appear.
III. Chlorophyll makes a leaf appear green.
parts.hint: Start with how a leaf looks before autumn. Then ask what changes, and last, what you can see after that.

steps.explain: Which step happens first? Before autumn the leaves are green.
steps.work: III: Chlorophyll makes a leaf appear green comes first.

steps.explain: What changes next? Autumn begins, the temperature and daylight change and the chlorophyll breaks down.
steps.work: I: temperature changes and the chlorophyll disappears comes second.

steps.explain: What happens last? Once the chlorophyll has gone, the other colours that were always there can be seen.
steps.work: II: the orange colours appear comes last.

steps.work: MOSCOW is a city (the capital of Russia). MONTREAL is a city in Canada. That leaves MALTA and MOROCCO, which are both countries.

questions.stem:
Questions 20 to 24 refer to the following poem.

This is a different kind of poem. Many of the real words have been changed. Read it carefully then answer the questions. The small numbers at the beginning of each verse stand for the line number in the poem.

GESTIMI

¹Dolo nem crakeing
Tizling at crafays
Krinkling their zoulo
And donpering the laves.

⁵Loung lirgs tafling
To the lavige tore
Wingsing their kasbets
Along the marbour nore.

⁹Inon the toumain
The stonamry is twair
Lony the sourists
Now moc and ter.

¹³Ikan varet kurch leb
Keho down the bane
Larkinem to lechap
Cum their queet ferain.

¹⁷Daslin of my tarenps
Mar lu may be joor
Lastecorizo, Gestimi
Sirt wen nath I daror.

parts.stem: Who is ‘krinkling their zoulo’ and ‘donpering the laves’ (lines 3 and 4)?
parts.hint: Read lines 1 to 4 as one sentence. The first words of the sentence tell you who does the actions.

steps.explain: Read lines 1 to 4 together.
steps.work: Dolo nem crakeing / Tizling at crafays / Krinkling their zoulo / And donpering the laves.

steps.explain: In the first line the sentence names who does the action: “Dolo nem”. The last two lines are what “Dolo nem” does.
steps.work: Dolo nem are the ones who are “krinkling their zoulo” and “donpering the laves”.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Read the lines as a sentence: who comes first in the sentence?

parts.stem: What is described as ‘twair’ (line 10)?
parts.hint: Find line 10 in the poem and see which word comes just before “is twair”.

steps.explain: Find line 10.
steps.work: The third verse starts at line 9. Line 9: “Inon the toumain”. Line 10: “The stonamry is twair”.

steps.explain: Which word is described as twair?
steps.work: The word before “is” is “stonamry”.

steps.explain: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Find line 10 and look at the words before “is”.

parts.stem: What would you say is true about this poem?
options: it is written in a foreign language
it is an example of how to write verse
it uses some nonsense words and rhymes
parts.hint: The poem uses words that are not real words, but it still has a rhythm and lines that sound alike at the end. What does that tell you?

steps.explain: Look at the words.
steps.work: The passage says that many of the real words have been changed, so there are words like “zoulo” and “laves” that do not exist.

steps.explain: Look at the sounds at the end of lines.
steps.work: Lines end in sounds like “zoulo” / “laves” and “tore” / “nore”: some lines rhyme, so it is a rhyming poem.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: It is not a foreign language or a code (the question says many of the real words have been changed), and it is not an example of how to write verse.

steps.explain: The poem uses some nonsense words and rhymes.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Pick the statement that is supported by what you can see in the poem.

questions.stem:
Read this short passage.

When Darin tries to protect Tiger from his own feline curiosity some surprising things happen. Tiger will need all nine lives to survive.

Source: Elizabeth Best, That Proverbial Cat, Sydney, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1990

Which word best gives the meaning of FELINE?
questions.hint: The passage is about Tiger, a cat. It also says Tiger will need “all nine lives”. What word describes things that belong to cats?

steps.explain: Read the sentence with the word in it.
steps.work: “…protect Tiger from his own feline curiosity…” and “Tiger will need all nine lives to survive.”

steps.explain: Who is Tiger?
steps.work: Tiger is a cat (the story is about a cat with “nine lives”), so feline curiosity is the curiosity of a cat.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: peculiar means odd. cunning means clever at tricking. animal is too general: it does not say what kind.

steps.explain: Feline means cat-like.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Look for clues about what kind of animal Tiger is.

questions.stem:
If these words are put into the right order they will make a sentence. What is the sixth word of this sentence?

A AT FARMER FIELDS HARVEST HAVE HIS IS LAZY NOTHING PLOUGH RIGHT THE TIME TO TO TOO WHO WILL
questions.hint: Look for groups: “A farmer who is …”, “to plough his fields at the right time” and “will have nothing to harvest”.

steps.explain: Find the groups that go together.
steps.work:
“A farmer who is” starts the sentence.

“too lazy to plough his fields” says what is wrong.

“at the right time” says when.

“will have nothing to harvest” says what will happen.

steps.explain: Join the groups in order.
steps.work: A farmer who is too lazy to plough his fields at the right time will have nothing to harvest.

Which number comes next in the series?

2  3  5  8  13  21  ?
questions.hint: Work out how much is added each time: 1, 2, 3, 5, … Do these gaps look like the numbers in the series itself?

questions.stem: It cost \(\$44\) for one adult and one child to visit an amusement park and \(\$58\) for one adult and two children. How much is the cost for one adult to visit the amusement park?
questions.hint: Compare the two prices. What is different about the two groups of people, and how much more does the second group cost?

steps.explain: Write the two facts so they can be compared. Both groups have one adult; the second group has one more child.
steps.work:
1 adult + 1 child \(=\$44\)

1 adult + 2 children \(=\$58\)

questions.stem: You have 71 square tiles for an area. Make these into the largest possible square area using as many of the tiles as you can. How many tiles would you have left over?
questions.hint: A square area uses a square number of tiles: 1, 4, 9, 16, … Find the biggest square number that is not more than 71.

steps.explain: A square made of tiles has the same number of tiles along each side, so it uses a square number of tiles. List the square numbers near 71.
81 is more than 71, so 9 by 9 is too big. The largest square we can make is 8 tiles by 8 tiles.
steps.work: \(8\times8=64\) tiles

questions.stem: Sixty-four stamps cost \(\$28.80\). Which calculation do you use to work out the cost of one stamp?
questions.hint: To find the cost of ONE item when you know the total cost, share the total equally between all the items. Which operation shares equally?

steps.explain: First find the total price and the number of stamps. We need the price of one stamp.
steps.work:
Known: total cost \(=\$28.80\) for 64 stamps.

Wanted: the cost of 1 stamp.

steps.explain: To share the total equally, divide the total price by 64.
steps.work: Price of 1 stamp: \(\$28.80\div64\)

steps.explain: Check the choices. We need total money divided by number of stamps, not the reverse.
steps.work:
A: \(45\text{c}\times64\) gives the total if one stamp costs 45c.

C: \(64\div\$28.80\) puts the number of stamps on top, so it does not find dollars per stamp.

D: \(64\times\$28.80\) would mean each stamp costs \(\$28.80\).

steps.explain: Now divide and match the result to the choices.

keyPoints.note: You want the price of ONE: divide the total cost by the number of items.

questions.stem: Each shelf can hold up to five packets. How many shelves will I need to store nineteen packets?
questions.hint: Share the packets out five at a time. How many full shelves can you make, and what happens to the packets that are left over?

steps.explain: Each shelf holds at most 5 packets, so divide the 19 packets into groups of 5.
steps.work:
\(19\div5=3\) remainder \(4\)

3 full shelves hold \(3\times5=15\) packets. 4 packets are left over.

steps.explain: The 4 left-over packets still have to be stored, so they need one more shelf.

questions.stem: My father married when he was 31 years old. My mother was born in 1925. They were married in 1947. How do you calculate the difference in their ages?
questions.hint: First work out the year the father was born. Then find the difference between the two birth years.

steps.explain: Find the year the father was born. He was 31 when they married in 1947.

steps.explain: The mother was born in 1925. Put both birth years on the line.

steps.explain: The difference in their ages is the later birth year take away the earlier birth year.
Check the other options.
Only option C is a correct calculation that gives 9 years.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: married when he was 31 years old
keyPoints.note: Take 31 away from the year of the wedding to find the father’s birth year.
A difference is found by subtracting the smaller birth year from the larger one.

questions.stem:

| Food | \(\$42\,553\) |
| Transportation | \(\$35\,461\) |
| Child care/education | \(\$21\,276\) |
| Clothing | \(\$16\,548\) |
| Health care | \(\$16\,548\) |

questions.stem:
What is the largest number that you can make from these seven digits?

1  1  3  5  8  2  9
questions.hint: The biggest digit in the first place makes the biggest number. Compare the four options place by place, from the left.

steps.explain: All choices have seven digits. Compare the digits from left to right; the first place that differs decides which number is larger.
The first two digits are 5 and 1 in every choice. Compare the third digit next.
steps.work:
A: 5119382; B: 5191832; C: 5118239; D: 5192813.

A and C have 1 in the third place. B and D have 9, so A and C are smaller.

steps.explain: B and D both start 519. Compare their fourth digits.
steps.work:
B has 1 in the fourth place; D has 2.

Since \(2>1\), D is larger than B.

steps.explain: D is the largest number among the four choices.
steps.work: \(5\,192\,813\) is the largest option, so the answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Compare the numbers from the left: the first place where they differ decides which is bigger.

questions.stem: At an exhibition there were 432 men, 368 women and 59 children. Then 68 men, 32 women and 9 children left. How do we calculate how many remained?
questions.hint: People who left must be taken away, not added. Work out the total at the start, the total who left, and then subtract.

steps.explain: Find the total number of people at the start.
Find the total number who left.
The people who remained are the ones at the start take away the ones who left.
Check the options: the calculation must use subtraction between the two totals, and the result must be 750.
steps.work:
A gives \(850\) and C gives \(650\) — wrong results.

D adds the people who left, which is wrong.

B: \((432+368+59)-(68+32+9)=750\) ✓

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: People who left are taken away from the number at the start.
Remained means how many are still there, so subtract.

questions.stem: These weights are placed on a plank. How much does the block marked X weigh?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 462 242" width="60%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t1-q26.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="462" height="242"/></svg>

questions.hint: Look at which end of the plank is lower. The heavier block pushes its end of the plank down.

steps.explain: Look at the plank. One end is lower than the other.
steps.work: The end with block X is lower. The end with the 12 kg block is higher.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 148" width="65%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><polygon points="150,100 128,138 172,138" fill="#334155" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1" stroke-linejoin="round" /><g transform="rotate(9 150 100)"><rect x="20" y="94" width="260" height="8" rx="0" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="25" y="48" width="70" height="46" rx="0" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="60" y="78" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >X</text><rect x="205" y="48" width="70" height="46" rx="0" fill="#fff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="240" y="78" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >12 kg</text></g></svg>

steps.explain: On a balance, the heavier side goes down and the lighter side goes up.
steps.work: X is on the side that has gone down, so X is heavier than the 12 kg block.

steps.explain: Check the options.
steps.work: If X weighed exactly 12 kg, the plank would be level (B). If X weighed less than 12 kg or about 10 kg, the 12 kg block would be on the side that goes down (C, D).

steps.explain: X weighs more than 12 kg.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: How much does the block marked X weigh
keyPoints.note: You are not given a number: use the tilt of the plank to compare the weights.

questions.stem:
Look at this clock. It is afternoon.

How many hours has it been since midnight?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 198 180" width="30%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t1-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="198" height="180"/></svg>

questions.hint: First read the time on the clock. Then count the hours from midnight to midday, and from midday to that time.

steps.explain: Read the time. The short (hour) hand points to 5 and the long (minute) hand points to 12.
steps.work: The time is 5 o’clock.

steps.explain: It is afternoon, so it is 5 pm. Count the hours since midnight in two parts.
steps.work:
Midnight to midday: \(12\) hours

Midday to 5 pm: \(5\) hours

steps.explain: Add the two parts.
Check: 5 hours would be the time since midday, and 15 or 16 hours would be 3 pm or 4 pm.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: In the afternoon, add 12 hours to the clock time to count the hours since midnight.
Midnight is 12:00 at night. Count from there.

questions.stem:

Which calculation below shows how to share the money equally?

questions.hint: First find how much money there is altogether. Then think: how do you share an amount equally between 5 children — multiply or divide?

steps.explain: Add up all the notes to find the total amount of money.

steps.explain: Sharing equally between 5 children means dividing the total by 5.
steps.work: \(185\div5=37\), so each child gets \(\$37\).

steps.explain: Write the calculation. The brackets are needed so that all the notes are added before dividing.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \((185)\times5=925\) — multiplying makes the amount bigger, it does not share it.

B: with no brackets only the last note \(5\) is divided by \(5\) (division is done first): \(100+50+20+10+1=181\).

D: \((100+50+20+10+5)\times5\) multiplies instead of dividing.

steps.explain: Only option C shows the total shared equally between five children.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Sharing equally means dividing.
Divide by 5, after finding the total of all the notes.

Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or while travelling.
Most people had their first cup of coffee at their home or at a coffee shop.

questions.stem: Every day from Monday to Friday, Anthony works from 7.30 am until 4.30 pm (including breaks for morning and afternoon tea plus lunch). How many hours is he at work altogether, including breaks?
questions.hint: First find how many hours Anthony is at work in ONE day. Then work out how many days he works.

steps.explain: Find the length of one working day: from 7.30 am to 4.30 pm.
steps.work:
7.30 am to 12.30 pm is \(5\) hours.

12.30 pm to 4.30 pm is \(4\) hours.

\(5+4=9\) hours each day

steps.explain: Count the days: Monday to Friday is 5 days.
steps.work: \(9\) hours \(\times\) \(5\) days

questions.stem: Which calculation shows you how to find the number of hundreds in 39 000?
questions.hint: To find how many hundreds fit into a number, ask: how many groups of 100 can you make from it? Which operation finds the number of groups?

steps.explain: “How many hundreds in 39 000?” means how many groups of 100 make up 39 000. Finding the number of groups is division.
Work it out and check with multiplication.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(39\,000\times100=3\,900\,000\) — far too big.

C: one-tenth of \(39\,000\) is \(3\,900\), and \(3\,900\times100=390\,000\) — too big.

D: \(100\div39\,000\) is a tiny number, much less than 1.

steps.explain: There are 390 hundreds in 39 000, found by dividing by 100.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This is a “how many groups” question. Groups are found by dividing.

questions.stem: In which general direction would you travel if you went directly from Sydney to Singapore?
questions.hint: Picture a map with north at the top. Is Singapore above or below Sydney, and is it to the left or to the right?

steps.explain: Picture a map of the world. Sydney is in the south of the world (southern hemisphere). Singapore is close to the equator.
steps.work: Singapore is NORTH of Sydney. (It is closer to the equator, so it is higher up the map.)

questions.stem: There are 53 pupils who have to be divided into groups. The teacher first tries to divide them into 8 equal groups but there are some pupils left over. How many pupils would be left after the 8 groups?
questions.hint: Divide 53 by 8. How many pupils go into each group, and how many are left over? Use your 8 times table.

steps.explain: Find the biggest number that 8 groups can be made of, without going over 53 pupils. Use the 8 times table.
steps.work: \(8\times6=48\)   \(8\times7=56\) — too many.

steps.explain: So each group has 6 pupils, and 48 pupils are in groups.
The pupils left over are the ones not in a group.
Check: 48 + 5 = 53 ✓. The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Make as many equal groups as you can, and count the ones that do not fit.
The pupils left over are the remainder.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in the series?

questions.stem: Angela paid \(\$378\) in advance for her school fees and \(\$24\) for books. The school reduced the school fees to \(\$262.00\). How much will the school now refund to Angela?
questions.hint: A refund is money given back. Compare what Angela paid for school fees with what the school fees now cost. Does the cost of books matter?

steps.explain: Find the facts about the school fees only. The books were paid for separately and their price did not change.
steps.work:
Paid for fees: \(\$378\)

Fees now: \(\$262\)

(The \(\$24\) for books is not part of the refund.)

questions.stem: In the city, Anthony travelled 107 km on half a tank of petrol. How far could he travel on a full tank? Show the correct calculation.
questions.hint: A full tank is how many times more than half a tank? Which operation gives that many times as far?

steps.explain: Compare a full tank with half a tank.
steps.work: A full tank is TWICE half a tank (two halves make a whole).

steps.explain: He travels 107 km on each half tank, so double it.
Check each option by working it out.
Only option B is a correct calculation.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A full tank is two half tanks.
Work out each option: only the correct one really equals 214.

questions.stem: The date today is the 6th February 1999. Angelena was born on the 5th April 1955. How old would she be today?
questions.hint: Count whole years from her birth date to her last birthday. Then count the months from that birthday to today. Has her birthday in 1999 happened yet?

steps.explain: Her birthday is 5 April. February comes before that birthday, so she is still 43 in 1999.
steps.work:
Last birthday: 5 April 1998.

\(1998-1955=43\) years.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 122" width="95%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="20" y1="70" x2="340" y2="70" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2.4" /><line x1="24" y1="62" x2="24" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="210" y1="62" x2="210" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="300" y1="62" x2="300" y2="78" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="24" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="start" >5 Apr 1955</text><text x="24" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="start" >born</text><text x="212" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5 Apr 1998</text><text x="212" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >43rd birthday... 43 years</text><text x="332" y="96" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="end" >6 Feb 1999</text><text x="332" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="end" >today</text><path d="M24 60 Q117 10 212 60" fill="none" stroke="#4338ca" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="118" y="30" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >43 years</text></svg>

steps.explain: Count from 5 April 1998 to 5 February 1999, one month at a time.
steps.work:
5 Apr → 5 May (1) → 5 Jun (2) → 5 Jul (3) → 5 Aug (4) → 5 Sep (5) → 5 Oct (6) → 5 Nov (7) → 5 Dec (8) → 5 Jan (9) → 5 Feb (10).

On 6 February, one extra day has passed.

steps.work: 43 years and 10 months (plus 1 day) = about 43 years 10 months.

steps.work: The answer is D: 43 years 10 months.

questions.stem: I had a meal with Terry and his wife at a Mexican restaurant. The cost came to \(\$51.00\) and I added a tip of ten per cent (10%), making it \(\$56.10\). Which is the correct calculation for the answer of \(\$56.10\)?
questions.hint: The tip is worked out on the cost of the meal. Find 10% of the meal, then add it to the meal cost.

steps.explain: Find 10% of the cost of the meal. 10% is the same as one-tenth, so divide by 10.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$56.10 altogether</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="309.09090909090907" height="34" rx="4" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="164.54545454545453" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >meal $51.00</text><rect x="319.09090909090907" y="30" width="30.909090909090903" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="334.5454545454545" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >tip $5.10</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add the tip to the cost of the meal.
So the calculation is the meal cost plus 10% of the meal cost.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(10\%\) of \(56.10\) is the tip on the total, which is not how the tip was found.

C and D use \(51.45\), which is not an amount in the question.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: A 10% tip is worked out from the cost of the meal, then added to it.

questions.stem: How far (in sea miles) would a steamship like the Mauretania travelling at a speed of 27 knots cover in three hours?
questions.hint: A speed of 27 knots means 27 sea miles every hour. Work out the distance for 3 hours.

steps.explain: A knot is one sea mile per hour, so 27 knots means the ship travels 27 sea miles in each hour.
steps.work: After each hour the ship has gone another \(27\) sea miles.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 112" width="65%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#6366f1"/></marker></defs><rect x="8" y="46" width="44" height="44" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="30.0" y="74.0" font-size="18" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >27</text><rect x="78" y="46" width="44" height="44" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="100.0" y="74.0" font-size="18" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >54</text><rect x="148" y="46" width="44" height="44" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="170.0" y="74.0" font-size="18" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >81</text><path d="M30.0 44 Q65.0 8 100.0 44" fill="none" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="65.0" y="22" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >+27</text><path d="M100.0 44 Q135.0 8 170.0 44" fill="none" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="135.0" y="22" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >+27</text><text x="100.0" y="108" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >after 1, 2 and 3 hours</text></svg>

steps.explain: Multiply the distance in one hour by the number of hours.
steps.work: distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time \(=27\times3\)

steps.explain: Calculate.
steps.work: \(27\times3=20\times3+7\times3=60+21=81\) sea miles

steps.explain: Check the other options: 54 is two hours, and 71 and 91 are not multiples of 27.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: A speed in knots is the number of sea miles travelled in one hour.
Multiply the distance travelled in one hour by 3.

questions.stem: Homer was a famous epic poet. He lived around 700 BC. How would you calculate the number of years from 700 BC to the year 2000?
questions.hint: BC years count backwards towards the year 0. Draw a time line with 700 BC on the left, year 0 in the middle and 2000 on the right.

steps.explain: Draw a time line. 700 BC is before the year 0, so it is 700 years to the left of 0. The year 2000 is 2000 years to the right of 0.
steps.work: The year 0 splits the time line into two parts.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 128" width="95%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="20" y1="78" x2="340" y2="78" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2.4" /><line x1="20" y1="70" x2="20" y2="86" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="20" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >700 BC</text><text x="20" y="120" font-size="11" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Homer</text><line x1="102.96296296296296" y1="70" x2="102.96296296296296" y2="86" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="102.96296296296296" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >year 0</text><line x1="340" y1="70" x2="340" y2="86" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3" /><text x="340" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >2000</text><path d="M20 66 Q61.48148148148148 24 102.96296296296296 66" fill="none" stroke="#4338ca" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="61.48148148148148" y="28" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >700 years</text><path d="M102.96296296296296 66 Q221.48148148148147 8 340 66" fill="none" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="221.48148148148147" y="22" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >2000 years</text></svg>

steps.explain: Find the length of each part.
steps.work:
700 BC to year 0: \(700\) years

year 0 to 2000: \(2000\) years

steps.explain: Add the two parts together.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(2000+(2000-700)=3300\) — adds the wrong amounts.

B: \(700+(2000-700)=2000\) — does not count from 700 BC.

D: \(2000-700=1300\) would be the answer if both years were AD (after the year 0), but 700 BC is before the year 0.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: BC means before the year 0, so the years are on the other side of 0 from 2000.
Add the years before year 0 to the years after year 0.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

These are the chances of winning that have been quoted for different types of gambling. These figures show the chances of winning the first prize.

| Gambling | Chances |
|---|---|
| Jackpot \(\$2\) | 1 in 180 000 |
| Jackpot \(\$5\) | 1 in 140 000 |
| Lotto Strike | 1 in 3.2 million |
| Lucky 7 | 1 in 200 000 |
| Oz Lotto | 1 in 8 million |
| Pools | 1 in 3.8 million |
| Powerball | 1 in 25 million |
| Scratchie \(\$2\) | 1 in 480 000 |

parts.stem: Assume that the figures in the table are correct. Which form of gambling listed in the table has the worst chance of winning?
parts.hint: “1 in 25 million” means you have to be very lucky: only one ticket in 25 million wins. The bigger the number after “1 in”, the worse the chance. Which number is biggest?

steps.explain: Each chance is written as “1 in …”. The more tickets there are for each winner, the harder it is to win.
steps.work: “1 in 140 000” is much easier than “1 in 25 million”.

steps.explain: Change the “million” numbers to ordinary numbers so that they are easy to compare.
Put the chances in order from the best chance (smallest number) to the worst chance (biggest number).
steps.work: The biggest number is 1 in 25 million: Powerball.

questions.stem:
Which number comes next in this series?

128  64  32  ?
questions.hint: The numbers are getting smaller. Is the same amount taken away each time, or is something else happening?

steps.explain: Compare neighbouring numbers.
steps.work: \(128\to64\) is half. \(64\to32\) is half. (The amounts taken away, 64 and 32, are not the same.)

questions.stem:
Look at the desks which are numbered from A to Y in the chart below.

The pupil in seat V moves three desks forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat W moves three desks to the left then one desk forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat X moves three desks forward and changes places.
The pupil in seat Y moves two seats forward and three across and changes places.

Which pupil is now in seat I?

“Forward” means towards the top row of the chart.

questions.stem: One of the longest tennis games ever played at Wimbledon was in 1969. It took around 5¼ hours. R. Gonzales (USA) beat C. Pasarell (USA), losing 22 to 24 in the first set; then losing 1 to 6 in the second set; winning 16 to 14 in the third set; winning 6 to 3 in the fourth set; and winning 11 to 9 in the fifth set. How do you calculate the number of games played by Gonzales?
questions.hint: In each set, Gonzales’s score is written first (“losing 22 to 24” means he scored 22 games and Pasarell 24). Add up Gonzales’s number in each of the five sets.

steps.explain: Read Gonzales’s score first in each set. Write down only those five scores.
Add Gonzales’s five scores.
Check what each other total counts.
steps.work:
A adds both players: \(56+56=112\).

C uses Gonzales’s scores but says 58, not 56.

D adds Pasarell’s scores, not Gonzales’s.

steps.explain: The total of Gonzales’s scores is 56.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: number of games played by Gonzales
keyPoints.note: Use only Gonzales’s number in each set, then add them all.

questions.stem: These are the sides of a box. They are folded so that the side with the star is at the top. Which side will now be at the bottom of the box?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 583 600" width="70%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t4-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="583" height="600"/></svg>

questions.hint: In a flat net, a row of four squares wraps around the box. In that row, the square two places away from the star is on the opposite side of the box.

steps.explain: The four squares in a row wrap around the sides of the box. The two extra squares become the top and bottom.
steps.work: Faces that are opposite each other in the box are the ones that end up on opposite sides.

steps.explain: In a row of four side faces, faces two places apart become opposite. The star is third in the row.
steps.work:
Star (3rd) is opposite pencil (1st).

Phone (2nd) is opposite envelope (4th).

Hand and scissors are opposite each other.

questions.stem: USA coins usually come in 1 cents, 5 cents, 10 cents, and 25 cents. I have to pay the salesperson \(\$1.07\). What is the least number of coins that I can give him/her?
questions.hint: To use the fewest coins, start with the biggest coin (25 cents) as many times as you can. Then use the next biggest coin for what is left.

steps.explain: Change the money to cents so that it is easy to work with.
Use as many 25-cent coins as you can without going over 107 cents.
steps.work:
\(4\times25=100\), and \(5\times25=125\) is too much.

So use four 25c coins. \(107-100=7\) cents are still to pay.

questions.stem: John works at the M & C Deli. He earns \(\$5.48\) an hour. He works three hours on Monday and three hours on Wednesday. How much does he earn each week?
questions.hint: First find the total number of hours John works in a week. Then multiply by the amount he earns in one hour. Check that the answer to each calculation is really right.

steps.explain: Find the total hours he works in a week.
steps.work: 3 hours on Monday + 3 hours on Wednesday \(=3\times2=6\) hours

steps.explain: He earns \(\$5.48\) for each hour, so multiply by the hours.
Write the calculation in the same form as the options.
Check the other options by working them out.
steps.work:
A: \(5.48\times3\times2=32.88\), not \(34.88\) — the calculation is right but the answer is wrong.

B: \(16.44\times3=49.32\), not \(32.88\).

D: \(5.48\times6=32.88\), not \(34.88\).

steps.explain: Only option C has a correct calculation and a correct answer.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: three hours on Monday and three hours on Wednesday
keyPoints.note: Add up the hours first: that is 3 × 2.
Multiply the total hours by the pay for one hour.

questions.stem:
At the university, the rate for mileage allowance is around 53 cents per kilometre. This is the kilometre reading at the beginning of a trip.

6 3 5 0 4

And this is the reading at the end of a trip.

6 3 5 3 4

How much mileage allowance should be paid?
questions.hint: First find how many kilometres were travelled: subtract the start reading from the end reading. Then multiply by 53 cents.

steps.explain: Find the distance travelled: end reading take away start reading.
steps.work: \(63\,534-63\,504=30\) km. Only the tens digit changed (0 to 3), so the trip was 30 km.

questions.stem:
Which is the correct way to solve this problem?

\(3\times8+6\div2=\;?\)
options: multiply 3 by 8 then add this answer to 6 and divide it all by 2
divide 6 by 2 then multiply 3 by 8; then add the two answers
multiply 3 by 14 (8 + 6) then divide the answer by 2
divide 14 (8 + 6) by 2 then multiply that answer by 3
questions.hint: Remember the rule for the order of operations: do multiplication and division first, then addition and subtraction. Which parts of the sum are multiplication or division?

steps.explain: Find the operations in the sum.
steps.work: \(3\times8\) is a multiplication, \(6\div2\) is a division, and the \(+\) in the middle is an addition.

steps.explain: Multiplication and division are done first (in either order). Addition is done last.
Now do the addition with the two answers.
Check the other options.
steps.work:
A: \(24+6=30\), then \(30\div2=15\) — it adds before dividing.

C: \(3\times14=42\), \(42\div2=21\) — adds \(8+6\) first.

D: \(14\div2=7\), \(7\times3=21\) — adds \(8+6\) first.

steps.explain: Only option B follows the order of operations (and gives 27).
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: correct way to solve this problem
keyPoints.note: Multiplication and division come before addition.

questions.stem: An area of 243 hectares has to be divided into nine equal lots. How many hectares would there be for each of the lots?
questions.hint: Dividing into equal lots means dividing by 9. How many times does 9 fit into 243? Try your 9 times table.

steps.explain: Dividing 243 hectares into 9 equal lots means dividing by 9.
Work it out in steps. How many 9s are in 24? Then in the rest?
steps.work:
\(9\times2=18\), and \(24-18=6\), then bring down the 3 to make \(63\).

\(9\times7=63\), so \(243\div9=27\).

steps.explain: Check by multiplying back.
Check the other options: 26 × 9 = 234, 30 × 9 = 270 and 33 × 9 = 297. Only 27 gives 243.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Dividing into equal lots means dividing by the number of lots.

questions.stem: Nicholas has \(\$1.90\), John has \(\$1.20\) and Angela has 80 cents. How much should we take from Nicholas and give to John and Angela, so that everyone will have the same amount?
questions.hint: First find how much money there is altogether. Then work out how much each person should have so they all have the same.

steps.explain: Add up all the money.

steps.explain: Share it equally between the three people.

steps.work: \(\$1.90-\$1.30=\$0.60\), so Nicholas gives away \(60\) cents.

questions.stem: Jim owed David Jones \(\$288.85\) last month. He paid David Jones \(\$113.95\) and spent another \(\$79.95\) this month. How do you calculate how much he owes David Jones now?
questions.hint: Think about whether each amount makes the debt bigger or smaller. Paying money back reduces what he owes. Spending more at the shop increases it.

steps.explain: Start with what Jim owed at the beginning.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 72" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M10 24 L10 18 L350 18 L350 24" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="180.0" y="13" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >at the start</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="340.0" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#4f46e5" stroke-width="1.6" /><text x="180.0" y="52.0" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >owed $288.85</text></svg>

steps.explain: He PAID David Jones \(\$113.95\). Paying back means he owes LESS, so take it away.
He SPENT another \(\$79.95\) at the shop. Spending more means he owes MORE, so add it.

steps.work:
He now owes \(\$254.85\).

A takes both amounts away (\(\$95.05\)), B adds both (\(\$482.75\)), and D starts with the small amounts, so each is wrong.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Paying money back makes the amount owed smaller: subtract.
Spending more makes the amount owed bigger: add.

questions.stem:
This chart shows the typical costs for a textbook of around 250 pages. The book sells for \(\$40.00\). Half of the \(\$40.00\) goes to the bookseller.

BOOK PROFITS FOR A TYPICAL 250 PAGE BOOK

| Cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Printing and bookbinding | \(\$3.20\) |
| Warehouse and distribution | \(\$3.20\) |
| Bookseller | \(\$20.00\) |
| Rent, salaries | \(\$3.20\) |
| Advertisements | \(\$2.40\) |
| Author’s payment | \(\$4.00\) |
| Publisher’s profit | \(\$4.00\) |
| TOTAL | \(\$40.00\) |

Source: Adapted from Anne R. Carey & Jerry Mosemak, USA Today, October 1998

parts.stem: How much profit does the publisher make on each book sold?
options: around one-tenth of the book’s price
around one-quarter of the book’s price
around one-fifth of the book’s price
around one-sixth of the book’s price
parts.hint: Find the publisher’s profit in the table. Then compare it with the price of the book as a fraction.

steps.explain: Find the publisher’s profit and the price of the book.
steps.work: Publisher’s profit \(=\$4.00\) Book price \(=\$40.00\)

parts.stem: How much does each book cost the publisher to produce (do not include the payment to the author)?
parts.hint: The cost of producing the book is the printing, the warehouse, the rent and salaries and the advertisements. Which items in the table are NOT part of the cost to the publisher?

steps.explain: Decide which items count as the cost to produce the book.
steps.work:
Printing and bookbinding, warehouse and distribution, rent and salaries, and advertisements are the publisher’s costs.

The bookseller’s share, the author’s payment and the publisher’s profit are NOT costs of producing it.

questions.stem: This week John worked on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday from 4 pm until 7 pm at a delicatessen. How many hours did he work this week?
questions.hint: First find how long John works each day. Then find how many days he works.

steps.explain: Find the hours in one working day: from 4 pm to 7 pm.
Find how many days he works: Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.
Multiply the hours each day by the days.
steps.work: \(3\text{ hours}\times3\text{ days}=9\text{ hours}\)

questions.stem: Each day I drink a 375 ml can of soft drink in the summer. Which calculation shows how many LITRES I drink over 12 weeks?
questions.hint: Work in steps: how many days are in 12 weeks, then how many millilitres in total, then change millilitres into litres.

steps.explain: Find the number of days in 12 weeks.
steps.work: 1 week \(=7\) days, so 12 weeks \(=12\times7=84\) days.

steps.explain: Find the total number of millilitres. One can a day for 84 days.
steps.work: \(375\text{ ml}\times84\) days

steps.explain: Change millilitres into litres. There are 1000 ml in 1 litre, so divide by 1000.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A multiplies by \(1000\) and divides by \(84\) (the wrong way round). C uses 12 (weeks) instead of 84 (days). D does not use the 375 ml correctly.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: how many LITRES I drink over 12 weeks
keyPoints.note: Weeks must be changed into days, and millilitres into litres.

questions.stem: How many square tiles, that are 10 cm long, can you fit into a space that is 200 cm by 200 cm?
questions.hint: First find how many tiles fit along one side of the space. Then think about how many rows of tiles you need.

questions.stem: An object falls to the ground at around 9 metres per second. How long would it take to fall from a plane that was 9 000 metres in the air?
questions.hint: First find how many seconds it takes. Then change seconds into minutes by dividing by 60.

steps.explain: The object falls 9 metres every second. Find how many seconds it takes to fall 9 000 metres.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 144" width="80%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="30" y1="20" x2="30" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="30" y="14" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >plane</text><text x="30" y="136" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >ground</text><line x1="26" y1="40" x2="34" y2="40" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="60" x2="34" y2="60" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="80" x2="34" y2="80" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="100" x2="34" y2="100" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="120" x2="34" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="150" y="40" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 m to fall</text><text x="150" y="62" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9 m every second</text><text x="150" y="86" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 ÷ 9 = 1 000 seconds</text><text x="150" y="108" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >1 000 ÷ 60 = 16 r 40 → between</text><text x="150" y="124" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >16 and 17 minutes</text></svg>

steps.explain: Change seconds into minutes. There are 60 seconds in one minute.
16 full minutes use up 960 seconds, and there are 40 more seconds.
steps.work:
\(16\times60=960\)   \(1\,000-960=40\)

So the time is 16 minutes and 40 seconds, which is between 16 and 17 minutes.

steps.explain: Check the other options: 26–27 minutes would be 1 560–1 620 seconds, and 9–10 and 6–7 minutes are far too short.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This tells you how far it falls in one second.
The answer is in minutes, but you will first get seconds.

questions.stem: One can of tomato paste takes up one-tenth of a row in a supermarket shelf. How many cans of tomato paste would be needed to stock (or fill up) three rows on that supermarket shelf?
questions.hint: If one can takes up one-tenth of a row, how many cans fill one whole row? Then find three rows.

keyPoints.note: If one can is one-tenth of a row, find how many cans make a whole row.
Multiply the cans in one row by 3.

questions.stem: Angelena uses a 375 gram packet of fettuccine and one-third of another 375 gram packet. How do you calculate how much fettuccine she used for the meal?
questions.hint: She uses one whole packet. Then she uses a third of ANOTHER packet. How big is that other packet?

steps.explain: She uses one whole packet.
She uses one-third of another packet, and that packet is also 375 g.

steps.explain: Add the two amounts.
steps.work: \(375+125=500\) g, so the calculation is \(375+(\frac13\text{ of }375)=500\).

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A takes a third of \(750\) (two packets), which is \(250\). B takes a third of \(500\), which is not one of the packets. D multiplies instead of adding.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The other packet is also 375 g. Find a third of 375.

questions.stem:
Here are the wage rates for an apprentice that works in shopfitting and kitchen detail joinery. Two sets of wages are shown. Some apprentices are indentured, that is they have a type of permanent contract. The other apprentices are trainees. There are different rates of pay for indentured and trainee apprentices. The pay also changes from first year to the fourth year.

APPRENTICE JOINER

| Year | Indentured | Trainee |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(\$172.60\) | \(\$193.00\) |
| 2 | \(\$234.00\) | \(\$259.50\) |
| 3 | \(\$306.20\) | \(\$336.10\) |
| 4 | \(\$371.90\) | \(\$392.30\) |

Look at the chart of these wage rates.
