questions.stem:
Look at this sum. Each letter stands for a number. Which number stands for the letter M?

MU × 4 = CU8

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 176 148" width="28%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q17.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="176" height="148"/></svg>

questions.hint: Look at the units digit first: U × 4 ends in 8. Which digit U gives a product ending in 8?

steps.explain: Start with the ones column. The product must end in 8, so U can be 2 or 7.
steps.work: \(2\times4=8\), and \(7\times4=28\); both end in 8.

steps.explain: Test U = 7 first, then U = 2. Carry the tens digit into the next column.
steps.work:
If \(U=7\), the tens digit of \(7\times4\) is 2, so the product cannot have 7 in its tens place.

If \(U=2\), then \(M2\times4\) must end in 28. For the listed choices, test M.

steps.explain: Among the choices, M = 3 works: 32 multiplied by 4 gives 128.
steps.work: \(32\times4=128\), which matches \(CU8\): \(C=1, U=2\). So the listed answer is \(M=3\), choice D.

steps.explain: Check the other listed choices by multiplying their two-digit numbers by 4.
steps.work:
\(12\times4=48\), \(22\times4=88\), and \(52\times4=208\); none matches the pattern with the same U in both places.

Among the listed choices, the answer is D (\(M=3\)). Note: \(82\times4=328\) also fits the written pattern, so the question has another solution if 8 is allowed, even though 8 is not offered as a choice.

keyPoints.text: Each letter stands for a number
keyPoints.note: The same letter is always the same digit. Start with the ones column.

questions.stem: Although we can never know all the prime numbers, what do you think we might be able to say about the sum of two prime numbers? (Hint: a prime number is a number that can only be divided evenly by itself and/or one.)
options: the sum is always an even number
the sum is an even number for all prime numbers except two
the sum is an odd number for all prime numbers except two
the sum is always an odd number
questions.hint: Write down a few prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 … Which of them is even? Try adding some pairs and see whether the sums are odd or even.

steps.explain: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The only even prime is 2; all other primes are odd.

questions.hint: Compare the three circles. What is happening to the thickness of the outline and to the size of the circle?

steps.explain: Look at the thickness of the black outline in I, II and III.

steps.work: The circles get smaller each time: I is the biggest and III is the smallest.

steps.explain: So the next circle (IV) is smaller still and its line is thicker still: almost all black, with only a small white dot in the middle.
steps.work: A small black circle is what comes next.

steps.explain: Find the option that is small and almost completely black.
steps.work: A is a small black circle. B is large. C and D have thin lines. The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Two things change at once: the thickness of the outline and the size of the circle.

questions.stem:
A tiler wants to make a pattern of grey and white triangle tiles. They would look something like this:

How many grey triangles could fit into this space? Start each row with a grey triangle.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 596 281" width="95%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q26.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="596" height="281"/></svg>

questions.hint: Count how many triangles are in one row and how many of them are grey when the colours take turns, starting with grey. Do this for one row, then use all the rows.

steps.explain: Look at the space. It has 3 rows of triangles, and in each row the triangles point up, down, up, down … so the colours take turns: grey, white, grey, white …
steps.work: Every row begins with a grey triangle, as the question says.

steps.explain: Count the triangles in one row. There are 9 triangles that point up and 8 that point down between them, which makes 17 triangles in a row.
steps.work: \(9+8=17\) triangles in each row

steps.explain: Grey is every second triangle, starting with the first one, so the grey triangles are the 1st, 3rd, 5th … 17th.
steps.work: \(1,3,5,\dots,17\) is \(9\) grey triangles in one row

steps.explain: There are 3 rows, and every row starts with grey, so each row has the same number of grey triangles.
steps.work: \(9\times3=27\) grey triangles

steps.explain: Check the other options: 30 would be 10 grey in each row, 25 is not a multiple of 3 and 36 would be 12 in each row.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Start each row with a grey triangle
keyPoints.note: The colours take turns, so find how many triangles are in each row.
Count the grey triangles in one row, then multiply by the number of rows.

questions.stem: Anthony works at the AMI Factory as a second year apprentice. He earns around \(\$7\) an hour. He works \(8\frac12\) hours each day from Monday to Thursday plus 4 hours on Friday. Which calculation shows correctly how much he earns each week?
questions.hint: First find how many hours he works in the week. Then multiply by the pay for one hour. Check that the hours really add to the number used in the calculation.

steps.explain: Find the hours from Monday to Thursday.
steps.work: \(4\text{ days}\times8\frac12\text{ hours}=4\times8.5=34\) hours

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 344 88" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="58" height="48" rx="8" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="37" y="26" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Mon</text><text x="37" y="46" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >8.5 h</text><rect x="74" y="8" width="58" height="48" rx="8" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="103" y="26" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Tue</text><text x="103" y="46" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >8.5 h</text><rect x="140" y="8" width="58" height="48" rx="8" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="169" y="26" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Wed</text><text x="169" y="46" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >8.5 h</text><rect x="206" y="8" width="58" height="48" rx="8" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="235" y="26" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Thu</text><text x="235" y="46" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >8.5 h</text><rect x="272" y="8" width="58" height="48" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="301" y="26" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >Fri</text><text x="301" y="46" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4 h</text><text x="170" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >4 × 8½ = 34 hours, plus 4 hours = 38 hours</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add the 4 hours on Friday.
steps.work: \(34+4=38\) hours in the week

steps.explain: Multiply the hours by the pay for one hour.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A multiplies the hours together, which is wrong (and \(7\times4\times8.5\times4\) is not \(258\)). B works out to \(\$238+\$28=\$266\), not \(\$264\), so its answer is wrong. D uses \(37\) hours, but he works \(38\).

steps.explain: Only option C has the right number of hours and the right total.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: \(8\frac12\) hours each day from Monday to Thursday
keyPoints.note: That is 4 days at 8½ hours. Find the total, then add Friday.
Check the hours and the final amount of each option.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

The Plimsoll line is a safety line that is painted on both sides of a ship. A ship may be safely loaded until this line is reached. The circle with the line through it stands for the original Plimsoll Mark. The top line is the deck line. The other symbols (TF, F, TS, S, W, WNA and LR) also have special meanings.

The figures show the amount of water the ship is drawing. This is the amount of water needed for the ship to float. The Plimsoll line is named after Samuel Plimsoll (1824–1898) who was responsible for its introduction.

Look at the chart showing some Plimsoll marks.

questions.stem:
Here are some facts:

• A company made 1000 toys.
• They cost \(\$12\) each.
• The company sold them to stores for \(\$16\) each.

How many would the company need to sell in order to cover the cost of the 1000 toys that were made?
questions.hint: First find the total cost of making all 1000 toys. Then find how many toys have to be sold at \(\$16\) to earn that much money.

steps.explain: Find the total cost of making the toys.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 110" width="90%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="340" height="30" rx="4" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#e11d48" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="178" y="28" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >cost to make 1 000 toys: 1 000 × $12 = $12 000</text><rect x="8" y="46" width="340" height="30" rx="4" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="178" y="66" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$16 each → toys needed to earn back $12 000</text><text x="178" y="100" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >12 000 ÷ 16 = 750 toys</text></svg>

steps.explain: Each toy is sold for \(\$16\). Find how many sales are needed to earn \(\$12\,000\).
Check by multiplying: 750 toys at \(\$16\) each.
Check the other options: 250 toys earn only \(\$4\,000\), 500 toys earn \(\$8\,000\) and 1000 toys earn \(\$16\,000\) (more than the cost).
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.text: cover the cost of the 1000 toys
keyPoints.note: Find the total cost first, then how many toys must be sold to get that much money back.

questions.stem: The US dollar is worth about one and two-thirds what an Australian dollar is worth. If I have to pay 75 US dollars, then how would I calculate this in Australian dollars?
questions.hint: One US dollar is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars, so each of the 75 US dollars is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars. Find 1⅔ of 75.

steps.explain: Each US dollar is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars.
steps.work: 1 US dollar \(=1\frac23\) Australian dollars

steps.explain: So 75 US dollars are worth 75 lots of 1⅔ Australian dollars.
steps.work: \(1\frac23\text{ of }75\)

steps.explain: Work it out: 1 of 75 is 75, and ⅔ of 75 is 50.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A takes \(1\frac23\) of \(125\), which is \(208\frac13\), not \(75\). C and D are not the right way to turn US dollars into Australian dollars.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

steps.work: Piece IV has one slanted side. Piece V has two. Piece VI is a square. Pieces I, II and III do not fit the slanted outline.

steps.explain: Turn pieces IV, V and VI to fit the outline. The slanted sides make the outside edges; VI fills the centre.
steps.work: The pieces fit together without gaps.

steps.explain: The three pieces are IV, V and VI.
steps.work: The answer is A.

steps.work: \(4\times3=12\) cubes, \(\times1\) deep \(=12\) cubes

steps.explain: Count the cubes in the small shape. The front has 3 cubes: two at the bottom and one on top at the left. The top shows that it is 1 cube deep.

questions.stem: A children’s book has a total of 28 printed pages plus the front and back covers are also printed. There are illustrations on 22 pages and on the two outside covers (but not the inside covers). On how many pages (including the covers) are there no illustrations?
questions.hint: Count everything that is printed: the 28 pages and the covers. Then find how many of them have pictures. Remember each cover has an outside and an inside.

steps.explain: Find the total number of printed surfaces. There are 28 pages, and each cover has an outside and an inside, so four more surfaces.
steps.work: \(28+2+2=32\) pages in all (28 pages, 2 outside covers and 2 inside covers)

steps.explain: Count the pages that have illustrations: 22 pages and the 2 outside covers.
Subtract the pages with illustrations from all the pages.

steps.explain: Check by counting the pages without pictures directly: 6 of the 28 pages (28 − 22 = 6) plus the 2 inside covers.
steps.work: \(6+2=8\) ✓ The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Each cover has an outside and an inside. The inside covers have no illustrations.

keyPoints.note: Count all the surfaces, then take away the ones with illustrations.

questions.stem:
Which signs (+, −, ×, ÷) can take the place of the symbols ✧, □ and ○ in the sum below? (Each symbol stands for only one sign.)

\(19\;✧\;4\;□\;3\;○\;1=4\;□\;2\)
questions.hint: The right side is 4 □ 2. Think which sign makes a sensible number there. Then try each option on the left side and see which one gives the same answer.

steps.explain: The same sign □ is used on both sides. Work out the right side for each option, then the left side.
steps.work: In every option except A the sign □ is ×, so the right side is \(4\times2=8\). (In A, □ is +, giving \(4+2=6\).)

steps.explain: Work out the left side with the signs in option C: ✧ is −, □ is × and ○ is +.
steps.work:
\(19-4\times3+1\). Do the multiplication first: \(4\times3=12\).

\(19-12+1=7+1=8\)

steps.explain: Compare the two sides.
steps.work: Left side \(=8\) and right side \(4\times2=8\). They are equal ✓

steps.explain: Check the other options.
Only option C makes both sides equal.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: Each symbol stands for only one sign
keyPoints.note: The same symbol stands for the same sign everywhere, including the □ on the right side.

questions.hint: Each box has marks in the top row and marks in the bottom row. Count the straight lines and the slanted lines in each row. Do the numbers follow a pattern?

steps.explain: Count each kind of mark separately in boxes 1, 2 and 3. Keep the top and bottom rows separate.
steps.work:
The bundle of 3 lines stays the same in every top row.

Box 1: top has 2 slanted marks; bottom has 2 slanted and 3 straight.

Box 2: top has 1 straight and 3 slanted; bottom has 3 slanted and 4 straight.

Box 3: top has 2 straight and 4 slanted; bottom has 4 slanted and 5 straight.

steps.explain: Compare each count with the same count in the next box. Each group grows by 1.
steps.work:
Top slanted: \(2,3,4\).

Top straight: \(0,1,2\).

Bottom slanted: \(2,3,4\).

Bottom straight: \(3,4,5\).

steps.explain: Add 1 to each group to get box 4.
steps.work:
Top: 3 straight and 5 slanted marks.

Bottom: 5 slanted and 6 straight marks.

steps.explain: Find the option with those four counts and the bundle of 3 lines.
steps.work: D matches all four groups. The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Count each kind of line separately in every box and find how each count changes.

Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

A national survey involving 503 children aged 8 to 13 has found that 44 per cent of girls and 31 per cent of boys expressed concern about their weight, and two-thirds felt they needed more exercise.

It found that children spent more time watching TV or playing computer games than playing sport, although team sport was their favourite activity. On average they watched television for 80 minutes per day; spent 20 minutes playing computer games and on other computer uses, including the Internet; spent 48 minutes playing organised and social sports; and 29 minutes doing homework.

questions.stem:
Six is considered a perfect number. This is because when you add up all the numbers (except 6) that divide into it properly then they add up to six. For instance 1, 2, and 3 all divide properly into six (1 × 2 × 3 = 6; or 2 × 3 = 6).

The next perfect number is 28. What are the numbers (proper divisors) that make 28 a perfect number? (Hint: Do not include 28.)
questions.hint: Find every number that divides exactly into 28 (except 28 itself). Then check that they add up to 28.

steps.explain: Find the numbers that divide into 28 without a remainder. Test the numbers from 1 upwards.
The numbers that divide 28 exactly are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14 (not counting 28).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 84" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="10" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="38" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >1</text><rect x="76" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="104" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >2</text><rect x="142" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="170" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4</text><rect x="208" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="236" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >7</text><rect x="274" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="302" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >14</text><text x="180" y="72" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add them to check that 28 is perfect.
Check the other options: A leaves out 2, B leaves out 1 and C has 5 and 6, which do not divide 28.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: A divisor divides into the number with nothing left over.

questions.stem:
In a binary number system you only count with zero (0) and one (1). There are no other numbers. Here are our ordinary decimal numbers and the binary number for each one of them.

What would be the binary number for nine (9)?
questions.hint: Each binary digit stands for 8, 4, 2 or 1 (from left to right). Which of these places do you need to add up to 9?

steps.explain: Look at how the table works. Each column of the binary number stands for a number: from the left 8, 4, 2 and 1.
steps.work: A 1 means “use this number”, a 0 means “do not use it”.

questions.stem: In this square the numbers (from 4 to 12) add up to 24 across and down. Find the missing number in the square marked with the asterisk (★). (Hint: you may have to find some of the other numbers before you can find the number you want.)

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 256 197" width="41%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q18.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="256" height="197"/></svg>

questions.hint: Every row and column adds up to 24. Find a row or column with only one missing number first.

steps.explain: Check the first row. It already has all three numbers.
Check the left column.
The numbers 4 through 12 are each used once. Cross out the five numbers already shown.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 148 148" width="45%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9</text><rect x="52" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5</text><rect x="96" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >10</text><rect x="8" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >11</text><rect x="52" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="96" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="8" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4</text><rect x="52" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="96" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#e11d48" text-anchor="middle" >?</text></svg>

steps.explain: The middle row needs two numbers that add to 13, because its total must be 24.
steps.work:
\(24-11=13\), and \(6+7=13\). So the middle and right entries are 6 and 7, in some order.

If the middle entry were 6, the middle column would need \(24-5-6=13\) at the bottom. But 13 is not left to use. So the middle entry is 7 and the right entry is 6.

steps.explain: Now finish the middle column, then the bottom row.

steps.explain: Check the right column to make sure the square works.
steps.work: \(10+6+8=24\). ✓ The missing number is 8, so the answer is B.

steps.explain: Look at the two arrows in the top line of each picture, from picture to picture.
steps.work: The arrows in the first line of each shape turn clockwise (the same way as the hands of a clock).

steps.explain: Look at the two arrows in the bottom line of each picture, from picture to picture.
steps.work: The arrows in the second line turn counter-clockwise (the other way round).

steps.work: Top line: one more clockwise turn. Bottom line: one more counter-clockwise turn.

steps.explain: Find the option that matches.
steps.work: A has the top arrows and the bottom arrows in the positions given by these two turning rules. ✓ The answer is A.

questions.stem: What triangular shape would you form if you travelled directly from Sydney to Adelaide then from Adelaide directly to Melbourne and then back to Sydney?
options: a triangle with three sides of different length
a triangle with three sides of equal length
a triangle with a right angle
a triangle with two sides of equal length
questions.hint: Picture the three cities on a map of south-east Australia. Compare the three straight-line distances: are any two the same?

steps.explain: The three straight lines are Sydney to Adelaide, Adelaide to Melbourne and Melbourne to Sydney.
steps.work: Look at them on a map: they are three different journeys.

steps.explain: Compare their lengths. Sydney to Adelaide is the longest. Melbourne is close to both Adelaide and Sydney, but the two distances to Melbourne are not the same as each other.
steps.work: The three sides are all different in length.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Equal sides would need two cities to be the same distance from a third. The angles are not square, so there is no right angle.

steps.explain: The triangle has three sides of different length.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Picture the three cities on a map and compare the three straight lines.

questions.stem:
Look at this clock. It is evening in Sydney. The time in Sydney is about 15 hours ahead of the time in the United States.

What would the time be in the United States?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 180 168" width="29%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="180" height="168"/></svg>

questions.hint: First read the time on the clock. It is evening, so it is pm. Then go back 15 hours.

steps.explain: Read the clock. The hour hand is near 5 and the minute hand is on 12, so the time is 5 o’clock. It is evening, so it is 5 pm.
steps.work: 5 pm in Sydney

steps.explain: The United States is 15 hours BEHIND Sydney, so take 15 hours away. Go back to midnight first: from 5 pm back to 12 midnight at the start of the day.
steps.work: 5 pm is \(17\) hours after midnight, so \(17-15=2\) hours after midnight.

steps.explain: 2 hours after midnight is 2 am, on the same day (Sydney’s date).
steps.work: 5 pm − 15 hours = 2 am, the same day.

steps.explain: Check the other options: the next day would be going forward, and 1 am or 3 am would be 16 or 14 hours earlier.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Sydney is ahead, so the United States is earlier: take away 15 hours.

These scientific terms or names are arranged in a special series. Which term comes next in the series?

Acid  Electron  Joule  Pressure  ?

steps.work: Acid → A, Electron → E, Joule → J, Pressure → P.

questions.stem:
Scientists suggest decreasing phone time is beneficial to all children and that parents should restrict screen time.

Which one of the statements, if true, best supports the Scientists' claim?
options: Decreasing phone time allows children to participate in more activities
Decreasing phone time will allow parent's phones to have more battery
Phones should only be used to play Fortnite
questions.hint: Find the option that gives children a direct benefit from spending less time on phones. A reason unrelated to children’s wellbeing does not support the claim.

steps.explain: The scientists say children benefit when they spend less time on phones. A good answer should tell us one way the children benefit.
steps.work: Claim: less phone time $\longrightarrow$ a benefit for children.

steps.explain: Choice A mentions sport but does not say less phone time leads to more sport. Choice C helps parents’ phones, not children. Choice D does not explain why less screen time helps.
steps.work: A: no stated link to reduced phone time.\quad C: benefit is to parents’ phones.\quad D: does not support the stated benefit.

steps.explain: Choice B gives a clear link: less phone time leaves children with more time for other activities.
steps.work: Less phone time $\longrightarrow$ more time for activities $\longrightarrow$ benefit to children.

steps.explain: So choice B gives the best reason for the scientists’ advice.
steps.work: Correct choice: B — Decreasing phone time allows children to participate in more activities.

keyPoints.note: Look for a consequence caused by less phone use.
The support should explain a benefit to children, not to someone else.

questions.stem:
Ella, Bella and Nella all keep games. Ella owns FIFA, Battlefield and Rocket League. Bella owns Rocket League, FIFA and Roblox. Nella owns Minecraft, Call of Duty and FIFA.

Which games does Ella or Bella own that Nella does not?
questions.hint: Compare the games owned by Ella or Bella with Nella’s list. Remove any game Nella also owns, even if both groups own it.

steps.explain: Write down the games Ella and Bella have. Do not write a game twice: FIFA, Battlefield, Rocket League and Roblox.
steps.work:
List Ella/Bella: FIFA, Battlefield, Rocket League, Roblox.
Nella: Minecraft, Call of Duty, FIFA.

steps.explain: Now compare this list with Nella’s list. FIFA is on both lists, so remove it. Minecraft and Call of Duty belong only to Nella.
The games left from Ella and Bella are Battlefield, Rocket League and Roblox.
That list is choice C.

Next year in sports class, I need to choose 4 sports to learn.
I have to choose one sport from each of the following lists.

LIST 1
Soccer
Basketball
Cricket
Dancing

LIST 2
Badminton
OZ-Tag
Quidditch
Rowing

LIST 3
Swimming
Touch Football
Soccer
Badminton

LIST 4
Cricket
Rugby
Table Tennis
Quidditch

I know that I want to choose Soccer, Cricket and Basketball.
Which one of the following can I NOT choose as my final sport?
questions.hint: The three chosen sports can come from Lists 1, 3 and 4. Your fourth sport must come from the list that still has no chosen sport.

steps.explain: Basketball is in List 1, so it uses the List 1 choice. Soccer is in List 3. Cricket can be chosen from List 4.
Each list needs one sport. Lists 1, 3 and 4 are now used, so the fourth sport must come from List 2.
Look at List 2: it has Badminton, OZ-Tag, Quidditch and Rowing. Dancing is not there.
You cannot choose Dancing as the last sport. The answer is C.

questions.stem:
To become a worthy dragon warrior, you need to have excellent agility as well as discipline.

Sam: “Sally is extremely quick and has amazing reflexes. The only problem is that she is sometimes unable to follow rules and is stubborn. Regardless, she will become the dragon warrior.”

Sally: “Sam was brought up to have good disciplinary skills, however, has slow agility. He will become the dragon warrior.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The requirement uses “as well as”: a dragon warrior needs both excellent agility and discipline. Check whether each person meets both requirements.

steps.explain: To become a dragon warrior, a person needs both excellent agility and discipline. “Both” means one good quality is not enough by itself.
Sally is quick and has good reflexes, so she has agility. But the story says she does not follow rules well, so she does not have the discipline she needs.
Sam has good discipline, but the story says he is slow. So he does not have the agility he needs.
Neither person has both required qualities. The answer is D.

questions.stem:
Katy, Taylor and Meghan are standing in a horizontal line.

If Taylor is to the left of Meghan, and Meghan is to the right of Katy, which one of the following must be true?
options: Meghan is on the furthest right
Katy is in the middle of the other two
Katy is to the furthest right
Taylor is in the middle of the other two
questions.hint: Translate “to the left of” and “to the right of” into an order from left to right.

steps.explain: Taylor is to the left of Meghan. So Meghan is to the right of Taylor.
Meghan is also to the right of Katy. That means both Katy and Taylor are somewhere to Meghan’s left.
We do not know whether Katy or Taylor is farther left, but Meghan is farther right than both of them.
Meghan must be at the far right. The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Katy, Taylor and Meghan are standin

questions.stem:
Jimmy and Kendell are in a classroom.

Jimmy: “Sally asked me to get her phone for her but I can’t seem to find it here. It’s a black coloured iPhone.”

Kendell: “Ooh look I see a black iPhone there. That must be Sally’s phone.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Kendell has made?
options: There are many black iPhones, so it might not be Sally’s
Sally must be the one who should come get her phone and not make Jimmy do it
Kendell purposely pointed at the wrong phone because she does not like Sally
Kendell isn’t too sure what an iPhone looks like.
questions.hint: Ask whether the description “black iPhone” identifies one unique phone or could fit several phones.

steps.explain: Sally’s phone is described as a black iPhone. We are not told about a special case, sticker, or other mark.
Kendell sees a black iPhone. It matches the description, but there could be other black iPhones in the classroom too.
Choices B, C and D add ideas that the story never tells us. The problem is that Kendell treats a matching description as proof that it is Sally’s phone.
Choice A explains the mistake: there may be many black iPhones.

keyPoints.text: Jimmy and Kendell are in a classroo
keyPoints.note: Read this condition literally and use it in the reasoning.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Sports specialists say that: “All Soccer players must wear shin pads/shin guards”.

Which one of the statements, if true, best supports the sports specialists’ claim?
options: Shin pads are uncomfortable to wear
Shin pads decrease the risk of leg injuries
Soccer players need to make sure they only kick the ball
Goalkeepers don’t need to wear shin pads/shin guards
questions.hint: Look for a reason that explains why shin guards are useful for soccer players.

steps.explain: The sports specialists want every soccer player to wear shin guards. Look for a choice that explains how shin guards help players.
Choice B says shin guards lower the chance of leg injuries. That gives a safety reason for wearing them.
Choice A says they are uncomfortable, which is not a reason to wear them. Choice C is about kicking. Choice D disagrees with the rule that all players need them.
Choice B best supports the rule.

keyPoints.note: Read this condition literally and use it in the reasoning.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
As Sachin was learning to play cricket, his coach told him: “To even have the slightest chance to play for an international team, you must know how to hold the bat properly.”

If Sachin’s coach is correct, which one of these statements will be true?
options: Everyone who knows how to hold a bat will be an international player
You must also know how to hold a ball to be an international player
All international players know how to hold a bat
Swinging the bat is also encouraged to be known
questions.hint: Look for what the coach says a player must know. Do not turn that rule around.

steps.explain: Read the coach’s sentence carefully. The coach says that a player needs to know the right way to hold the bat before they can have a chance to play internationally.
steps.work: International player → knows how to hold the bat properly.

questions.stem:
Alan owns a playlist with all of Justin Bieber’s songs.

Alan: “If you tell me the name of a song, I will tell you when Justin Bieber sang it.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Alan has made?
options: There can be more than one song with the same name
questions.hint: Ask whether one song name could belong to two different songs.

steps.explain: Alan says he will tell the singing time when someone gives him a song name. Ask: could the same name belong to two different songs?
steps.work: Check whether one song name always points to just one song.

questions.stem:
At the basketball competition, whoever makes the top 5 will be allowed to move into the next round. Additionally, whoever can prove that their trampoline was faulty, can proceed to the next round.

Louise: “A maximum of 6 people can make it to the next round”

What mistake has Louise made in her statement?
options: More than one person can prove that their trampoline was faulty
We are not told how many people will be in the competition
Everyone in the top 5 could have had faulty trampolines
Some people may not want to participate next round
questions.hint: Count the top-five places, then check whether the faulty-trampoline rule sets a limit.

steps.explain: The first rule lets the top five competitors move on. That gives five places through the competition result.
steps.work: Top-five places: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → no more than 5 people from this rule.

questions.stem:
Adam, Billy, Charlie and Donna play in a sports team. The coach said that “If Adam does not play tomorrow, then Billy will start on and play. If Adam plays, then Charlie will replace Donna and play.”

steps.explain: The coach gives two rules. If Adam does not play, Billy must play. But we are told Billy will not play.

questions.stem:
Kate has 20 coins which add to make $5. She only has 10c, 20c and 50c coins. She has more 50c coins than 10c coins.

steps.explain: If all 20 coins were 10 cents, they would make 200 cents. Kate has 500 cents, so the other coins must add 300 cents more.

Each 20-cent coin adds 10 cents extra. Each 50-cent coin adds 40 cents extra. Fewer than 3 fifty-cent coins cannot add enough; 8 or more add too much. So check 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 fifty-cent coins in the table.
steps.work:
Extra value above twenty 10-cent coins: $300\text{ cents}$.

steps.explain: Only 4 fifty-cent coins works: it leaves 14 twenty-cent coins and 2 ten-cent coins. Check: 4 + 14 + 2 = 20 coins, and 4 is more than 2.
steps.work: Start with 20 × 10¢ = 200¢. Need 500¢ − 200¢ = 300¢ extra. A 20¢ coin adds 10¢; a 50¢ coin adds 40¢. Try 4 × 50¢: 4 × 40¢ = 160¢ extra. Remaining extra: 300¢ − 160¢ = 140¢, so 14 coins are 20¢. Then 20 − 4 − 14 = 2 ten-cent coins. Check: 4 > 2.

questions.hint: Every face on a cube has 4 adjacent (neighbouring) faces and 1 opposite face. Check Views 2 and 3 to identify all 4 faces adjacent to X.

questions.stem:
Merrylands is north of Fairfield and northeast of Guildford. Fairfield is north of Parramatta and west of Granville. Harris Park is east of Granville.

What suburb is northwest of Parramatta?
questions.hint: Set Parramatta as the reference point. Place Fairfield directly north of it, then use “north of Fairfield” and “northeast of Guildford” to locate the remaining suburbs.

steps.explain: Put Parramatta at the origin. “Fairfield is north of Parramatta” places Fairfield directly above it.
steps.work: Parramatta → north → Fairfield.

questions.stem:
Gabriel thinks that helmets should be free when people buy bikes so that people are more likely to wear helmets and stay safe.

Which one of the following statements, if true, best supports Gabriel's idea?
options: Providing helmets would be very expensive for shops selling bikes
Helmets are uncomfortable and it is wasteful to give helmets to everyone
Some people will still not wear helmets
This would mean there are less head injuries that occur
questions.hint: Choose the statement that directly links free helmets to Gabriel’s safety goal, rather than one that weakens or is unrelated to it.

steps.explain: find the claim: giving a helmet with a bike should increase helmet use and help people stay safe.
steps.work: Claim → more helmet use → greater safety.

steps.explain: Check each option against that chain. Cost and discomfort oppose the proposal; “some may still not wear one” weakens it.
steps.work: A and B weaken; C challenges effectiveness.

steps.explain: Fewer head injuries is direct clue of greater safety, so it most strongly supports the idea.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Choose the statement that directly links free helmets to Gabriel’s safety goal, rather than one that weakens or is unrelated to it
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Whenever Royce’s sister does not get her laundry done on the weekend, she gets angry. And when she gets angry, she steals Royce’s lollies.

Royce: “My lollies are missing, this must mean that my sister did not get her laundry done on the weekend”.

Royce’s mother: “Just because your lollies are missing does not mean she took them”.

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Write the stated chain in the forward direction: laundry not done → angry → steals lollies. Missing lollies do not prove the chain happened.

steps.explain: The given information says that not doing laundry leads to anger, and anger leads to stealing lollies.
steps.work: Not done → angry → steals.

steps.explain: Royce reasons backwards from missing lollies to laundry not done. The facts do not say that only his sister can take the lollies, or that laundry is the only reason she gets angry.
steps.work: A result does not prove its possible cause.

steps.explain: His mother correctly notes that another explanation could account for missing lollies.
steps.work: Answer: B, Royce’s mother only.

keyPoints.text: Write the stated chain in the forward direction: laundry not done → angry → steals lollies
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Andrew’s jigsaw puzzle is not finished.

Which piece will complete the puzzle?
questions.hint: Compare the four sides of the empty space: each tab must meet a notch, and each straight edge must continue the outside silhouette. Rotate the options before deciding.

steps.explain: Look at the empty space. Its top and right sides have bumps to join. Its bottom and left sides have dips to fit over bumps. These four edge shapes tell us what the missing piece must have.
steps.work: Required piece features: Top tab, Right tab, Bottom hole, Left hole (2 tabs, 2 holes).

steps.explain: Compare the edges of each choice with the empty space. A, B and C have at least one edge that does not fit. D has bumps and dips in the matching places.
steps.work: Check each marked edge or clue.

steps.explain: Put D in the gap: all four edges join. So D completes the puzzle.
steps.work: Piece D matches all four interlocking edges. Correct answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Compare the four sides of the empty space: each tab must meet a notch, and each straight edge must continue the outside silhouette
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Three gold balls are lined up in the middle of the field. They are either red or pink. Adam hits the red ball and it rolls to the ball in the middle which moves the last ball which is pink.

On the basis of this information, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: There is only one pink ball
There is only one red ball
A pink ball hit a red ball
A red ball hit a pink ball
questions.hint: Follow the collisions in order: the first ball is red, it hits the middle ball, and the middle ball hits the last ball, which is pink.

steps.explain: Label the balls from first to last. The first is red; the third (last) is pink.
steps.work: Ball 1 = red; Ball 3 = pink.

steps.explain: Ball 2 can be red or pink. Check both cases to see what must happen.
steps.work: Case 1: Ball 2 is pink. Case 2: Ball 2 is red.

steps.explain: If Ball 2 is pink, the red first ball hits it. If Ball 2 is red, that red middle ball hits the pink last ball. Either way, a red ball hits a pink ball. Answer D.
steps.work: Either way: red ball hits pink ball. Answer D.

keyPoints.text: Follow the collisions in order: the first ball is red, it hits the middle ball, and the middle ball hits the last ball, which is pink
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Sammy believes that schools should invest in art as a subject at school rather than a fun activity children do in their spare time.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Sammy’s idea?
options: This will encourage creative students to pursue their passions
Art is a fun activity to reward students for concentrating
Not all students will like art or be good at the subject
Some children will be discouraged by doing badly in the subject
questions.hint: Look for a benefit that follows from teaching art as a school subject. A statement that calls art only a reward or lists a disadvantage does not support the claim.

steps.explain: Sammy wants art to be taught as a subject, so a relevant supporting reason should describe a learning or development benefit from formal study.
steps.work: Claim: teach art as a subject.

steps.explain: Option A gives a direct benefit: creative students can develop their interests and abilities. B treats art only as a reward; C and D argue against the proposal.
steps.work: A supports; B–D do not.

steps.explain: so the strongest support is option A.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: Look for a benefit that follows from teaching art as a school subject
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Michael is taller than Amy. Rodney is shorter than Debbie but taller than Michael.

Who is the tallest?
questions.hint: Translate each comparison into an inequality, then connect them into one height order.

steps.explain: “Michael is taller than Amy” gives Michael > Amy.
steps.work: M > A.

steps.explain: “Rodney is taller than Michael” gives Rodney > Michael, and “Rodney is shorter than Debbie” gives Debbie > Rodney.
steps.work: D > R > M > A.

steps.explain: Debbie is above everyone else in the chain, so she is tallest.
steps.work: Answer: Debbie (D).

keyPoints.text: Translate each comparison into an inequality, then connect them into one height order
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Only people that have bought the unlimited rides tickets are allowed on all the rides at the Easter show. If they don’t, they can’t get on the Swoopy rollercoaster without paying $5.

Molly: “Jessie was allowed on the Swoopy rollercoaster but not the Big Drop chair so she must have the unlimited rides ticket”.

Kimmy: “No, she must have paid the $5 dollar admissions ticket because she could not get on all the other rides”.

If the information in the box above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: An unlimited ticket gives access to all rides. Being allowed on one ride does not prove that someone has the unlimited ticket.

steps.explain: Unlimited ticket → allowed on every ride. Without it, the Swoopy ride requires an extra $5 payment.
steps.work: Unlimited → all rides; no unlimited → $5 for Swoopy.

steps.explain: Jessie could not ride the Big Drop, so she did not have a ticket that allows all rides. This disproves Molly’s answer.
steps.work: Not all rides → not unlimited.

steps.explain: Jessie could have paid $5 for Swoopy without buying the unlimited ticket, which fits the information. Kimmy’s reasoning is correct.
steps.work: Answer: B, Kimmy only.

keyPoints.text: An unlimited ticket gives access to all rides
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem: Which of the shapes can be added to the shape below to complete a rectangle?
questions.hint: Trace the outline of the given shape and ask: what piece fills the remaining space inside the rectangle?

steps.explain: The gap has two rounded bumps and one narrow straight slot. The missing piece needs matching dips and a narrow bump to fit them.
steps.work: The complementary piece needs: two arch-shaped notches going downward at its base (to match the two humps) plus a narrow rectangular slot on the right (to slot around the chimney).

questions.stem: Alex, Alyssa and Kenny are sitting in the front row of the concert. If Alex is to the right of Alyssa and Kenny is to the left of Alex, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: Alyssa is furthest to the right
Kenny is the furthest to the left
Alex is furthest to the right
questions.hint: Place Alex relative to each person. Both conditions put Alex to the right of someone; test whether either person can still be between the other two.

steps.explain: “Alex is to the right of Alyssa” means Alyssa must be somewhere to Alex’s left.
steps.work: Alyssa < Alex.

steps.explain: “Kenny is to the left of Alex” also places Kenny somewhere to Alex’s left. The two left-side people may switch order.
steps.work: Possible orders: Alyssa–Kenny–Alex or Kenny–Alyssa–Alex.

steps.explain: In both possible orders, Alex is at the far right.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Place Alex relative to each person
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Mike: “The owner of the store told me that Matcha the German Shepherd is grey with white patches under his chin”.

Kelly: “Oh I saw a grey German Shepherd in the cage near the door! That must be Matcha the dog”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Kelly made?
options: There are no German Shepherds in the store
Even though the German Shepherd is grey it may not have white patches
There may be more than one person looking for Matcha
Mike may be looking for someone else’s dog
questions.hint: Kelly used only the colour and breed. Check which identifying feature from the description she failed to verify.

steps.explain: Matcha is described by three details: German Shepherd, grey, and white patches under the chin.
steps.work: Required details: breed + grey coat + white chin patches.

steps.explain: Kelly saw a grey German Shepherd, but she does not mention checking the white patches. Another grey German Shepherd could be there.
steps.work: The observed details are not enough to find Matcha uniquely.

steps.explain: Option B states the missing detail and so identifies Kelly’s mistake.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: Kelly used only the colour and breed
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
A teacher says: “Students should make sure to sit in the seats they are given and answer when their names are called in class”.

Which one of the following statements, if true, best supports the teacher’s rule?
options: This means the teacher will know who is missing and can act quickly
Students like to sit next to their friends and may learn better together
Students may not hear the teacher call their name
This means the teacher can count the students more easier
questions.hint: Choose the reason that explains why the teacher needs students to use assigned seats and respond when called.

steps.explain: The rule is about identifying which students are present.
steps.work: Teacher calls names + assigned seats → attendance check.

steps.explain: Option A explains a practical benefit: the teacher can find an absent student quickly. The other choices are irrelevant or weaken the rule.
steps.work: A links directly to the purpose.

steps.explain: so the best support is option A.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: Choose the reason that explains why the teacher needs students to use assigned seats and respond when called
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
This graph shows how the rainfall and temperature vary throughout the year in Sydney. Temperature is shown as a line graph and rainfall is shown as a column graph.

Which statement is true about the weather in Sydney?
options: As the temperature decreases, the rainfall increases.
As the temperature increases, the rainfall increases.
This graph shows no relationship between rainfall and temperature.
The rainfall is mostly lower than the temperature.
questions.hint: Follow the temperature line through the cooler months and compare the rainfall columns over the same months. Read the two scales separately.

steps.explain: Use the legend: bars show rainfall on the left scale; the line shows temperature on the right scale. From about May to July, the line moves down.
steps.work: Temperature falls from autumn into winter.

questions.stem:
When Kristy was trying out for the Debate team, the teacher told her “To have a chance at making the team, you must come to the team meetings every week at least twice”.

If Kristy’s teacher is right, which one of the following statements will be true?
options: Everyone that turns up to the meetings will make the team
None of the students that didn’t turn up to meetings will make the team
Some of the students that only turned up sometimes will make the team
Only students that were on the team last year will make the team this year
questions.hint: The statement gives a necessary condition: to have a chance, a student must attend at least twice each week. It does not say attendance guarantees selection.

steps.explain: Let C = “has a chance to make the team” and M = “attends at least twice weekly”. The teacher says C requires M.
steps.work: C → M.

steps.explain: Read the rule this way: if a student does not meet M, then they do not have a chance (and so cannot make the team).
steps.work: Not M → not C.

steps.explain: Option B says this clearly. Option A wrongly treats attendance as a promise that the student will make the team.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: The statement gives a necessary condition: to have a chance, a student must attend at least twice each week
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Melanie’s monkey is small and brown. He likes to get loose and run around the park.

Kelsie: “This small, brown monkey on the tree next to me must be Melanie’s monkey”.

Preston: “There may be more than one small, brown monkey in the park!”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: A description can identify an animal only if it is unique. Ask whether the given features rule out every other monkey.

steps.explain: Melanie’s monkey is small, brown, and runs around the park. Kelsie saw a monkey matching two visible features, but she has not shown it is the only one.
steps.work: Matching features do not promise identity.

steps.explain: Preston points out that another monkey could share the same size and colour. Then Kelsie’s answer would not follow.
steps.work: There may be multiple matching monkeys.

steps.explain: Preston’s reasoning is valid; Kelsie’s “must be” claim is too strong.
steps.work: Answer: B, Preston only.

keyPoints.text: A description can identify an animal only if it is unique
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
The total amount of money it takes for the renovation of a house is $20,000.

How much does it cost for Kitchen?
questions.hint: The kitchen sector is one eighth of the circle. Find one eighth of the total budget.

steps.explain: In the pie chart, the Kitchen wedge is a 45° sector. A full circle is 360°, so its fraction is 45/360 = 1/8.
steps.work: Kitchen fraction = 45° ÷ 360° = 1/8.

questions.stem:
The table shows the “digit difference” of some two-digit numbers.

| Number | Working | Digit difference |
|---|---|---:|
| 15 | 5 − 1 = 4 | 4 |
| 28 | 8 − 2 = 6 | 6 |
| 50 | 5 − 0 = 5 | 5 |
| 73 | 7 − 3 = 4 | 4 |

How many two-digit numbers between 10 and 50 have a digit difference of 3?
questions.hint: For each tens digit, find the units digits whose absolute difference from it is 3. Stay within the numbers 10 through 50.

steps.explain: Digit difference means subtract the smaller digit from the larger digit. Start with tens digit 1: 14 has difference 4−1=3.

questions.stem:
At lunch time, I have to choose what sports I want to do for the next 4 weeks. I have to choose one sport from each of the following lists:

List 1: Javelin, Squash, Golf, Badminton

List 2: Javelin, Softball, Basketball, Swimming

List 3: Javelin, Squash, Gymnastics, Dance

List 4: Basketball, Gymnastics, Badminton, Dance

I know I want to do Swimming, golf and gymnastics. Which of the following can I not choose as my final sport?
questions.hint: Check which lists can supply the three chosen sports. Then see which option appears only in a list already needed for one of those sports.

steps.explain: Swimming appears only in List 2, so List 2 is already used. Golf appears only in List 1, so List 1 is used.
steps.work: Chosen: Swimming → List 2; Golf → List 1.

steps.explain: Gymnastics appears in both List 3 and List 4. One of those lists remains available for the fourth sport.
steps.work: Choose List 3 or List 4 for gymnastics.

steps.explain: Softball appears only in List 2, which is already used for Swimming. It cannot be the fourth choice.
steps.work: Answer: Softball (C).

keyPoints.text: Check which lists can supply the three chosen sports
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Mr Giggles: “I know that 11 of my students speak Korean, but I only hear 6 students speaking Korean to each other in class today, that must mean the rest of the class does not know enough Korean to speak in a conversation”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mr Giggles has made?
options: He did not count the students speaking Korean accurately
He may not be in the right classroom
Some students might have chosen to speak English only today
Mr Giggles may not know enough Korean to recognise it
questions.hint: Knowing a language does not mean someone must use it in every conversation. Look for a reason the other students may not have spoken Korean today.

steps.explain: The information says 11 students know Korean. It does not say they always speak Korean in class.
steps.work: Can speak Korean ≠ must speak Korean.

steps.explain: Only 6 students spoke Korean today. The other 5 may have chosen to use English on this occasion.
steps.work: 11 − 6 = 5 students not heard speaking Korean.

steps.explain: Option C identifies the unsupported assumption.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: Knowing a language does not mean someone must use it in every conversation
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Bryan, Trevor, Amy and Chris are seated around a table on a train. Two of them are facing forwards and two are facing backwards. Two have aisle seats and the other two have window seats.

I know that:
- Trevor is next to Bryan
- Bryan is sitting diagonally opposite Amy
- Chris is facing forwards

Which one of the following do I also know?
questions.hint: Draw the four positions around a 2 × 2 table. Put Bryan and Amy in opposite corners, then use Trevor-neighbour and Chris-facing clues.

steps.explain: In a 2 × 2 order, diagonally opposite people occupy opposite corners. Put Bryan and Amy on one diagonal.
steps.work: Bryan ↘ Amy.

questions.stem:
Nate believes that: “The local library should invest in a more extensive collection of encyclopedias”.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Nate’s argument?
options: Encyclopedias will take up a lot of space in the library
It is very expensive for the library to invest in more encyclopedias
Many people never use encyclopedias from the library
With more encyclopedias, people can become more educated
questions.hint: Choose a statement that gives a benefit of expanding the encyclopedia collection, not a cost or drawback.

steps.explain: Nate recommends buying more encyclopedias. A supporting statement should show a useful result of having more copies.
steps.work: Claim: expand collection → benefit.

steps.explain: Options A–C describe disadvantages or reduced use. Option D gives a positive educational outcome.
steps.work: Only D strengthens the recommendation.

steps.explain: so D is the best support.
steps.work: Answer: D.

questions.hint: A square pyramid has exactly one square base and four triangular side faces. Check how many faces of each shape each net contains and whether the triangles can meet at the apex.

steps.work: Check face counts: 1 square + 4 triangles required.

questions.stem:
When the lockdown bell rings, there could be an intruder on the school grounds or it could be a drill.

Jackie: “If you hear the lockdown bell there may be an intruder on school grounds”.

Keshan: “Yes, but we don’t need to worry yet as it may just be a drill”.

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is true?
questions.hint: The clue gives two possibilities. The word “may” means possible, not certain. Check whether each speaker preserves that uncertainty.

steps.explain: The information says the bell could mean an intruder, or it could be a drill. Both are possible cases.
steps.work: Possible cause ∈ {intruder, drill}.

steps.explain: Jackie says there may be an intruder. Keshan says it may be a drill. Each statement matches one of the stated choices.
steps.work: “May” does not claim certainty.

steps.explain: Both pieces of reasoning are valid.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem: Vincent and Sofia have the same birthday. On their birthday this year, Sofia’s age is three times Vincent’s age in years. Both Vincent and Sofia are less than 10 years old and Sofia’s age is an odd number. Which of these could be Vincent’s age?
questions.hint: Multiply each possible age by 3. The result must be an odd age below 10.

steps.explain: Test the choices using Sofia = 3 × Vincent.
steps.work: If Vincent is 2, 3, 5, or 7, Sofia would be 6, 9, 15, or 21.

steps.explain: Sofia must be younger than 10 and have an odd age. Only 9 meets both conditions.
steps.work: 3 × 3 = 9; 9 is odd and less than 10.

steps.explain: Vincent could be 3 years old.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Jason is at the punch table. One of them is normal and the rest are mixed with salt. He must bring back the punch without salt but he can only choose one flavour of juice. Janet gives him 5 clues to help him choose a juice.

- The blueberry juice is not next to the banana or kiwi juice.
- The apple juice is to the left of the kiwi one.
- The orange juice is not next to the jar without salt.
- The banana juice is at the far right and 2 places away from the kiwi juice.
- The kiwi juice is 2 places away from the juice without salt.

Which juice should Jason choose to bring home?
questions.hint: Place Banana at the far right. Then put Kiwi two places to its left, Apple to the left of Kiwi, and use the remaining positions to satisfy the two “not next to” clues.

steps.explain: Number the five positions 1–5 from left to right. Banana is at position 5. Since it is two places away from Kiwi, Kiwi is at position 3.
steps.work: Banana = 5; Kiwi = 3.

steps.explain: Apple must be before Kiwi. Put the fruits in the open places and check the clues about Blueberry, Banana and the juice without salt. The order that fits is Blueberry, Apple, Banana, Kiwi, Orange.
steps.work: Order: Blueberry – Apple – Kiwi – Orange – Banana.

steps.explain: The clue lineup is Blueberry, Apple, Kiwi, Orange, Banana. The normal (salt-free) juice is highlighted in the source key: Blueberry.
steps.work: Answer: Blueberry (option A).

questions.stem:
Inez’s class can choose what colour they want their next classroom uniform to be. They could vote to have orange, yellow or brown uniforms. Everyone could only choose for one colour and the colour would only be chosen if everyone chose the same colour.

Knowing one of the following would allow us to know the result of the vote. Which one is it?
options: Only three people voted for brown
No one voted for orange or yellow
Everyone voted for orange or yellow
Brown was the most popular vote
questions.hint: The outcome is selected only if everyone chooses the same colour. Which fact guarantees all votes are for one colour?

steps.explain: The rule says one colour is chosen only when all students vote for the same colour.
steps.work: Need unanimous votes.

steps.explain: If nobody voted orange or yellow, every vote must be brown because those are the only three options.
steps.work: No orange + no yellow → all brown.

steps.explain: That makes the result certain is brown. The other statements do not promise a unanimous result.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: The outcome is selected only if everyone chooses the same colour
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Ian, Janet, Kendall and Lexi are on the National Swimming team. The Swimming coach has announced that: “If Ian does not swim tomorrow, then Janet will swim. If Ian does swim then Kendall will take Lexi’s place”.

So, if Janet does not swim tomorrow, which of the other three swimmers will be at practice?
questions.hint: Use the first conditional backwards: if Janet does not swim, Ian cannot be absent. Then apply the second rule.

steps.explain: Rule 1: if Ian does not swim, Janet will swim. Read the rule this way: if Janet does not swim, Ian does swim.
steps.work: Not Ian → Janet; so not Janet → Ian.

steps.explain: Since Ian swims, apply rule 2: Kendall takes Lexi’s place. That means Kendall swims and Lexi does not.
steps.work: Ian swims → Kendall replaces Lexi.

steps.explain: The swimmers at practice among the other three are Ian and Kendall.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Use the first conditional backwards: if Janet does not swim, Ian cannot be absent
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
Jenny: “To even have a shot at being a regional champion of the year, you need to be on at least 3 state teams”.

Mary: “I am on 3 local teams so I have a chance at becoming the regional championship”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mary made?
options: Mary needs to try out for the teams she is on again this year
There may not be a regional champion this year
Mary is only a player on the local level, not the state level
The regional champions are older than Mary
questions.hint: The requirement specifies state teams. Does being on local teams prove membership on state teams?

steps.explain: Jenny’s condition is at least 3 STATE teams.
steps.work: Required level = state.

steps.explain: Mary counts 3 LOCAL teams. The question gives no rule saying local teams count as state teams.
steps.work: Local ≠ state based on the information.

steps.explain: Mary’s mistake is treating local-team membership as satisfying the state-team condition.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem: Mayor Julia wants to buy 1000 chairs for her town hall, but she is not sure she can fit them all into storage. She knows that one storage room can fit in 15 chair racks and each chair rack can hold 35 chairs. If the hall has 2 storage rooms, can she fit 1000 chairs in?
questions.hint: Calculate the capacity of one room, then double it for two rooms. Compare that total with 1000.

steps.explain: One room holds 15 racks, and each rack holds 35 chairs. Multiply to find one-room capacity.
steps.work: 15 × 35 = 525 chairs per room.

steps.explain: There are two rooms, so total capacity is 2 × 525 = 1050 chairs.
Since 1050 ≥ 1000, the chairs will fit.
steps.work: Answer: Yes (A).

keyPoints.text: Calculate the capacity of one room, then double it for two rooms
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues and check that the conclusion must follow.

questions.stem:
From birth to the age of 21, the number of bones in your body changes naturally.

Lacey: “So that means if I break my arm when I am 30, then the number of bones in my body changes naturally.”

Avi: “I don’t think so, since not everyone between birth to 21 breaks their arm or any other bone but still the number of bones still changes.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The given time condition is from birth up to age 21. Do not extend it to age 30, and do not assume a break is needed for natural change.

steps.explain: The fact in the box limits the natural change to ages from birth to 21. It does not say that an injury causes the change.
steps.work: Age interval: birth → 21.

steps.explain: Lacey applies that information to age 30, outside the stated interval, so the answer does not follow. Avi correctly notes that changes can happen without a break.
steps.work: Natural change does not require a fracture.

steps.explain: Only Avi’s reasoning matches the information given.
steps.work: Answer: A, Avi only.

keyPoints.text: The given time condition is from birth up to age 21
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.hint: Reflect the 4 by 4 grid across the vertical dashed line. Each symbol moves to the opposite column; its orientation is mirrored too.

steps.explain: A mirror on the left-right line swaps the columns: 1 with 4, and 2 with 3. The rows stay where they are. For example, the mark in row 1, column 1 moves to row 1, column 4.
steps.work: Check outer symbols: Black circles at (1,4) and (4,1); trapezoid at (4,4).

questions.stem:
A health specialist suggests a greater need for more organic farmers rather than the current mono farmers who use a significant amount of chemicals in comparison to the little to no chemicals by organic farmers.

Which of these statements, if true, best supports the health specialist’s claims?
options: Mono farmers produce the vegetables or fruits which are highly demanded by consumers
The chemicals used by mono farmers have been linked to health problems
Organic farming is more tedious and expensive to continue
Not many individuals know the difference between organic and mono-farmed produce
questions.hint: The claim favours organic farming because it uses fewer chemicals. A strong support should show why reducing mono-farm chemical use matters.

steps.explain: The specialist’s key comparison is chemical use: mono farmers use many chemicals, organic farmers use few or none.
steps.work: Claim: fewer chemicals is preferable.

steps.explain: Option B links mono-farm chemicals to health problems, giving a direct reason to prefer less chemical use.
steps.work: A and C favour mono farming; D is unrelated.

steps.explain: so option B most strongly supports the specialist.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: The claim favours organic farming because it uses fewer chemicals
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem:
Jessica bought some shoes, socks and shirts.

Which graph shows that Jessica spent the most money on shoes?
questions.hint: In each segmented bar, the width of a category represents the amount spent. Find the graph where the shoes segment is the widest.

steps.explain: Compare the widths of the three labelled sections in each graph. A larger section represents more money spent on that item.
steps.work: Shoes must be the widest section.

questions.stem:
Polly, Lisa and Jenny all plant various flowers in their backyard. Polly has Gardenias, Roses, Azaleas, Baby Breath and Geraniums. Lisa has Roses, Daffodils, Lilies and Azaleas. Jenny has Geraniums, Orchids, Daisies and Roses.

Which flowers does Lisa have, but neither Polly nor Jenny plant?
questions.hint: Start with Lisa’s flower list and cross out any flower that also appears on Polly’s or Jenny’s list.

steps.explain: Lisa has Roses, Daffodils, Lilies and Azaleas.
steps.work: Lisa = {Roses, Daffodils, Lilies, Azaleas}.

steps.explain: Roses and Azaleas also appear on Polly’s list. Roses also appears on Jenny’s list. Remove those shared flowers.
steps.work: Remove shared: Roses, Azaleas.

steps.explain: The flowers remaining are Daffodils and Lilies.
steps.work: Answer: C.

questions.stem:
A doctor says: “exercise is good for your health.”

Which of the following statements supports the doctor’s claims?
options: Exercising makes people’s immune systems weaker.
People who exercise are less likely to be sick.
Those who do not exercise are healthier.
Exercise only benefits a specific age group.
questions.hint: Choose the evidence that directly connects exercise with improved health.

steps.explain: The claim is that exercise benefits health. A supporting statement should describe a positive health effect.
steps.work: Exercise → health benefit.

steps.explain: Option B says people who exercise are less likely to be sick, which is direct clue of improved health.
steps.work: A and C oppose the claim; D narrows it.

steps.explain: So option B supports the doctor.
steps.work: Answer: B.

questions.stem:
These are four views of the same cube.

Which view would come next?
questions.hint: Track the three visible faces and the orientation of the symbol on top. Apply the alternating 90° rotations shown in the sequence.

steps.explain: Compare views 1 and 2: the front symbol changes while the right-side triangle remains in place, showing a quarter-turn in one direction.
steps.work: Follow the unchanged face to find the turn.

questions.stem:
A chicken egg and duck egg have a similar colour of white or brown. However, the duck egg is slightly bigger at 65 mm, while a chicken egg is 3 mm smaller.

Sofia: “The egg is brown so it has and looks like the right size for an egg so it is a chicken egg!”

Aldrich: “Well I measured the egg and it’s 62 mm so it is a chicken egg.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Use the measurable difference, not the colour. Calculate the chicken egg size from the duck egg size and compare it with Aldrich’s measurement.

steps.explain: A duck egg is 65 mm. A chicken egg is 3 mm smaller, so calculate 65 − 3.
Aldrich measured 62 mm, which matches the stated chicken egg size. Sofia relies on colour, which the clue says can be similar for both types.
steps.work: Measurement identifies; colour does not.

steps.explain: Aldrich’s reasoning is supported; Sofia’s is not.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: Use the measurable difference, not the colour
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Lisa’s vocal instructor said, “To have a chance to place in the top three, you must in the last three days before the competition only practice in spaced out intervals to not overuse one’s vocal cords by competition night.”

If Lisa’s instructor is correct, which of the following statements is true?
options: Only those who practice in intervals throughout the last three days till competition night will not be able to place.
Those who only sing off tune the last two days before the performance will give themselves the best opportunity for the competition.
Someone who practiced consistently at their peak level of performance for five days before the competition will not be able to place.
None of the statements above is true.
questions.hint: The rule says spaced-out practice over the last three days is necessary to have a chance. Continuous peak practice for five days conflicts with that advice.

steps.explain: The instructor’s condition is required practice spacing during the last three days.
steps.work: Need spaced practice; avoid overuse.

steps.explain: Option C describes continuous peak practice for five days, which conflicts with spacing and risks overusing the vocal cords. Options A and B do not follow the stated rule.
steps.work: Compare each option with the rule that must be followed first.

steps.explain: so the true consequence is option C.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: The rule says spaced-out practice over the last three days is necessary to have a chance
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Macey and Darren are standing in the kitchen.

Macey: “Well I’ve been looking for the salt but I can’t find it!”

Darren: “Here it is! I found it next to your teas on the counter.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Darren has made?
options: He tasted it before he gave it to Macey.
There may be a lot of people who don’t like salt.
Salt is not the only white crystal present in the kitchen.
There might be no containers holding salt in the kitchen.
questions.hint: Darren identified the item by where it was found. Ask whether being next to tea uniquely identifies a white crystal as salt.

steps.explain: Darren concludes that the white crystal beside the tea is salt.
steps.work: Location beside tea is his clue.

steps.explain: But both salt and sugar are white crystals, and sugar is often kept near tea. So the location alone does not tell us which substance it is.
steps.work: Same appearance/location can fit another item.

steps.explain: Option C points out the alternative that undermines Darren’s answer.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: Darren identified the item by where it was found
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem: Choose a graph that shows Matt leaving his home, cycling at a constant speed to meet a friend in a park for a short play, resting once before reaching there, and then cycling home.
questions.hint: Read distance from home over time: cycling away at constant speed is a straight rising segment; each rest is horizontal; returning home is a falling segment to zero.

steps.explain: On the way out, Matt’s distance from home gets bigger, so the line goes up. When he stops, time passes but distance stays the same, so the line is flat.
steps.work: Cycling away → straight upward-sloping line.
