questions.stem:
Leila: “Molly knows that there are 8 runners in her class. If any of the runners are ever away, it tends to be for an athletics competition. Today 2 runners were away, so it was for an athletics competition.”

Which of the following sentences shows the mistake Molly has made?
options: Molly forgot to ask the runners to double check whether they actually had a competition today
No one else attended school today since it was a holiday.
Runners don’t have to be away just because of an athletics competition.
questions.hint: “Tends to” means often, not always. Find an alternative reason the two runners could be absent.

steps.explain: The clue says absences tend to be for competitions. That describes a usual pattern, not a rule that every absence is caused by a competition.
steps.work: Often ≠ always.

steps.explain: The two runners might be away for another reason, so their absence alone does not prove there is a competition.
steps.work: Absence does not uniquely imply a competition.

steps.explain: Option C identifies this mistaken assumption.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
The scientist said during a conference: “The more we shift towards green energy, the more we slow down the harmful effects of greenhouse gases on the environment.”

Which of the following statements, if true, best supports the scientist’s claim?
options: Using more green energy means reducing the use of carbon dioxide which produces greenhouse gases.
Greenhouse gases have an everlasting effect on the planet and even the reduction of their use will not change the current state of the earth.
Green energy is good and takes longer to collect than carbon dioxide which produces greenhouse gases.
Shifting to green energy is worse in the long run as the resources which produce it are not infinite.
questions.hint: The claim is that green energy slows harmful greenhouse effects. Look for a direct link between using green energy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

steps.explain: The scientist claims a shift to green energy slows harmful greenhouse effects.
steps.work: Green energy → slower greenhouse impact.

steps.explain: Option A explains how it helps: using more green energy reduces carbon dioxide use/emissions. B says reductions will not help; C and D weaken the proposal.
steps.work: Only A supports how the plan is meant to help.

steps.explain: so option A best supports the claim.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: The claim is that green energy slows harmful greenhouse effects
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Whenever John’s mum sells a house, she is in a good mood. And when she is happy, she will bake cookies.

John: “My mum wasn’t in a good mood last week, meaning mum didn’t sell a house.”

Jacob: “Well if your mum makes cookies this week, she will have sold a house.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Follow the arrows in the direction stated. A conditional can be reversed only by taking its contrapositive, not by swapping its two parts.

steps.explain: Write each stated if-then rule in its given direction. A house sale implies a good mood, and a good mood implies cookies.
steps.work: Sale → good mood → cookies.

steps.explain: John says “not a good mood, so no sale.” This is the same rule read backward from sale → good mood, so it follows from the rule.
steps.work: Sale → good mood; so not-good-mood → no sale.

steps.explain: Jacob reads the rule backwards: cookies do not always mean a house is for sale. John follows the rule correctly. Only John is right.
steps.work: Answer from the logic: A (John only). Source-key discrepancy: printed key D.

keyPoints.text: Whenever John’s mum sells a house, she is in a good mood.
keyPoints.note: The valid contrapositive is “not in a good mood → did not sell.”

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1
meta.answerKeyNote: Printed source answer key gives D, but the stated implications make John’s contrapositive valid and Jacob’s reversal invalid; the logically correct option is A.

questions.stem:
Peter’s clock is not working properly. The hour changes every 30 minutes instead of every 60 minutes.

Peter’s clock was correct at 12:00 pm. It now shows this time: 3:00 pm.

What is the correct time?
questions.hint: The displayed clock advances twice as fast: every real 30 minutes it gains one clock hour. Convert the displayed 3-hour advance into real time.

steps.explain: Peter’s clock advanced from 12:00 to 3:00, which is 3 displayed hours.
steps.work: Clock advance = 3 hours.

steps.explain: Each displayed hour takes 30 minutes of real time. Multiply 3 by 30 minutes.
steps.work: 3 × 30 = 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes.

questions.stem:
Molly is playing with four coloured marbles, with the starting marble being white and the other three being either blue or green. The starting marble hits a green marble. That ball hits another marble. The third marble then hits the final marble which is blue.

On the basis of this information, which of the following statements must be true?
options: Two of the marbles were white.
The blue marble hit a white marble.
The blue marble hit a green marble.
The green marble hit a blue marble.
questions.hint: Follow the collision chain and consider both possible colours for the unknown third marble. Look for a statement true in every case.

steps.explain: The impact order is fixed: the starting white marble hits a green marble; that second marble hits a third; then the third hits the last blue marble.
steps.work: White → green → ? → blue.

steps.explain: The third marble can be either blue or green. If it is blue, the green second marble hits a blue third marble. If it is green, the green third marble hits the last blue marble.
steps.work: Either way, a green marble hits a blue marble.

steps.explain: That statement is true in both cases.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Follow the collision chain and consider both possible colours for the unknown third marble
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem:
Stefi, Kole, Troy and Gabby are sitting together at a table in the cafeteria. Two are sitting facing towards the aisle while the other two are facing the wall. Two are on the side that has an empty table and the other two are on the side where the table is occupied.

I know that:
- Troy is sitting diagonally of Stefi
- Kole is sitting against the aisle
- Kole and Stefi are not sitting next to each other.

Which of the following do I also know?
options: Stefi is facing towards the aisle.
Gabby is sitting next to Troy.
Kole is sitting on the side of the empty table.
Troy is sitting on the side of the occupied table.
questions.hint: Draw four places in a 2 by 2 arrangement. Put Troy diagonally opposite Stefi; the “not next to” clue then fixes Kole’s position.

steps.explain: Troy and Stefi sit in opposite corners. The two empty seats are the other corners.
steps.work: Troy and Stefi: opposite corners.

questions.stem:
An economist says: “It is good to save money, not just for the saver, but for the others in the economy as well.”

Which one of these, if true, best supports the economist’s claim?
options: The more money one saves, the less money one can spend, not being able to buy things one wants.
The bank will lend out people’s savings at interest to others who need money.
The only people who have access to a savings account is the owner themselves.
Saving is an expensive practice, which is why people like giving out their money to charity instead.
questions.hint: The claim includes a benefit to people other than the saver. Look for a way savings can reach or help other people.

steps.explain: The economist says saving benefits both the saver and other people in the economy.
steps.work: Need benefit beyond the saver.

steps.explain: If banks lend deposited savings to borrowers, then the savings can help other people access money for their needs.
steps.work: Savings → bank lending → borrowers benefit.

steps.explain: Option B directly explains that wider benefit.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: The claim includes a benefit to people other than the saver
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Harry, Carrie and Barry share 9 cupcakes, and each of them receives at least one cupcake. Harry has 4 more than Barry.

Which of the following statements is true?
options: The greatest amount of cupcakes Barry can have is 2.
Harry could have either 2 or 5 more cupcakes than Carrie.
Carrie always has the least cupcakes.
Both A and B are true.
questions.hint: Let Barry have b cupcakes. Then Harry has b+4, so Carrie has 9−(2b+4). Test positive whole-number values for b.

steps.explain: Let Barry = b. Harry = b+4. Since the total is 9, Carrie = 9−b−(b+4) = 5−2b.
All three must have at least one cupcake. So 5−2b≥1, which gives b≤2. The positive choices are b=1 or b=2.
Barry’s maximum is 2, and Harry exceeds Carrie by 2 in the first case and 5 in the second. Both A and B are true.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Car P travels 30 km in 20 minutes. Car Q travels 90 km in 60 minutes. Car R travels 25 km in 15 minutes. Car S travels 45 km in 30 minutes.

Which car has the highest average speed?
questions.hint: Convert every time to hours, then divide distance by time. A common km/h unit makes the four speeds comparable.

steps.explain: Convert minutes into hours. P and S take 20 and 30 minutes; Q takes 60 minutes; R takes 15 minutes.
Car R has the highest average speed at 100 km/h.
steps.work: Answer: C.

questions.stem:
Solar, Moon, Star, Nebi and Sunny are part of the debate team. A usual debate only allows for three members, so two members must sit out per debate. Their debate coach told them: “If Moon will sit out then Sunny will debate. If Nebi debates then Solar will sit out instead of Star. If Solar doesn’t debate then Moon will debate.”

So if Sunny sits out for the next debate, who else will also be sitting out?
questions.hint: First use the contrapositive to establish that Moon debates. Then test whether the remaining rules force one unique second person to sit out; do not reverse a conditional.

steps.explain: There are 5 people and 3 debate, so 2 sit out. Sunny sits out. If Moon sat out, Sunny would debate. Since Sunny sits out, Moon must debate.
steps.work: Sunny sits out → Moon debates.

steps.explain: The clue does not say that Solar must sit out whenever Moon debates. So check all the clues instead of turning that rule around.
steps.work: Do not turn “Solar sits out → Moon debates” around.

steps.explain: Two groups fit the clues: Sunny and Nebi sit out, or Sunny and Solar sit out. So the clues do not choose one second person. The printed answer is B, but A also fits the written clues.
steps.work: Both listed teams fit the rules; the question has two possible answers.

keyPoints.text: If Moon will sit out then Sunny will debate.
keyPoints.note: Contrapositive: if Sunny sits out, Moon must debate.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1
meta.answerKeyNote: The printed key gives B, but the conditions allow both A (Nebi) and B (Solar) as the second person sitting out. The item is underdetermined as written.

questions.stem:
Henry: “You need to practise driving the potential three test routes at least 3 times before your exam, as you will be tested on one of them on the day.”

Julie: “Well I’ve driven two of the routes five times already so I should pass the exam!”

Which of the following sentences shows Julie’s mistake?
options: Driving potential routes more than the recommended times will guarantee a pass on the test.
She has practised the routes ten times altogether.
Julie hasn’t attempted all possible routes that she could be tested on.
She will need to learn how to drive all three routes as she will be tested on all three.
questions.hint: The condition requires practice on each of the three possible routes. Julie practised only two routes.

steps.explain: There are three possible exam routes, and the advice is to practise each one at least three times.
steps.work: Need cover all three routes.

steps.explain: Julie has repeated two routes five times each, but she has not practised the third possible route.
steps.work: 2 routes practiced; 1 route missing.

steps.explain: Since the test could use the unpractised route, she has not prepared for every choice.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: The condition requires practice on each of the three possible routes
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem:
There are six friends (Louise, Kay, Han, Jie, Tami and Carrie) standing in the handball court. Han is standing in the centre of the court. Tami is southwest of Han. Jie is northwest of Kay. Carrie is north of Louise. Tami is east of Louise. Jie is north of Han.

Who is east of Han?
questions.hint: Place Han at the centre. Position Jie north of him and Tami southwest. Use the two remaining direction clues to place Kay and the others.

steps.explain: Set Han as the origin (0,0). Jie is north of Han, and Tami is southwest of Han.
steps.work: Han centre; Jie north; Tami southwest.

steps.explain: Tami is east of Louise, so Louise is west of Tami. Carrie is north of Louise. Jie is northwest of Kay, which places Kay southeast of Jie.
steps.work: Use “northwest of” in reverse: Kay is southeast of Jie.

steps.explain: The completed order places Kay directly east of Han.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem:
This figure is made of small cubes. All surfaces of this figure are painted blue.

How many faces on the small cubes have been painted blue?
questions.hint: Count all cube faces, then subtract the two faces hidden at each shared join. The source shape has 8 cubes and 9 joins.

steps.explain: Each small cube has 6 faces. A face where two cubes touch is hidden inside and cannot be painted.
steps.work: Total cubes = 8. Total cube faces before joining = 8 × 6 = 48.

The reward was in one of the five coloured boxes on the table, with the other four being empty. From left to right, each box is numbered 1 (most left) to 5 (most right). These were the clues:

- The pink box is furthest to the left.
- The yellow box is two spaces left of the black box.
- The yellow box is also two boxes away from another colour box on the opposite side.
- The red box has to its right, the colour of the night sky.
- The immediate left of the yellow box is a box that is the colour of the grass.
- The reward is in the box next to the middle box.
- The reward is in the second box.

Which box should Toby open to find the reward?

questions.stem:
I have to choose four electives for the next two years of school.

I need to choose a subject from each of the following lists:

| List A | List B | List C | List D |
|---|---|---|---|
| Photography | Food technology | Modern history | Statistics |
| Design technology | Legal studies | Art history | Business |
| PE | Business | Design technology | Photography |
| Visual art | Statistics | Photography | Ancient history |

I want to study Photography, Design technology and Legal studies.

Which one of the following can I not choose as my final subject?
questions.hint: Assign each wanted subject to a list. Legal studies appears only in List B, so the fourth subject must come from an unused list.

steps.explain: Legal studies appears only in List B, so List B is used. Photography can be selected from List A, C, or D; Design technology from A or C.
steps.work: Legal studies → List B.

steps.explain: The other three subjects can be arranged using Lists A, C, and D. Food technology appears only in List B, which is already used.
steps.work: Food technology unavailable because it shares List B with Legal studies.

steps.explain: so Food technology cannot be the last subject.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Assign each wanted subject to a list
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem: One morning Luisa, Noor and Manling counted their pencils. They found that Luisa had three times the number of pencils that Manling had and Noor had twice the number of pencils that Manling had. By the end of the day, Noor had lost four pencils, and had 34 pencils left. How many pencils did Luisa have that morning?
questions.hint: Work backwards from Noor’s ending amount to her starting amount. Use the two ratios to find Manling’s and then Luisa’s counts.

steps.explain: Noor finished with 34 after losing 4, so she started with 34+4=38 pencils.
steps.work: Noor start = 38.

steps.explain: Noor had twice Manling’s amount, so Manling had 38÷2=19. Luisa had three times Manling’s amount.
steps.work: Manling = 19; Luisa = 3×19.
Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: Work backwards from Noor’s ending amount to her starting amount

questions.stem:
Only those who attend the photography class, today after school will be able to take photos for tomorrow’s school event.

Liam: “Well I don’t think Min will be taking pictures with us tomorrow since he will be able to attend the meeting after school today.”

Kate: “Well Corey will be able to go since he has a piano lesson after school but his mum moved his lesson to after the class so he can attend.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Attendance at the photography class is necessary. Check whether Min and Corey can attend today; do not reverse the rule.

steps.explain: The rule says only attendees of today’s photography class can take pictures tomorrow. Attending the class is needed.
steps.work: Attend class → eligible.

steps.explain: Min can attend today, so Liam’s answer that Min will not take pictures does not follow. Corey’s piano lesson was moved until after class, so Corey can attend.
steps.work: Min can attend; Corey can attend.

steps.explain: Kate is correct about Corey’s eligibility; Liam’s reasoning is incorrect.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: Attendance at the photography class is necessary
keyPoints.note: Check each clue against the conclusion; use only what the question states.

questions.stem:
Toby is standing to the left of Lisa. Kristen is to the right of Toby.

Which of the following statements is true?
options: Kristen is furthest to the right.
Lisa is always in the middle.
Lisa is furthest to the right.
Toby is furthest to the left.
questions.hint: Both Lisa and Kristen are to Toby’s right. Decide whether their order can vary, and identify the position that cannot vary.

steps.explain: Toby is left of Lisa, so Lisa is to Toby’s right. Kristen is also right of Toby.
steps.work: Toby < Lisa and Toby < Kristen.

steps.explain: Lisa and Kristen can switch order, so neither one is guaranteed to be furthest right. But Toby is left of both in every allowed order.
steps.work: Possible orders: Toby–Lisa–Kristen or Toby–Kristen–Lisa.

steps.explain: Toby is always furthest left.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Both Lisa and Kristen are to Toby’s right

questions.hint: Convert each bar to a fraction of 200, then compare those percentages with the sector sizes. The counts are 80, 60, 40, and 20.

steps.explain: The bar chart shows four shares: Maths 35%, Thinking Skills 30%, English 25%, and Writing 10%. Together they make 100%.

questions.stem:
Adelaide time is one and a half hours behind Sydney time.

A plane leaves Sydney at 10:00 am and flies to Adelaide. The flight takes 2 hours. What time is it in Adelaide when the flight arrives?
questions.hint: First add the flight duration using Sydney time. Then convert the arrival time to Adelaide time by subtracting 1 hour 30 minutes.

steps.explain: The flight leaves at 10:00 am Sydney time and takes 2 hours.
steps.work: 10:00 am + 2 hours = 12:00 pm Sydney time.

steps.explain: Adelaide is 1 hour 30 minutes behind Sydney. Subtract that time difference: 12:00 pm − 1 hour = 11:00 am; 11:00 am − 30 minutes = 10:30 am.
steps.work: 12:00 pm Sydney − 1 h 30 min = 10:30 am Adelaide.

steps.explain: The plane arrives at 10:30 am Adelaide time.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: First add the flight duration using Sydney time
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
People who play a musical instrument are less stressed than those who do not. Maddy’s dad is encouraging Maddy to go to music lessons to help improve her discipline.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Playing a musical instrument is challenging but needed.
Playing a musical instrument will fill in spare time.
Playing a musical instrument is quick and easy to learn.
Playing a musical instrument will build greater confidence and improve skills.
questions.hint: Choose the option that adds a relevant benefit of learning an instrument and supports the reason for lessons.

steps.explain: The claim links music lessons with better discipline, and says instrument players experience less stress.
steps.work: find the claimed positive effects: less stress and improved discipline.

steps.explain: A strong supporting statement gives another direct benefit of playing an instrument. Confidence and skill development are relevant positive outcomes; spare time or ease of learning do not support the claim as directly.
steps.work: Relevant support: music → improved confidence and skills.

steps.explain: Option D provides the strongest additional benefit.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Choose the option that adds a relevant benefit of learning an instrument and supports the reason for lessons
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
Max, Calum and Arvin all have cars. Max has a red, white and blue car, and Calum has a red, white and yellow car. Arvin has a red, white and yellow car.

Which car colour does Max have that neither Calum nor Arvin have?
questions.hint: Compare the colour lists. Find the colour that appears in Max’s list but not in either of the other two lists.

steps.explain: Max has red, white, and blue. Calum and Arvin each have red, white, and yellow.
steps.work: Max: {red, white, blue}; others: {red, white, yellow}.

steps.explain: Red and white appear in all three lists. Yellow is not one of Max’s colours. The only colour in Max’s list that is not in the other lists is blue.
steps.work: Only Max has blue.

steps.explain: so the answer is Blue.
steps.work: Answer: C.

questions.stem:
Whenever Jim is angry, he goes on a walk. When he goes on a walk, he always listens to sad music.

Dan: “Jim is listening to sad music, so he must be angry.”

Pat: “If Jim is angry, he will listen to sad music.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Translate the statements as one-way implications: angry → walk → sad music. Do not reverse the arrows.

steps.explain: The two clues make a chain: angry → goes for a walk → listens to sad music. Follow the arrows from left to right.
steps.work: Follow the arrows: Angry → Walk → Sad music.

questions.stem:
When the last piece is put into this puzzle it shows 3 triangles.

Which piece is missing from this puzzle?
questions.hint: Count the triangular regions formed by the line segments. Mentally rotate each option and see which completes exactly three triangles.

steps.explain: Look at the three line ends around the empty middle square. The marked ends are ① on the left, ② near the top-right, and ③ near the bottom-right. The missing piece must join all three lines smoothly.
steps.work: Three line ends to join: ① left, ② upper right, ③ lower right.

questions.stem:
There is a car crash where 5 cars (red, white, blue, green and yellow) crashed into each other in a row. The first car is blue, two cars next to it is a red car. Next to the white car on the end is the green car.

On the basis of this information, which of the following orders of the car crash is true?
questions.hint: Fix Blue in the first position. “Two cars next to it” means Red is two places from Blue; then use the White-at-an-end and Green-next-to-White clues.

steps.explain: Make five spaces and number them 1 to 5. The blue car is first. The red car is two spaces after blue, so red is in space 3.
steps.work: Slot 1 = Blue; Slot 3 = Red.

questions.stem:
Only people who score higher than 80% on their exam can go on school camp.

Jemma: “I am going on camp, so that means I got higher than 80%.”

Tom: “Alex is not allowed to go camping because he is busy that day.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: “Only people above 80% can go” means above 80% is necessary for camp. Being busy is not given as a camp rule.

steps.explain: To go on camp, a student must score above 80%. The rule does not say that every student above 80% will go.
steps.work: Going on camp → score above 80%.

questions.stem: Bella, Molly and Alex are standing in a row. If Alex is on the left of Bella and Molly is furthest from Alex, which of the following statements is true?
options: Bella is furthest on the left.
Molly is furthest to the right.
questions.hint: Alex is left of Bella. “Molly is furthest from Alex” places Molly at the opposite end of the three-person row.

steps.explain: Number the places from left to right: 1, 2, 3. Alex is left of Bella, so Alex cannot be in place 3.

steps.explain: A cube has 6 faces. One is black, four touch it, so 1 + 4 = 5 faces are accounted for. The one face left is blank. It is opposite the black square.
steps.work: The cube has 6 faces: 1 black + 4 touching + 1 opposite. The face left is blank, so blank is opposite black.

questions.stem:
Sarah has lost her car in the shopping centre parking and asks security to help her find it.

Sarah: “My car is small and blue, it is also on the second floor.”

The security: “There is a blue car on the second floor which must mean that it is your car.”

Which of the following sentences shows the mistake of the security?
options: The security might be looking at someone else’s car.
Even if the car is blue, it might not be small.
There might be more than one blue car on the first floor.
The security is looking at the wrong floor.
questions.hint: Sarah gave two identifying features, size and colour, plus the floor. Security checked colour and floor but did not check size.

steps.explain: Sarah’s description contains three details: small, blue, second floor.
steps.work: Required features: small + blue + second floor.

steps.explain: Security found a car matching blue and second floor but has not established that it is small. Another, larger blue car could be there.
steps.work: Missing check: size.

steps.explain: so the security’s answer is not certain.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: Sarah gave two identifying features, size and colour, plus the floor
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem: Peter spent all of his pocket money on food, toys, lollies and books. He spent the most money on food. Which graph shows this?
questions.hint: In a pie chart, compare the sector sizes. The food sector must be larger than each of toys, lollies, and books.

steps.explain: The question says food received the greatest amount of money, so its sector must be the largest slice.
steps.work: Largest amount ↔ largest pie sector.

questions.stem:
Jen’s mother suggests Jen go to tutoring to get better marks.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Jen’s mother’s suggestion?
options: Tutoring is expensive but will help her learn faster.
Getting help from her parents will also help her get better marks.
Jen is not guaranteed better marks.
Tutoring will help Jen understand things she struggles with at school.
questions.hint: Choose the statement that explains how tutoring could lead to better marks, rather than a different method or a limitation.

steps.explain: The suggestion is tutoring → better marks. Look for a reason that connects tutoring to learning.
steps.work: Tutoring should help learning, which can improve marks.

steps.explain: Tutoring that clarifies difficult school concepts gives a direct pathway to better understanding and so better marks.
steps.work: Tutoring → understanding difficult topics → better marks.

steps.explain: Option D gives the strongest support.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Choose the statement that explains how tutoring could lead to better marks, rather than a different method or a limitation
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Kate’s mother said in order to have a big birthday party she must get more than 50% in Maths and English.

If Kate’s mother has this rule, which of the statements must be correct?
options: Kate gets more than 50% in Maths so she will have a big party.
Kate gets 45% in Maths and 80% in English so she will have a big party.
Kate gets less than 50% in General ability but 70% in both Maths and English so she will have a big party.
Kate will not have a big party if she gets 60% in both Maths and English.
questions.hint: The required condition is strictly more than 50% in both named subjects. Check that each option satisfies both conditions and ignore General Ability.

steps.explain: The rule requires Maths > 50% AND English > 50%.
steps.work: Both scores must exceed 50%.

steps.explain: Option C has Maths 70% and English 70%, so both required conditions hold. General Ability is not part of the rule.
steps.work: 70>50 in Maths and 70>50 in English.

steps.explain: Thus C is the statement that must be correct under the rule.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: The required condition is strictly more than 50% in both named subjects
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem: A rectangular piece of paper is folded once and the shaded section is cut out. What is the shape of this unshaded part when the shaded part has been removed?
questions.hint: Unfold the paper by reflecting the cut edge across the fold. The final outline must preserve the cut’s flat top, slanted edge, and vertical section.

steps.explain: find the fold line and the shaded cut on the folded paper. When unfolded, the cut is flipped across the crease, so matching edges appear on both halves.
steps.work: The cut is mirrored across the fold.

steps.work: Look for the mirrored outline with the flat top and slanted-to-vertical sides.

questions.stem:
Sam’s house is 2 stories, brown with a white door. The only other brown house on his street is Matt’s house.

Jeff: “This house is brown so it must be Sam’s house.”

Harry: “The house which is white cannot be Sam’s or Matt’s house.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Brown identifies two houses (Sam and Matt), so it cannot identify Sam uniquely. Only Sam’s house has the specified white door.

steps.explain: Sam’s house is brown and has a white door. Matt’s is the only other brown house on the street.
steps.work: Brown house options: Sam or Matt.

steps.explain: Jeff cannot find Sam using brown alone. Harry is correct that a white house cannot be either Sam’s or Matt’s because both are brown.
steps.work: White exterior does not match both known brown houses.

steps.explain: Only Harry is correct.
steps.work: Answer: B.

keyPoints.text: Brown identifies two houses (Sam and Matt), so it cannot identify Sam uniquely
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Amanda: “There are 3 children in the class who catch the same bus that ran late to school, however, 5 students were late to class, this means there are now 5 students on the bus.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Amanda made?
options: Amanda did not count students from the other class.
Amanda counted the number of late children incorrectly.
Not all late people come by bus; some come by car which also has traffic.
Amanda did not say which students were usually on the bus.
questions.hint: Being late and riding the bus are different groups. Some of the five late students may have travelled by another method.

steps.explain: Three children on the bus were late. The class had five late students in total.
steps.work: Bus-late students = 3; total late students = 5.

steps.explain: The two additional late students are not necessarily bus passengers. They may have arrived by car or another way.
steps.work: Late ≠ necessarily on the bus.

steps.explain: Option C identifies the unsupported assumption.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: Being late and riding the bus are different groups
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

meta.source: Essential Opportunity Class Thinking Skills Book 1

questions.stem:
Emma, Jen, Rosie and Jack are seated at a table for dinner, two people on either side. We know that:

• Rosie is sitting next to Jack.
• Jack is directly opposite Jen.

Which of the following must be true?
options: Rosie is directly sitting opposite Jen.
Emma and Jen are sitting next to each other.
Jack is sitting next to Emma.
questions.hint: Place Jack and Jen opposite each other. Rosie sits beside Jack, so the remaining seat beside Jen must be Emma.

steps.explain: Draw four seats around a table. Put Jack in one seat and Jen directly opposite him.
steps.work: Opposite seats: Jack ↔ Jen.

questions.stem:
The table shows the final scores of four teams in a competition.

| Red | 37.9 |

How many more points were scored by the team that came first than the team that came second?
questions.hint: Rank the four point totals from highest to lowest, then subtract second place from first place.

steps.explain: Compare the scores: Blue 71.0, Red 37.9, Green 50.8, Yellow 43.6. Blue is first with 71.0 and Green is second with 50.8.
Find the difference: 71.0 − 50.8. Write decimals in columns: 71.0 − 50.0 = 21.0, then 21.0 − 0.8 = 20.2.
The difference is 20.2 points.
steps.work: Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Next month Emma is getting four pets to improve her wellbeing. Emma has to pick one pet from each list:

| List 1 | List 2 | List 3 | List 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dog | Fish | Fish | Horse |
| Pig | Horse | Pig | Rat |
| Cat | Chicken | Rat | Bird |
| Bird | Snake | Spider | Spider |

Emma knows that she wants a fish, cat and rat.

Which of the following can Emma not choose as her last pet?
questions.hint: Assign Fish, Cat, and Rat to lists that contain them. The remaining available list determines the last pet.

steps.explain: Cat appears only in List 1, so List 1 is used for Cat. Fish can be chosen from List 2 or List 3; Rat can be chosen from List 3 or List 4.
steps.work: Cat → List 1.

steps.explain: If Dog is the answer, Dog must come from a list that contains Dog. Check each list. The lists that could give Dog are already needed for other animals, so Dog cannot be chosen.
steps.work: Dog is only in List 1, which is already used for Cat.

steps.explain: Emma cannot choose Dog as her fourth pet.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: Assign Fish, Cat, and Rat to lists that contain them

questions.stem: In 5 days’ time, which will be a Monday, I will go visit my grandmother for a week and a half. If the forecast today says that it will be raining for the next 15 days, which of the following is certain?
options: It will not be raining when I arrive home.
It will rain on Tuesday, the day I return home.
It will not rain on Monday, the day I return home.
questions.hint: Count back five days from Monday to find today. The rain forecast does not tell you which individual days will be rainy.

steps.explain: Five days after today is Monday. Count backward: Sunday (1), Saturday (2), Friday (3), Thursday (4), Wednesday (5).
steps.work: Today must be Wednesday.

steps.explain: The visit lasts a week and a half, but “raining for the next 15 days” does not tell us which exact days will be rainy or whether rain will continue through the return date.
steps.work: The only certain fact is the weekday today.

steps.explain: Today is Wednesday.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.text: Count back five days from Monday to find today
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
A police officer says: “Whoever commits a crime should face the consequences, even if it is small.”

Which one of these statements best supports the police officer’s claim?
options: It is only fair that everyone gets punished for crimes, so it doesn’t happen again.
Not all consequences will solve crime rates.
Even if criminals face consequences, crimes will still occur.
Small crimes are not serious and should not have consequences.
questions.hint: Choose a reason that supports consequences for all crimes and explains why applying consequences is useful.

steps.explain: The officer argues that consequences should apply to every crime, including small ones.
steps.work: Claim: crime → consequence.

steps.explain: Option A supports fair and consistent consequences and gives a deterrent reason. The other options weaken or does not match the claim.
steps.work: Consistent consequence → fairness and discouragement of repeat crimes.

steps.explain: so A best supports the officer.
steps.work: Answer: A.

questions.stem:
There are 2 red and 2 white marbles in a bag. Mary picks her 2 marbles first without looking and picked a red marble on her second go. Sam gets the remaining 2 marbles.

Mary: “If I picked a red marble on my first go, that means after my second go there will be no red marbles left.”

Sam: “If there is a white and red marble left that means Mary picked a white marble first.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Mary’s second marble is known to be red. Consider both possibilities for her first pick; then examine what remains if one red and one white are left.

steps.explain: Mary’s second pick is red. If her first pick was also red, both red marbles have been taken, leaving two white marbles. So Mary’s answer is correct.
steps.work: First red + second red uses both red marbles.

steps.explain: If the remaining marbles are one red and one white, Mary must have taken one red and one white. Since her second pick was red, the first pick had to be white. Sam’s answer also follows.
steps.work: Remaining R+W means Mary took R+W; second was R, so first was W.

steps.explain: Both Mary and Sam reason correctly.
steps.work: Answer: C.

keyPoints.text: Mary’s second marble is known to be red
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
John, Max and Tom play soccer together. The coach says, since John is injured, then a new player James has to replace him. If James plays then Max will not play.

Who will play on the team now according to the coach?
questions.hint: Replace injured John with James. James playing rules Max out; with three team places, Tom fills the remaining place.

steps.explain: John is injured, so he is replaced by James. John is so not in the playing group.
steps.work: John out → James in.

steps.explain: If James plays, Max does not play. The team has three players, so among the remaining players Tom must fill the third position.
steps.work: James in → Max out; Tom takes the remaining place.

steps.explain: Tom and James play (with the third spot occupied according to the team rule). The listed option D is the intended selection.
steps.work: Answer: D.

keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
John: “In order to get into the Olympics for swimming, you need to train at least 2 hours for 4 times a week.”

Tim: “I train 5 times a week for 2 hours so I am sure I will make the Olympics.”

Which one of the mistakes does Tim make?
options: Training is not enough to guarantee a spot in the Olympics.
You must train for a year to be good enough for the Olympics.
Trying to get on the Olympic team is too difficult.
Only healthy people can get into the Olympics.
questions.hint: The training routine is stated as necessary, not sufficient. Meeting a required condition does not guarantee selection.

steps.explain: John says the training routine is needed to qualify. This means not meeting the routine prevents entry.
steps.work: Required condition: 2 hours × 4 times weekly.

steps.explain: Tim meets or exceeds the stated routine, but the statement never says that this alone guarantees a place. Other swimmers may meet it too, and selection may depend on other rules.
steps.work: A required number of races gives a chance; it does not promise a place.

steps.explain: Tim assumes the condition guarantees success. Option A identifies this error.
steps.work: Answer: A.

keyPoints.text: The training routine is stated as necessary, not sufficient
keyPoints.note: Use only the stated clues; check the conclusion against them.

questions.stem:
In a town, there is a Police station, a school, shops and a hospital. If the school is south of the hospital and south west of the shops. The police station is south of the shops.

What is east of the hospital?
questions.hint: Place the school south of the hospital, then northeast of the school place the shops. The police station is south of the shops.

steps.explain: Option C best supports the claim.
steps.work: Answer: C.

questions.stem:
A slow train departed from Lode at 1:00 pm and arrived at Braxton at 7:00 pm. An express train departed from Lode later and arrived at Braxton at the same time as the slow train. The express train was four times as fast as the slow train. Each train travelled at a constant speed and did not stop along the way.

When did the express train depart from Lode?
questions.hint: Work out how long the slow train took. If a train is four times as fast, it takes a quarter of the time for the same trip.

steps.explain: Find how long the slow train took for the trip.
steps.work: 1:00 pm to 7:00 pm is 6 hours.

steps.explain: Both trains travel the same distance. Going four times as fast means the trip takes one quarter of the time.
steps.work: \(6\text{ hours}\div4=1\frac{1}{2}\text{ hours}\)

steps.explain: The express train arrived at 7:00 pm, so count back 1½ hours to find when it left.
steps.work: \(7\text{:}00\text{ pm}-1\frac{1}{2}\text{ hours}=\)5:30 pm

keyPoints.note: Four times as fast over the same distance means a quarter of the time.

keyPoints.text: arrived at Braxton at the same time
keyPoints.note: Both trains finish at 7:00 pm — work backwards from there.

questions.stem:
A health specialist has suggested that dance lessons should be an important part of school life, and that school children should spend as much time learning to dance as they do playing sport.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the health specialist’s claim?
options: Some children cannot afford equipment to participate in sports.
Some children dream of becoming professional sportspeople.
Dancing has been taught in schools in the past.
questions.hint: The claim is that dance is valuable enough to deserve as much school time as sport. Look for the statement that gives a real benefit of dancing for children.

steps.explain: find the claim: dance should be an important part of school life, with as much time as sport.
Check each statement. A good supporting reason must show that dancing is good for children.
steps.work:
A: Dancing improves mental abilities — a clear benefit of dance. ✔

B: This is about the cost of sport, not a benefit of dance.

C: This is about sport, and if anything supports more sport.

D: Being taught in the past does not show it is worthwhile now.

steps.explain: Only A gives a reason why children should spend time dancing.
steps.work: Answer: A

keyPoints.note: Pick the statement that gives a reason to agree with the claim.

questions.stem:
Alex, Ben and Carlos all keep pets. Alex has snakes, fish, lizards, rats and frogs. Ben keeps cats, frogs and rats. Carlos keeps fish, parrots, rats, grasshoppers and frogs.

Which pets does Alex keep that neither Ben nor Carlos keep?
questions.hint: Go through Alex’s pets one at a time and cross out any that Ben or Carlos also keeps.

steps.explain: Copy Alex’s five pets, then compare each name with Ben’s and Carlos’s lists.
steps.work: Start with: snakes, fish, lizards, rats, frogs.

steps.explain: Cross out any pet kept by either other person: fish appears with Carlos, and rats and frogs appear with both Ben and Carlos.
steps.work: Only snakes and lizards remain.

steps.explain: The pets Alex keeps that neither Ben nor Carlos keep are snakes and lizards.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{snakes and lizards}}\)

keyPoints.note: A pet only counts if NO one else keeps it.

questions.stem:
Next year at school I need to choose four subjects to study.

I have to choose one subject from each of the following lists:

| List 1 | List 2 | List 3 | List 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| arts | English | English | maths |
| geography | maths | geography | science |
| history | design | science | PE |
| PE | health | technologies | technologies |

I know that I want to study English, history and science.

Which one of the following can I **not** choose as my final subject?
questions.hint: History is only in List 1, so List 1 is used up. Which lists are left for English and science, and which list is left over for the final subject?

steps.explain: History appears only in List 1, so history must use List 1.
steps.work: List 1 → history

steps.explain: English is in List 2 or List 3. Science is in List 3 or List 4. Try each way.
steps.work:
English (List 2) + science (List 3) → last from List 4: maths, PE, technologies

English (List 2) + science (List 4) → last from List 3: geography, technologies

English (List 3) + science (List 4) → last from List 2: maths, design, health

steps.explain: Arts is only in List 1, which is already taken by history, so arts can never be the last subject.
steps.work: Answer: arts

keyPoints.note: Each list can be used only once.
Place the subject that appears in only one list first.

questions.stem:
Only those students who attend the meeting at lunchtime today will be allowed to go on the excursion to the museum next week.

**Mia:** “Jayden is going to the meeting today, so he’ll definitely be able to go on the excursion.”

**Tyler:** “Noah’s going to cricket practice at lunchtime today, so he won’t be able to go on the excursion.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: “Only those who attend” means attending is needed — but does attending guarantee a place on the excursion?

steps.explain: The rule says attending the meeting is needed: if you miss it, you cannot go. It does not say everyone who attends will go.
Mia says attending means Jayden will definitely go. Attending is needed, but it does not promise he goes (he may be sick, may not have permission, etc.).
steps.work: Mia ✘

steps.explain: Tyler says Noah is at cricket at lunchtime, so he misses the meeting and so cannot go. That follows from the rule.
steps.work: Tyler ✔

steps.explain: Only Tyler’s reasoning is correct.
steps.work: Answer: Tyler only

keyPoints.note: “Only” means attending is required — it is not a guarantee.

questions.stem: Archie, Beau and Carter are standing in a row. If Archie is to the right of Beau and Carter is to the left of Archie, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: Beau is furthest to the right.
Carter is furthest to the left.
Archie is furthest to the right.
questions.hint: Both Beau and Carter are to the left of Archie. Where does that put Archie?

steps.explain: Archie is to the right of Beau, and Carter is to the left of Archie — so both of the others are to Archie’s left.
The order could be Beau, Carter, Archie or Carter, Beau, Archie. In both, Archie is on the right end.
steps.work:
Beau – Carter – Archie

Carter – Beau – Archie

steps.explain: We cannot tell who is furthest left, but Archie is always furthest to the right.
steps.work: Answer: Archie is furthest to the right.

questions.stem:
A show is to be performed from Wednesday 12th to Saturday 29th of the same month. There will be a performance every evening. On Wednesdays and Saturdays there will be an afternoon performance as well.

How many performances of the show will there be?
questions.hint: Count the evenings from the 12th to the 29th (include both). Then count how many Wednesdays and Saturdays fall in that time.

steps.explain: Count the evening shows. Every day from the 12th to the 29th inclusive has one.
steps.work: 29 − 12 + 1 = 18 evening shows

steps.explain: Find the Wednesdays and Saturdays. The 12th is a Wednesday, so add 7 each time.
steps.work:
Wednesdays: 12, 19, 26 → 3

Saturdays: 15, 22, 29 → 3

6 afternoon shows

steps.explain: Add them together.
steps.work: 18 + 6 = 24

keyPoints.note: Include both the first and last day when counting.

questions.stem:
Darryl and Jim are in the corridor.

**Darryl:** “Jane asked me to fetch her jacket, but I can’t seem to find it here. It’s blue, with a hood, she says.”

**Jim:** “Here’s a blue jacket with a hood – it must be hers!”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Jim has made?
options: Jane might prefer a different jacket.
Darryl might be looking for someone else’s jacket.
There might be more than one blue jacket with a hood.
Even if the jacket is blue, it might not have a hood.
questions.hint: Jim found a jacket that matches the description. Does matching the description prove it is Jane’s?

steps.explain: Jim treats “blue and has a hood” as if it describes the only jacket like that.
steps.work: The description gives two features, but it does not give the owner’s name.

steps.explain: Another jacket could also be blue and have a hood. So those two features alone cannot show that the jacket belongs to Jane.
steps.work: A matching description is not proof that it is Jane’s jacket.

steps.explain: Jim should check whether Jane’s jacket has another identifying feature. There may be more than one blue jacket with a hood.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{There might be more than one blue jacket with a hood.}}\)

keyPoints.note: “Must” is a strong claim — could another jacket fit the description too?

questions.stem:
A police officer says: “Anyone riding a motorcycle should wear a helmet.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the police officer’s claim?
options: Good helmets are cheaper and lighter than they used to be.
You are much less likely to suffer a serious injury if you are wearing a helmet.
People riding horses normally wear some sort of head protection.
Motorcycles can travel a lot faster than bicycles.
questions.hint: Look for the statement that gives the strongest reason WHY a motorcyclist should wear a helmet.

steps.explain: The police officer’s claim is a recommendation: motorcycle riders should wear helmets. Find clue that explains why.
steps.work: A direct safety benefit would support the recommendation.

steps.explain: Wearing a helmet makes serious injury much less likely. This links the action (wearing a helmet) to the benefit (reduced harm).
steps.work: The other statements discuss cost, horse riders or speed without showing helmet protection.

steps.explain: So the strongest support is that a helmet reduces the chance of serious injury.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{You are much less likely to suffer a serious injury if you are wearing a helmet.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Choose the reason that most directly backs up the claim.

questions.stem:
On a normal dice the numbers on each pair of opposite sides add up to 7.

Which one of the following nets shown below is the only one which makes a normal dice when folded?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 503" width="90%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts1-q10.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="503"/></svg>

questions.hint: In a net, two squares with exactly one square between them in a straight line end up opposite each other. Check that each opposite pair adds to 7.

steps.explain: In a straight row of squares, the 1st and 3rd squares fold to be opposite each other (as do the 2nd and 4th).
Check A, B and D, which each have a row or column of four squares.
steps.work:
A: row 1, 3, 4, 6 → 1 opposite 4 (5) ✘

B: column 2, 6, 1, 4 → 6 opposite 4 (10) ✘

D: row 4, 3, 2, 5 → 4 opposite 2 (6) ✘

steps.explain: Check C (the staircase net). With 3 as the base: 5 and 2 become front and back, 6 and 1 become the two sides, and 4 is the top.
steps.work:
5 + 2 = 7, 6 + 1 = 7, 3 + 4 = 7 ✔

Answer: C

keyPoints.note: The pairs must be 1–6, 2–5 and 3–4.

questions.stem:
When Kinta was learning to drive his instructor told him: “To have even a chance of passing your driving test you must have had at least 20 hours of driving practice.”

If Kinta’s instructor is correct, which one of these statements will be true?
options: All the learner drivers who have had 20 hours or more of practice will pass their test.
None of the learner drivers who have had less than 20 hours of practice will pass their test.
Some of the learner drivers who have had less than 20 hours of practice will pass their test.
Only the learner drivers who have had less than 20 hours of practice will pass their test.
questions.hint: 20 hours is needed just to have a chance. What happens to someone with less than 20 hours?

steps.explain: move the instructor’s condition carefully: at least 20 hours is needed to have any chance of passing.
steps.work: \(\text{less than 20 hours}\Rightarrow\text{no chance to pass}\)

steps.explain: The condition does not say that 20 hours guarantees a pass; it only says that below 20 hours passing is impossible.
steps.work: Do not reverse a rule that must be followed first into a promise.

steps.explain: so none of the learners with less than 20 hours can pass.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{None of the learner drivers who have had less than 20 hours of practice will pass.}}\)

keyPoints.note: 20 hours is required just to have a chance — it is not a promise of passing.

questions.stem:
An emu’s egg is dark green, speckled with white spots, and can measure up to 13 cm long. Only an ostrich’s egg is larger.

**Charlotte:** “This egg is dark green, and fairly large, so it must be an emu’s.”

**Oliver:** “But it’s only about 10 cm long, so it can’t be!”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Does being dark green and fairly large prove an egg is an emu’s? And does “up to 13 cm” mean an emu egg cannot be 10 cm?

steps.explain: Charlotte: other eggs might also be dark green and fairly large. The box does not say only emu eggs look like that, so “must be an emu’s” does not follow.
steps.work: Charlotte ✘

steps.explain: Oliver: the box says emu eggs can be up to 13 cm, so a 10 cm emu egg is possible. “It can’t be” does not follow.
steps.work: Oliver ✘

steps.explain: Neither answer follows from the information.
steps.work: Answer: Neither Charlotte nor Oliver

keyPoints.note: “Up to” gives the biggest size — smaller eggs are still possible.

questions.stem:
A piece of string is initially held end-to-end in a straight line. A mark is made in the middle of the string. The string is then folded in half and the new ends again pulled tight. A mark is made in the middle of the strands of folded string. This process is then repeated a third time.

The string is then unfolded and its ends pulled so that it is once again in its initial straight line.

The distance between marks on the string is found to be 4 cm.

How long is the piece of string?
questions.hint: Track the number of equal pieces the marks cut the string into after each step: 1 mark, then more, then more.

steps.explain: First mark: one mark in the middle cuts the string into 2 equal pieces.
steps.work: 2 pieces

steps.explain: Second mark: folded in half, the middle of the strands marks the middle of each half — at ¼ and ¾ of the way along.
steps.work: 4 pieces

steps.explain: Third mark: folded again (4 strands), marking the middle adds marks at ⅛, ⅜, ⅝ and ⅞.
steps.work: 8 pieces

steps.explain: Each piece is 4 cm long.
steps.work: 8 × 4 cm = 32 cm

keyPoints.note: Each time, the number of equal pieces doubles.

questions.stem:
**Mrs Hughes:** “I know that ten of the children in my class are short-sighted, but I only saw seven wearing glasses this morning. So some of the class must have been wearing contact lenses.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mrs Hughes has made?
options: She did not include the children in other classes.
She did not say which children must have been wearing contact lenses.
Some of the short-sighted children might not have been wearing either glasses or contact lenses.
Some of the children who have normal eyesight now might need glasses in the future.
questions.hint: Mrs Hughes thinks the 3 children without glasses must be wearing contact lenses. Is there another possibility?

steps.explain: Subtract the seven children wearing glasses from the ten known to be short-sighted.
steps.work: \(10-7=3\) short-sighted children were not seen wearing glasses.

steps.explain: Mrs Hughes assumes those three must be wearing contacts. But the facts do not rule out other choices, such as wearing no correction or being absent.
steps.work: Not wearing glasses does not prove they wear contact lenses.

steps.explain: Her mistake is treating contacts as the only alternative.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Some short-sighted children might wear neither glasses nor contact lenses.}}\)

keyPoints.text: must have been wearing contact lenses
keyPoints.note: Is wearing contact lenses the ONLY other possibility?

steps.explain: Kamilla is next to Jess, so they sit side by side on one side of the table. Lucy and Max are on the other side.
Lucy is diagonally opposite Jess, so Max must be in the seat directly opposite Jess.
steps.work:
Jess | Kamilla

———————

Max | Lucy

steps.explain: Max faces forwards, so Lucy (same side) also faces forwards — A is false. Which side is the window is not given, so B and C are unknown.
steps.work: Answer: Jess is sitting opposite Max.

Next to = same side of the table.

Check the options for a shape that does not belong.

questions.stem:
An environmentalist says: “Plastic pollution in our oceans is not just a problem for the creatures that live there − it affects us too.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the environmentalist’s claim?
options: Only a small proportion of plastic is recycled.
Many things made of plastic could be made from environmentally friendly alternatives.
Plastics are durable and can last for over 500 years.
Plastics have been found in fish sold in supermarkets.
questions.hint: The claim is that ocean plastic affects PEOPLE as well as sea creatures. Which statement shows a link to people?

steps.explain: The claim says ocean plastic affects people as well as marine creatures. Look for clue that connects ocean plastic with humans.
steps.work: The support must complete the link from ocean pollution to people.

steps.explain: Plastic found in fish sold in supermarkets provides that link: fish live in the ocean, and people buy and eat them.
steps.work: The other options describe recycling, alternatives or durability without showing a direct human effect.

steps.explain: so the supermarket-fish clue best supports the claim.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Plastics have been found in fish sold in supermarkets.}}\)

keyPoints.note: The support must link ocean plastic to people.

questions.stem:
When the fire alarm goes off, it could either be a real fire, or it could be a fire drill. Fire drills can be scheduled for any day of the week, but they always happen at exactly 2 o’clock in the afternoon.

**Yuri:** “If the fire alarm goes off during the morning, you know it must be a real fire!”

**Bindi:** “Even if the fire alarm is not going off, it doesn’t mean that there isn’t a fire.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Yuri: can a drill happen in the morning? Bindi: does the box say the alarm always goes off when there is a fire?

steps.explain: Yuri: an alarm is either a fire or a drill, and drills only happen at 2 pm. A morning alarm cannot be a drill, so it must be a real fire.
steps.work: Yuri ✔

steps.explain: Bindi: the box only says what an alarm could mean. It never says every fire sets off the alarm, so a silent alarm does not prove there is no fire.
steps.work: Bindi ✔

steps.explain: Both pieces of reasoning are correct.
steps.work: Answer: Both Yuri and Bindi

keyPoints.text: it could either be a real fire, or it could be a fire drill
keyPoints.note: Only two possibilities when the alarm sounds.
A drill can never happen at any other time.

questions.stem:
At a school, exams are held at the end of each year. A prize is awarded in each subject to the student who has made the biggest improvement in his/her exam mark since the previous year. In Year 9, the marks achieved by the six students in the mathematics class were as follows:

| Student | Year 9 mark |
|---|---|
| Uma | 84 |
| Finn | 82 |
| Lily | 75 |
| Arlo | 73 |
| Leon | 73 |
| Sophie | 69 |

At the end of Year 10, their marks were as follows:

| Student | Year 10 mark |
|---|---|
| Finn | 88 |
| Lily | 86 |
| Uma | 79 |
| Arlo | 78 |
| Sophie | 78 |
| Leon | 73 |

Which student won the Year 10 prize for mathematics?
questions.hint: The prize is for the biggest improvement, not the highest mark. Find Year 10 mark − Year 9 mark for each student.

steps.explain: The prize is for the largest change, so calculate Year 10 mark minus Year 9 mark for each student.
steps.work: \(\text{change}=\text{Year 10 mark}-\text{Year 9 mark}\)
The largest increase is 11 marks.

steps.explain: Lily has the greatest improvement, even though Finn has the highest Year 10 mark.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Lily}}\)

keyPoints.note: Compare the change in marks, not the marks themselves.

questions.stem:
Arthur, Bilal, Conor, and David play regularly in a sports team. The coach has just told them: “If Arthur does not play tomorrow, then Bilal will play. If Arthur does play, then Conor will play in place of David.”

So, if Bilal does not play tomorrow, which of the other three will be in the team?
questions.hint: If Arthur did not play, Bilal would play. Bilal is not playing — so what must be true about Arthur?

steps.explain: If Arthur did not play, Bilal would play. Since Bilal is not playing, Arthur must be playing.
steps.work: Arthur plays

steps.explain: If Arthur plays, Conor plays instead of David.
steps.work: Conor plays, David does not

steps.explain: So the players are Arthur and Conor.
steps.work: Answer: Arthur and Conor

keyPoints.text: If Arthur does not play tomorrow, then Bilal will play
keyPoints.note: Work backwards: no Bilal means Arthur must play.

questions.stem:
**Faisal:** “To have any chance of passing your piano exam, you will need to practise for at least fifteen minutes, four times a week.”

**Sajid:** “I practise every day for twenty minutes or more, so I’m sure to pass the exam.”

Which one of these sentences shows the mistake Sajid has made?
options: Taking an exam can be a stressful experience.
Learning to play an instrument well requires many years of practice.
Practising alone is not as useful as having a lesson with your teacher.
Doing the minimum practice required does not guarantee success in the exam.
questions.hint: Faisal says the practice gives you a chance. Does Sajid treat it as a guarantee?

steps.explain: Faisal says 15 minutes, four times a week is required just to have a chance of passing.
steps.work: This states a minimum condition, not a guaranteed result.

steps.explain: Sajid practises more than that minimum, but “I do enough to have a chance” does not imply “I am sure to pass”. Other factors can affect the result.
steps.work: The mistake is turning a rule that must be followed first into a promise of success.

steps.explain: The sentence that identifies this error is that meeting the minimum practice does not promise success.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Doing the minimum practice required does not promise success in the exam.}}\)

keyPoints.text: To have any chance of passing
keyPoints.note: The practice is needed — it does not promise a pass.

questions.stem:
Dominoes are to be arranged in a square, on a table, face up, as shown below. New dominoes are placed so that neither of the numbers on them is placed next to the same number on another tile.

The dominoes numbered 1−5 shown above may be used only once.

Which of the two-domino combinations shown below will **not** complete the square?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 581" width="90%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts1-q22.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="581"/></svg>

questions.hint: There are two gaps: one at the top right (lying flat) and one at the bottom right (standing up). Write down which numbers are NOT allowed in each half of each gap.

steps.explain: Read the dominoes as 1: 3|5, 2: 2|4, 3: blank(0)|2, 4: 2|2, 5: 0|5. Find the numbers next to each gap.
steps.work:
Top gap — left half is next to 0 and 5; right half is next to 4.

Bottom gap — top half is next to 2 and 4; bottom half is next to 2.

steps.explain: Check which dominoes can fit the bottom gap (top half not 2 or 4, bottom half not 2).
Only dominoes 1 and 5 fit the bottom gap. Option C uses 3 and 4 — neither can fill the bottom gap.
steps.work:
A: 3 top, 1 bottom ✔

B: 2 top (4|2), 5 bottom ✔

C: 3 and 4 ✘

D: 4 top, 5 bottom ✔

Answer: 3 and 4

questions.stem:
There are six towns (A, B, C, D, E and F) in a region.

Town B is north of Town C and northeast of Town A. Town C is north of Town D and west of Town E. Town F is east of Town E.

Which town is northwest of Town D?
questions.hint: Draw a quick map: put D at the bottom, C above it, B above C. Then place E, F and A.

steps.explain: B is north of C, and C is north of D, so B is directly north of D — not northwest.
B is northeast of A, so A is further west than B — and so further west than D.
E is east of C and F is east of E, so both E and F are further east than D. They cannot be northwest of D.
steps.work: The only town that can be northwest of D is Town A.

keyPoints.note: If B is northeast of A, then A is southwest of B.

questions.stem:
A politician said in a television interview: “The more trade that countries do with each other, the better it is for everyone.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the politician’s claim?
options: It is important for a country to have strong businesses.
Businesses do better when more people are buying their goods or services.
Countries that trade with each other are less likely to go to war against each other.
Different countries can sometimes make particular goods more cheaply than others.
questions.hint: The claim is about trade being good for EVERYONE. Which statement shows a benefit of trade that everyone shares?

steps.explain: The claim: more trade between countries is better for everyone.
A and B are about businesses, not everyone. D explains why trade happens but not that more trade helps everyone.
C: trading countries are less likely to go to war — peace benefits everyone in those countries.
steps.work: Answer: C

keyPoints.note: The support must show a benefit for everyone, not just some people.

questions.stem:
Daniel wants to make as many cupcakes as possible from the ingredients he has at home.

The recipe to make 8 cupcakes needs 100 g of flour, 100 g of sugar, 100 g of butter and 2 eggs.

At home, he has 600 g of flour, 500 g of sugar, 300 g of butter and 5 eggs.

What is the maximum number of cupcakes Daniel can make?
questions.hint: Work out how many cupcakes each ingredient alone would allow. The smallest answer is the limit.

steps.explain: Find how many cupcakes each ingredient could support if it were the only limiting ingredient.
steps.work: Flour: \(600\div100=6\) recipe quantities, so \(6\times8=48\) cupcakes.

steps.explain: Do the same for sugar, butter and eggs. For eggs, each cupcake needs \(2/8=1/4\) egg.
steps.work: Sugar: \(500\div100\times8=40\); butter: \(300\div100\times8=24\); eggs: \(5\div2\times8=20\).

steps.explain: The smallest capacity is 20 cupcakes, so eggs run out first.
steps.work: \(\boxed{20\text{ cupcakes}}\)

keyPoints.note: The ingredient that runs out first decides the answer.

questions.stem:
Whenever Mr Rudd’s favourite team loses, it always puts him in a bad mood. And when Mr Rudd is in a bad mood, he always gives us extra homework.

**Wei:** “We got extra homework last week – Mr Rudd’s team must have lost!”

**Dylan:** “If they lose this week, we’re sure to get extra homework again!”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The chain goes: team loses → bad mood → extra homework. Can you follow the chain backwards?

steps.explain: The box gives a chain: team loses → bad mood → extra homework.
Wei goes backwards: extra homework → team lost. But Mr Rudd could be in a bad mood for another reason, or give homework for another reason.
steps.work: Wei ✘

steps.explain: Dylan goes forwards along the chain: team loses → bad mood → extra homework.
steps.work:
Dylan ✔

Answer: Dylan only

keyPoints.text: Whenever Mr Rudd’s favourite team loses
keyPoints.note: This only tells us what happens AFTER a loss.

questions.stem:
Three balls – each of which is either red or yellow – lie in a straight line on a pool table. Aziz strikes the first ball, which is red. That ball hits the middle ball. The middle ball then hits the last ball, which is yellow.

On the basis of this information, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: Only one of the balls was red.
A red ball hit a yellow ball.
A yellow ball hit a red ball.
Only one of the balls was yellow.
questions.hint: We do not know the colour of the middle ball. Try it both ways and see which statement is true each time.

steps.explain: First ball red, last ball yellow. The middle ball could be red or yellow.
If the middle ball is red: red hits red, then red hits yellow. If the middle ball is yellow: red hits yellow, then yellow hits yellow.
steps.work: Either way, a red ball hits a yellow ball.

steps.explain: A, C and D are only true in one of the two cases.
steps.work: Answer: A red ball hit a yellow ball.

Which one of the following drawings represents the floor plan for this level of the building?

steps.work: There are four separate rooms.

Check each plan for those two rectangular rooms shown side by side.
steps.work:

questions.stem:
A girl is locked in the dungeon of a castle. There are 5 chests in a row in the dungeon, one of which contains a key to escape, but the others contain poisonous snakes. The girl can only open one chest. She has 5 clues to help her make her choice:

The white chest is 2 places away from the chest with the key.
The black chest is at the far right and 2 places away from the white chest.
The red chest is not next to the chest with the key.
The yellow chest is to the left of the white one.
The purple chest is not next to the black or white chests.

Which chest should the girl open to find the key?
questions.hint: Number the places 1 to 5 from the left. Place the black chest first, then the white one, then use the purple clue.

steps.explain: Black is at the far right (place 5). White is 2 places away from black, so white is in place 3.
Purple is not next to black or white, so it cannot be in places 2 or 4. Purple goes in place 1.
steps.work: P _ W _ B

steps.explain: Yellow is to the left of white, so yellow is in place 2 and red is in place 4.
steps.work: P Y W R B

steps.explain: The key is 2 places from white: place 1 (purple) or place 5 (black). Red (place 4) is next to black, so the key is not in black.
steps.work: Key → place 1 → purple

keyPoints.text: The black chest is at the far right
keyPoints.note: Start with the clue that fixes a chest in one exact place.

questions.stem:
Zara’s class wanted to decide what colour to paint their classroom. They decided to have a vote. Students could vote to change it to red, yellow or green. Everyone had to cast two votes, but they could not vote for the same colour twice. The colour would only be changed if everyone voted for the same colour; if this did not happen the room would be left unpainted. Every colour got at least one vote.

Knowing **one** of the following would allow us to know the result of the vote. Which one is it?
options: No student voted for both red and green.
Every student voted for either green or yellow, or both.
Red was the most popular vote.
Only two people voted for green.
questions.hint: Each student votes for exactly two different colours: red + yellow, red + green or yellow + green. Which statement forces one colour onto every ballot?

steps.explain: Each student picks a pair: red+yellow, red+green or yellow+green.
A: if nobody picked red+green, every student picked red+yellow or yellow+green — so every student voted yellow. The room is painted yellow. The result is known.
B, C and D each still allow different results (for example, some red+green and some red+yellow pairs), so they do not tell us the result.
steps.work: Answer: A

keyPoints.text: everyone voted for the same colour
keyPoints.note: The room changes only if ONE colour is on every student’s ballot.

questions.stem:
A community club offers the following sports:

| sport | days available |
|---|---|
| netball | Monday, Thursday |
| boxing | Monday, Friday |
| football | Tuesday, Wednesday |
| swimming | Wednesday, Thursday |
| tennis | Tuesday, Friday |

I want to do a sport on a Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

One of my sports must be football.

Which sport will I not be able to do?
questions.hint: Football can only fit on one of my three days. Which days are left for my other sports?

steps.explain: Football is only on Tuesday or Wednesday, so football must be my Wednesday sport.
steps.work: Wednesday → football

steps.explain: My other two sports must be on Monday and Friday.
steps.work:
Monday: netball or boxing

Friday: boxing or tennis

steps.explain: Swimming is only on Wednesday and Thursday — not Monday or Friday — so I cannot do it.
steps.work: Answer: swimming

keyPoints.text: One of my sports must be football
keyPoints.note: Place football first — it fits only one of your days.

questions.stem:
Four friends want to go to the movies. There are four kinds of movies showing: cartoon, comedy, drama and action. Andrew likes all movies except dramas and action. Rishi and Audrey only like comedies and dramas. Yifan would like to watch any movie so long as it is not a cartoon or an action movie.

Which kind of movie would all four friends like to see?
questions.hint: Cross out each kind of movie that at least one friend does not like.

steps.explain: Andrew does not like drama or action, so cross those out.
steps.work: Left: cartoon, comedy

steps.explain: Rishi, Audrey and Yifan do not like cartoons, so cross that out too.
steps.work: Left: comedy

steps.explain: Everyone likes comedy.
steps.work: Answer: comedy

questions.stem:
The school chess coach has told the team that if they want to do well in chess competitions, they should go running or play tennis every day.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the coach’s claim?
options: Chess is not a physical sport.
Chess players are often good tennis players.
Running builds physical strength and stamina.
questions.hint: The claim is that exercise will help with CHESS. Which statement links exercise to something that matters in chess?

steps.explain: The coach claims exercise improves chess performance. find a skill that matters in chess and an effect exercise can have on it.
steps.work: Concentration is relevant to making and evaluating chess moves.

steps.explain: Regular exercise improves concentration, so it provides a direct link between the suggested activity and better chess performance.
steps.work: The other options do not establish that connection.

steps.explain: Thus the best supporting statement is that regular exercise improves concentration.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Regular exercise improves concentration.}}\)

keyPoints.note: The reason must connect exercise to playing chess better.

questions.stem:
A piece of a construction kit is shown below.

Which one of the following shows a side view of the construction kit piece?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 800" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts2-q4.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="800"/></svg>

questions.hint: The four columns all have different heights. From which side could you see all four, and how would they line up?

steps.explain: Read the four columns’ heights and positions in the 3D picture. A side view collapses depth, so columns in the same line of sight overlap.
steps.work: The correct silhouette must show the visible columns in the right order and keep the taller and shorter heights distinct.

questions.stem:
There are five school teams: Red, Yellow, Green, Orange and Blue. A member of each team competes in the 100 m race. You don’t see the race but a friend tells you the following facts:

Yellow finished third.
Green finished after Red but before Yellow.
Blue beat Orange but finished after Yellow.

Who won the race?
questions.hint: Yellow is 3rd. Which two teams must be in 4th and 5th? Then which two fill 1st and 2nd?

steps.explain: Place Yellow in third place. Green finished after Red but before Yellow, so Red and Green must occupy first and second places in that order.
steps.work: \(\text{Red} < \text{Green} < \text{Yellow}\)

steps.explain: Blue finished after Yellow, and Blue beat Orange. so Blue is fourth and Orange is fifth.
steps.work: \(\text{Yellow} < \text{Blue} < \text{Orange}\)

steps.explain: The full order is Red, Green, Yellow, Blue, Orange. Red is first.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Red}}\)

keyPoints.note: Start with the fixed place, then fill in before and after it.
