questions.stem:
The arrow snake got its name because of its long and thin body and quick-as-lightning movements. It is a popular belief that an arrow snake can leap great distances, and even that its head can pierce the body of its prey.

**Gabriel:** “That can’t be true. I’ve seen arrow snakes plenty of times, and I’ve never seen one jump – let alone pierce its prey!”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Gabriel has made?
options: He has ignored the reason the arrow snake got its name.
He has denied the well-known fact that some snakes can jump.
He has denied something just because he has not witnessed it himself.
He has assumed that no popular belief can be true.
questions.hint: Gabriel says “it can’t be true” because of what he personally has seen. Is that enough to prove it never happens?

steps.explain: Gabriel’s clue is that he has seen arrow snakes many times but has never seen one leap or pierce prey.
steps.work: He is using personal experience as the basis for rejecting the claim.

steps.explain: Not observing an event does not prove it never appears; it may be rare or happen when he is not watching.
steps.work: This is the gap between “I have not seen it” and “it cannot happen”.

steps.explain: His mistake is denying something solely because he has not witnessed it himself.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{He has denied something just because he has not witnessed it himself.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Not having seen something is not proof that it never happens.

questions.stem:
You cannot write good poetry without having interesting life experiences.

**Rose:** “My brother has been on some adventures and met some interesting people, so his poetry is certain to be good.”

**Elsie:** “Well, my great aunt won prizes for her beautiful poetry, so she must have had an interesting life.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The box says interesting experiences are NEEDED for good poetry. Does having them guarantee good poetry? Does good poetry guarantee you had them?

steps.explain: The box says interesting life experiences are needed for good poetry.
Rose: having interesting experiences does not promise good poetry.
steps.work: Rose ✘

steps.explain: Elsie: her great aunt wrote prize-winning (good) poetry, so she must have had interesting life experiences.
steps.work:
Elsie ✔

Answer: Elsie only

keyPoints.text: You cannot write good poetry without
keyPoints.note: “Cannot … without” means it is needed — not that it is enough.

questions.stem:
Izzy is taller than Caitlin; Caitlin is shorter than Melissa. But when they stand on a short flight of three stairs, one on each step, their heads are all level.

Which one of these sentences **cannot** be true?

Melissa is on the middle step.
Caitlin is on the middle step.
Melissa is the tallest of the three girls.
questions.hint: If all their heads are level, the shortest girl must stand on the highest step. Who is the shortest?

steps.explain: If all heads are level, the height of each stair must compensate for the girl’s height: the shortest girl stands on the highest step.
steps.work: Caitlin is shorter than Izzy and Melissa.

steps.explain: so Caitlin must stand on the top step, not the middle step.
steps.work: The statement “Caitlin is on the middle step” cannot be true.

steps.explain: The impossible statement is choice C.
steps.work: \(\boxed{C}\)

questions.stem:
In a game, players take it in turns to draw shapes in a line.

The following rules apply (going from left to right):

● The shape immediately after a square must be a circle.
● The second shape after a triangle must be a square.

Which one of the following sequences is **not** allowed?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 511" width="75%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts2-q10.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="511"/></svg>

questions.hint: Check each triangle: count two shapes along — is it a square? Then check every square is followed by a circle.

steps.explain: Test the two rules separately in each sequence. For every square, inspect the very next shape; for every triangle, count two positions to its right.
steps.work: Rule 1: square → next shape is circle. Rule 2: triangle → second following shape is square.

steps.explain: In sequence D, the triangle is followed by a square and then a circle. The second shape after the triangle is so a circle, not a square.
steps.work: Triangle → square (1st) → circle (2nd), so Rule 2 is broken.

steps.explain: Since one rule is broken, D is the sequence that is not allowed.
steps.work: \(\boxed{D}\)

questions.stem:
Michael says: “I don’t like this book I’ve been told to read. I think students should be free to choose what books they study at school.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Michael’s claim?
options: Students are allowed to choose what they study in some other subjects.
Students often want to read books that have been made into films.
Other students in the class also disliked the book they were told to read.
Students learn more when they enjoy what they read.
questions.hint: The support must show a BENEFIT of letting students choose their own books.

steps.explain: Michael’s answer is that students should choose their own books. The strongest support should show a benefit of choosing a book they enjoy.
steps.work: Look for a statement that links enjoyment with learning.

steps.explain: If students learn more when they enjoy what they read, giving them choice can help them select books they enjoy and so learn more.
steps.work: Choice → more enjoyable reading → more learning.

steps.explain: That direct link supports Michael’s claim. The other statements do not show that choice improves learning.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Students learn more when they enjoy what they read.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Look for a reason that shows why choosing books would be better.

questions.stem:
Four boys are riding their bicycles and have a race to see who can go fastest. Marcel’s bicycle is blue and Ralph’s is purple. The boy on the red bicycle, Barry, finishes the race ahead of Ralph, but behind Will on his green bicycle. Marcel is level with the boy on the purple bicycle.

Which colour bicycle is the winner?
questions.hint: Ralph rides the purple bicycle, so Marcel is level with Ralph. Put Will, Barry and Ralph in order.

steps.explain: Will is ahead of Barry, and Barry is ahead of Ralph.
steps.work: Will – Barry – Ralph

steps.explain: Ralph is on the purple bicycle, so Marcel finishes level with Ralph.
steps.work: Will – Barry – Ralph = Marcel

steps.explain: Will wins, on the green bicycle.
steps.work: Answer: green

keyPoints.text: Marcel is level with the boy on the purple bicycle
keyPoints.note: Who rides purple? That tells you who Marcel tied with.

questions.stem:
The lights in four rooms of my house automatically switch on and off during day and night, when I am away from home, so that it always looks like there is someone at home.

The diagram below shows when lights are on or off for each room. (Each square is one hour.)

What is the longest continuous period of time that more than 1 light is on in my home?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 226" width="90%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts2-q13.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="226"/></svg>

questions.hint: Go along the diagram hour by hour and find the times when only one light (or no light) is on. The longest gap between those is your answer.

steps.explain: Find the times when only one light is on.
steps.work: 4 am – 5 am, 9 am – 11 am, 4 pm – 6 pm, 10 pm – 11 pm

steps.explain: Between 11 pm and 4 am no lights are on.
The longest stretch with more than one light on is from 11 am to 4 pm.
steps.work: 11 am → 4 pm = 5 hours

questions.stem:
Ms Chen’s class will be allowed to watch a movie on the last day of term. There are two classrooms available and two televisions, so the class can be split into two, and watch two different movies, if needed.

Ms Chen does a survey of the class, asking them what they would like to watch. She notices that most of the girls in the class want to watch Harry Potter, and most of the boys want to watch Star Wars.

**Ms Chen:** “There are the same number of boys and girls in the class. So I should put the girls in one classroom and show them Harry Potter, and put the boys in the other classroom to watch Star Wars.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Ms Chen has made?
options: Harry Potter and Star Wars may be different lengths.
There may be some boys who would prefer Harry Potter, and some girls who would prefer Star Wars.
Some of the boys might only have chosen Star Wars because their friends did.
Different numbers of boys and girls might miss the last day of term.
questions.hint: “Most” of the girls want Harry Potter — not all of them. Who would be unhappy with Ms Chen’s plan?

steps.explain: “Most girls” preferring Harry Potter and “most boys” preferring Star Wars describe majorities, not unanimous preferences.
steps.work: A majority can still leave some people in the minority.

steps.explain: For example, with 10 boys, 6 may prefer Star Wars and 4 Harry Potter; with 10 girls, 6 may prefer Harry Potter and 4 Star Wars.
steps.work: Both statements about the majorities remain true, while some boys and girls prefer the other film.

steps.explain: So Ms Chen should not assume that every boy and every girl wants a different film.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Some boys may prefer Harry Potter and some girls may prefer Star Wars.}}\)

keyPoints.note: “Most” is not “all” — some girls may want the other film.

meta.source: NSW Opportunity Class Placement Test · Thinking Skills

questions.stem:
A secret agent uses a code to send messages. It involves shifting each letter of the alphabet forwards or backwards two letters, so for example the letter ‘C’ could be represented by either ‘A’ or ‘E’. There are no spaces between words in this code.

You receive the following message from the secret agent:

YFCPBKFVFGWCTPKXG?

Which of the following could be the intended message?
questions.hint: Each code letter stands for the letter 2 before it or 2 after it. Check the first few letters of each option — Y could be W or A, F could be D or H …

steps.explain: Each code letter could stand for the letter two before it or two after it.
steps.work: Y → W or A, F → D or H, C → A or E, P → N or R, B → Z or D, K → I or M …

steps.explain: Try the options. The first four letters YFCP can be W, H, E, N — “WHEN”. Keep going: BKF → D, I, D; VFGW → T, H, E, Y …
steps.work:
YFCP BKF VFGW CTPKXG

WHEN DID THEY ARRIVE

steps.explain: Every letter fits.
steps.work: Answer: WHEN DID THEY ARRIVE?

keyPoints.note: Each code letter has exactly two possible meanings.

questions.stem:
I have recently tiled the wall of my bathroom using a set of identical tiles. I have laid the tiles so that the black sections on one tile do not join along the edge of the black sections on another tile.

I have one tile left to put in place.

Which way up will the last tile be placed?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 752" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts2-q16.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="752"/></svg>

questions.hint: Look at the tiles around the gap. Wherever a neighbour has black along the edge of the gap, the new tile must be white there.

steps.explain: At the empty position, inspect each shared edge. A black region on a neighbouring tile must meet a non-black region on the missing tile.
steps.work: The condition is checked edge by edge; touching at a corner is not an edge connection.

steps.explain: Rotate each option mentally so its edges line up with the gap. cross off a option whenever black meets black on any one of the four shared edges.
steps.work: Three ways of turning the options create at least one forbidden black-to-black join.

steps.explain: D is the only direction whose black sections avoid matching black sections on every next to tile.
steps.work: \(\boxed{D}\)

keyPoints.text: do not join along the edge
keyPoints.note: Black can only sit next to white across a tile edge.

questions.stem:
Patricia’s friend Aditya recently won a gold medal for the 200 metre freestyle. He trains for six hours per day, six days a week.

**Patricia:** “I’m going to start a new programme, swimming for six hours a day, six days a week. Then I’ll get a gold medal too!”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Patricia has made?
options: Some gold medallists may train far less than Aditya.
Patricia’s training programme alone may not guarantee her a gold medal.
The training programme may prevent Patricia from doing other things she likes.
Patricia may not be able to afford the cost of the training programme.
questions.hint: Patricia thinks doing the same training will definitely give the same result. Could other things matter?

steps.explain: Patricia copies Aditya’s training schedule and predicts she will also win gold. That prediction assumes the schedule alone causes the medal.
steps.work: Training for 6 hours × 6 days = 36 hours each week.

steps.explain: Even if this schedule helped Aditya, it does not promise the same result for Patricia: medals depend on ability, competition, coaching and other factors too.
steps.work: Same training programme does not mean they will get the same result.

steps.explain: The flaw is the mistake is thinking that following the programme guarantees Patricia will win a gold medal.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Patricia’s training programme alone may not promise her a gold medal.}}\)

keyPoints.text: Then I’ll get a gold medal too
keyPoints.note: Is the same training enough to guarantee the same result?

questions.stem:
An actor came to visit a local school. She gave the principal this advice: “It is important for children to be given the chance to perform in a school play or concert.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the actor’s claim?
options: The actor has given similar advice at many other schools.
Children spend a lot of time playing sports and other games.
Many people enjoy watching plays or listening to concerts.
Performing in front of other people helps to build confidence.
questions.hint: Look for a benefit to the CHILDREN who perform.

steps.explain: The actor recommends giving children opportunities to perform. A supporting reason should state a positive outcome children gain from performing.
steps.work: Connect performing to a benefit for children.

steps.explain: Performing in front of other people helps build confidence, which is a benefit of giving children a chance to take part.
steps.work: Recommendation → opportunity to perform → confidence.

steps.explain: This directly supports the actor’s claim. The other statements do not explain why the opportunity is important for children.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Performing in front of other people helps to build confidence.}}\)

questions.stem:
A dentists’ surgery opens at 8:00 am and closes at 5:00 pm each day. Each appointment is 20 minutes and every dentist has a 60-minute lunch break but no other breaks.

Three dentists work in the surgery.

What is the maximum number of appointments that can be made in the surgery in a day?
questions.hint: Find how many hours one dentist actually works, then how many 20-minute appointments fit in each hour.

steps.explain: The surgery is open from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm.
steps.work: 9 hours

steps.explain: Each dentist has a 1-hour lunch break.
steps.work: 9 − 1 = 8 working hours

steps.explain: Three 20-minute appointments fit in each hour.
steps.work: 8 × 3 = 24 appointments per dentist

steps.explain: There are three dentists.
steps.work: 24 × 3 = 72

keyPoints.note: Take the lunch break away from the working time.

questions.stem:
There are six lunch boxes lined up on a shelf and each is a different colour: blue, green, orange, purple, red and yellow. There is one box between the green box and the orange box. The purple box’s only neighbour is blue, and there are three boxes between the red box and the blue box.

What colour lunch boxes are at each end of the line?
questions.hint: A box with only one neighbour must be at an end. Start there.

steps.explain: Purple has only one neighbour, so purple is at one end, with blue next to it.
steps.work: Purple – Blue – _ – _ – _ – _

steps.explain: There are three boxes between red and blue, so red is in the 6th place — the other end.
steps.work: Purple – Blue – _ – _ – _ – Red

steps.explain: The ends are purple and red.
steps.work: Answer: red and purple

keyPoints.text: The purple box’s only neighbour is blue
keyPoints.note: Only one neighbour means it is at the end of the line.

questions.stem:
The school principal, Ms Flint, is looking at the school records for last term to see which class has the best-behaved students.

She notices that students in Class 1, who are taught by Mr Avery, were given 47 lunchtime detentions in total last term. Students in Class 2, who are taught by Mr Bailey, were only given 18.

**Ms Flint:** “That’s interesting – it clearly shows that students in Class 2 are much better behaved than students in Class 1.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Ms Flint has made?
options: Good behaviour may not be the most important thing for students in Class 1 to focus on.
There may be good reasons why students in Class 1 have problems with behaviour.
Students in Class 1 might do just as well as students in Class 2 in their examinations.
Students in Class 1 may be more likely to be given detention when they are badly behaved than students in Class 2.
questions.hint: Ms Flint uses the number of detentions to measure behaviour. Is that a fair measure if the two teachers are different?

steps.explain: Ms Flint compares total detentions: 47 in Class 1 and 18 in Class 2. A fair comparison also needs the number of students and how detentions are assigned.
steps.work: Totals alone are not rates per student.

steps.explain: The teacher is comparing the two classes fairly. But one class might get detention more often for the same behaviour. So the bigger detention total alone does not show that class behaved worse.
steps.work: A different detention threshold is a possible alternative explanation.

steps.explain: Thus the total does not establish which class behaves better; the stated alternative undermines the comparison.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Class 1 students may be more likely to be given detention for the same misbehaviour.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Ask whether the detention count is a fair way to compare the two classes.

Only C shows this.

questions.stem:
The Kingdom of Chromatica has five traditional festivals which are held every year. During these festivals, all the citizens of Chromatica wear the same colour. The colours are shown in this table:

| Festival | Colour |
|---|---|
| Chromatican Independence Day | Red |
| The King’s Official Birthday | Yellow |
| Women’s Day | Blue |
| The Ice Carnival | Blue |
| Chromatican New Year | Red |

Shiro is visiting Chromatica and sees that everyone is wearing the same colour, so he knows they are celebrating a festival, but he doesn’t know which one. Even after checking the table above, he’s still not sure.

What can we say about the colour that Shiro saw everyone wearing?
options: It was either red or yellow.
It was either yellow or blue.
It was either blue or red.
It could have been red, yellow or blue.
questions.hint: Which colour belongs to only one festival? If Shiro had seen that colour, would he still be unsure?

steps.explain: The table assigns colours to the five festivals. Red is used for two festivals, blue for two festivals, and yellow for only one.
steps.work: Red → Independence Day or New Year; blue → Women’s Day or Ice Carnival; yellow → King’s Birthday only.

steps.explain: Shiro knows a festival is being celebrated but cannot work out which festival. If everyone wore yellow, the table would find the King’s Birthday, so he would know. Yellow is so impossible.
steps.work: Yellow → exactly 1 festival, so it would find the festival.

steps.explain: Red and blue each leave two possible festivals, so either colour fits his uncertainty.
steps.work: Red → 2 choices; blue → 2 choices. so \(\boxed{\text{blue or red}}\).

keyPoints.note: The colour must match more than one festival.

questions.stem:
Darren has a deck of fifteen special playing cards:
Five red cards, numbered 1−5
Five blue cards, numbered 1−5
Five yellow cards, numbered 1−5
He shuffles the deck randomly, and then draws a number of cards from the top.

**Lily:** “To be certain of having all three colours, he has to draw eleven cards.”

**Tom:** “To be certain of having three different numbers, he needs to draw seven cards.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Think about the unluckiest draw. How many cards could you draw and still be missing a colour? Still have only two numbers?

steps.explain: Lily: with 10 cards you could get all 5 of two colours and none of the third. With 11 cards, only 4 are left, so at least one card of every colour has been drawn.
steps.work: Lily ✔

steps.explain: Tom: each number appears 3 times (once per colour). With 6 cards you could get all three cards of two numbers. With 7 cards, a third number must appear.
steps.work: Tom ✔

steps.explain: Both are correct.
steps.work: Answer: Both Lily and Tom

keyPoints.note: Imagine the unluckiest possible draw.

questions.stem:
In a competition, 10 students were allowed two attempts at running 200 metres as fast as possible. The fastest time in the two attempts was counted as their ‘result’. The attempts for the 10 students are shown in the table.

| student number | attempt 1 (in seconds) | attempt 2 (in seconds) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25.6 | 24.1 |
| 2 | 25.0 | 26.4 |
| 3 | 27.4 | 25.8 |
| 4 | 25.3 | 24.9 |
| 5 | 24.8 | 26.3 |
| 6 | 26.1 | 27.2 |
| 7 | 26.4 | 28.1 |
| 8 | 27.7 | 26.9 |
| 9 | 25.8 | 24.5 |
| 10 | 25.2 | 25.6 |

Which student came 3rd in the competition?
questions.hint: For each student, keep only the faster (smaller) time. Then put the results in order from fastest.

steps.explain: Each student’s result is their faster time.
Order the fastest results.
steps.work:
1st: student 1 (24.1)

2nd: student 9 (24.5)

3rd: student 5 (24.8)

steps.explain: Student 5 came 3rd.
steps.work: Answer: student 5

keyPoints.text: The fastest time in the two attempts
keyPoints.note: Use the smaller time for each student.

questions.stem:
Dylan was keen to get fitter and stronger so he took up running. His friend Angela said to him: “If you want to strengthen your whole body, you should take up swimming as well as running.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Angela’s claim?
options: Swimming uses more of the body’s muscles than running.
Swimming can be quite relaxing and help reduce stress.
Being able to swim well is good for your own personal safety.
People who run too much can sometimes damage their knees or ankles.
questions.hint: Angela’s claim is about strengthening the WHOLE body. Which statement shows swimming does that better than running alone?

steps.explain: Angela claims swimming plus running strengthens the whole body. The best support should compare the muscles used in swimming with running.
steps.work: Find clue about muscle coverage.

steps.explain: If swimming uses more of the body’s muscles than running, adding swimming exercises areas running may not target as much.
steps.work: Running + a wider range of muscles used in swimming → more whole-body strengthening.

steps.explain: That clue supports the recommendation directly.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Swimming uses more of the body’s muscles than running.}}\)

keyPoints.note: The support must be about strength across the whole body.

questions.stem:
The majority of the Bulbo trees in the world are in the Manu Forest in Peru.

**Ravi:** “So if you were to randomly choose a tree from all the Bulbo trees in the world, it would probably be in Peru.”

**Luca:** “And if you were to randomly choose a tree in the Manu Forest, it would probably be a Bulbo tree.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Most Bulbo trees are in the Manu Forest. Does that mean most trees in the Manu Forest are Bulbo trees?

steps.explain: Ravi starts by choosing a Bulbo tree. Since most Bulbo trees are in Manu Forest, a randomly chosen Bulbo is likely to be there. This is the same population in the given clue.
steps.work: “Most Bulbo trees are in Manu” means \(P(\text{Manu}\mid\text{Bulbo})>1/2\).

steps.explain: Luca reverses the groups: he starts with a randomly chosen Manu tree and concludes it is likely to be a Bulbo. The given clue gives no count of all Manu trees or of Bulbos within Manu.
steps.work: Knowing the chance of Manu given Bulbo is different from knowing the chance of Bulbo given Manu.

steps.explain: Ravi’s answer follows from the information; Luca’s reversed answer does not.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Ravi only}}\)

keyPoints.text: The majority of the Bulbo trees
keyPoints.note: This tells us about Bulbo trees — not about all the trees in the forest.

A pyramid of 9 layers is shown below.

Which **one** of the following arrangements shows all 9 layers of the pyramid?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 654" width="85%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/ts2-q28.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="800" height="654"/></svg>

questions.hint: Count the blocks in each layer of the pyramid (1, 3, 5, …). Each arrangement must use each of those widths exactly once.

steps.explain: The pyramid’s layers have widths 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 and 17 blocks.
Each correct order must use every one of those widths exactly once — no width repeated and none missing. Compare the rows in each option; look for widths that appear twice.
Only A has exactly the right set of widths.
steps.work: Answer: A

questions.stem:
The Crown Jewels of the Kingdom of Animalia have been stolen!

The horse says that the rabbit stole the jewels. The rabbit says that the tiger did it. The owl claims to be innocent. The tiger says that the rabbit is lying.

If only one of them is telling the truth, who stole the Crown Jewels?
questions.hint: The rabbit and the tiger contradict each other, so exactly one of them is telling the truth. What does that mean for everyone else?

steps.explain: The tiger says the rabbit is lying. Either the rabbit is truthful or the tiger is — exactly one of them.
Only one animal tells the truth, so the horse and the owl must both be lying.
The owl says it is innocent — that is a lie, so the owl stole the jewels.
steps.work: Answer: the owl

keyPoints.text: only one of them is telling the truth
keyPoints.note: Look for two statements that cannot both be true or both be false.

questions.stem:
There are three ways to cross the Korra River:
Archer Bridge is only open on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
Djorlom Bridge is only open on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.
The Korra Ferry is used on Sundays. It is also sometimes used on other days, but only if the bridge that would normally be open is damaged.

**Robbie:** “If the ferry operates for two days in a row, it must mean that both the bridges are damaged.”

**Declan:** “If you don’t use the Archer Bridge, you’ll never be able to cross the river on Friday.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Robbie: think about Sunday followed by Monday. Declan: what happens on a Friday when Archer Bridge is damaged?

steps.explain: Robbie: the ferry runs every Sunday anyway. If it also runs on Monday (Archer damaged), that is two days in a row with Djorlom Bridge fine.
steps.work: Robbie ✘

steps.explain: Declan: if Archer Bridge is damaged on a Friday, the ferry runs, so you can still cross without Archer Bridge.
steps.work: Declan ✘

steps.explain: Neither is correct.
steps.work: Answer: Neither Robbie nor Declan

keyPoints.text: The Korra Ferry is used on Sundays
keyPoints.note: The ferry runs every Sunday whether or not a bridge is damaged.

questions.stem:
Inge and Finn first met on a Tuesday. They met again 8 days later. They then met for the third time 4 days later.

On which day did Inge and Finn meet for the third time?
questions.hint: Add up the days from the first meeting. How does that compare with a whole number of weeks?

steps.explain: Start at Tuesday. The second meeting is 8 days later: 7 days returns to Tuesday, then 1 more day gives Wednesday.
steps.work: \(8=7+1\), so Tuesday + 8 days = Wednesday.

steps.explain: The third meeting is 4 days after Wednesday. Count forward: Thursday (1), Friday (2), Saturday (3), Sunday (4).
steps.work: Wednesday + 4 days = Sunday.

steps.explain: So their third meeting was on Sunday.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Sunday}}\)

keyPoints.note: Add the gaps to find the total days from the first meeting.

questions.stem:
After school, Cecilia likes to visit her favourite juice stand to buy a drink. The stand sells four types of juice, which are available on different days. Cecilia does not like apple or orange juice, but she will visit the stand as long as she can buy a drink that she likes.

| juice | days available |
|---|---|
| lemon | Monday and Wednesday |
| orange | Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday |
| apple | Thursday and Friday |
| grape | Monday, Tuesday and Friday |

On which day will Cecilia not visit the juice stand?
questions.hint: Cecilia only buys lemon or grape. Which days have at least one of those?

steps.explain: Cecilia avoids apple and orange, so she will visit only on days when lemon or grape juice is available.
steps.work: Lemon: Monday, Wednesday. Grape: Monday, Tuesday, Friday.

steps.explain: Combine those days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday are visit days. Thursday has only orange and apple, both disliked.
steps.work: Thursday: orange + apple; neither is acceptable.

steps.explain: so she will not visit on Thursday.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Thursday}}\)

keyPoints.text: does not like apple or orange juice
keyPoints.note: Only lemon and grape days count.

questions.stem:
Nick wants to learn to speak the Wiradjuri language, but he thinks it will take him a long time. Medika suggests a solution: “You should spend some time in Wagga Wagga. There are plenty of people there who can speak Wiradjuri.”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Medika’s claim?
options: Nick can travel to Wagga Wagga fairly easily.
Learning a language always takes hard work and concentration.
Medika has learned to speak three different languages.
Languages are easier to learn if you practise speaking them with other people.
questions.hint: Medika’s reason is that many people in Wagga Wagga speak Wiradjuri. Why would that help Nick learn faster?

steps.explain: Medika suggests going to Wagga Wagga because Wiradjuri speakers live there. To support that suggestion, the clue must explain how being there helps Nick learn.
steps.work: Access to speakers only helps if practising with people improves language learning.

steps.explain: If languages are easier to learn by practising with other speakers, spending time where many Wiradjuri speakers live gives Nick that practice.
steps.work: Wagga Wagga → opportunities to speak Wiradjuri → easier learning.

steps.explain: That statement provides the needed link; Medika’s own language skills do not prove the advice works for Nick.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Languages are easier to learn if you practise speaking them with other people.}}\)

questions.stem:
Simon is watching a news report which claims that nearly a third of Australians go swimming regularly.

**Simon:** “That can’t be true – I almost never go swimming, and neither do any of my friends.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Simon has made a mistake?
options: Simon may prefer other forms of exercise, such as running.
Swimming may have become more popular in recent years.
The news report that Simon is watching may be incorrect.
Simon may live in an area where there are few opportunities to go swimming.
questions.hint: Simon uses himself and his friends to judge all of Australia. Could his group be different from the rest of the country?

steps.explain: Simon’s clue is only that he and his friends rarely swim. This is a small group and may not represent all Australians.
steps.work: A personal sample can differ from the national population.

steps.explain: If Simon lives where swimming opportunities are limited, his local experience could be unusual even if many Australians elsewhere swim regularly.
steps.work: Local availability is a possible reason his observations are unrepresentative.

steps.explain: So he cannot reject a national statistic from his own circle alone.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Simon may live in an area where there are few opportunities to go swimming.}}\)

keyPoints.text: neither do any of my friends
keyPoints.note: A small group may not represent the whole country.

questions.stem:
Staff at a wildlife hospital are building a structure to house sugar gliders. The structure has three levels: one for food, one for a water bowl, and one for a hollow log that a sugar glider can use as a nest.

If the food is on a lower level than the water bowl and the log is higher than the food, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: The middle level has the log.
The lowest level has the food.
The highest level has the water.
The middle level has the food.
questions.hint: The food is lower than both of the other things. Where must it be?

steps.explain: Label the three levels from lowest to highest. The food must be lower than the water bowl, and the log must also be higher than the food.
steps.work: Food < Water and Food < Log.

steps.explain: Food cannot be on the middle level: then only the top would be above it, but both the bowl and the log must be above the food. So food must be on the bottom.
steps.work: The only remaining position for food is the lowest level.

steps.explain: Thus the statement that must be true is that the lowest level has the food. Water and log can occupy the middle and top levels in either order.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{The lowest level has the food.}}\)

questions.stem:
John is collecting a set of toy robots based on his favourite television program. The robots come in different colours and John still needs the red and green robots to complete his set. The local shop has an offer where they will sell any of the following packs of three robots for $10.

| pack | robot | robot | robot |
|---|---|---|---|
| pack 1 | red | blue | yellow |
| pack 2 | red | yellow | pink |
| pack 3 | green | pink | purple |
| pack 4 | blue | orange | pink |

John has a friend who has a spare green robot and will swap it for a pink robot.

Which pack should John buy to be able to complete his set?
questions.hint: John needs a red robot from the pack, and a pink robot to swap for the green one.

steps.explain: John needs a red robot and a green robot. His friend offers to swap a green robot for a pink robot, so John can obtain green by trading away a pink one.
steps.work: Needed: red + green. Trade: pink → green.

steps.explain: Pack 2 contains red and pink. John keeps the red robot and swaps the pink robot for green.
steps.work: Pack 2: red + yellow + pink; after trade: red + yellow + green.

steps.explain: so pack 2 alone supplies the two colours needed to complete his set.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{pack 2}}\)

keyPoints.text: will swap it for a pink robot
keyPoints.note: John needs a pink robot to get the green one.

questions.stem:
A scientist, Melanie, is trying to figure out why the number of fish in a nearby lake has decreased over the past year.

**Melanie:** “The lake has become more polluted over the past year as well, so it must be the pollution that is causing many fish in the lake to die.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Melanie has made a mistake?
options: The number of fish in other lakes might not have decreased over the past year.
Pollution may also cause health problems in humans.
The number of plants in the lake might not have decreased over the past year.
More people may have fished from the lake over the past year.
questions.hint: Two things happened at the same time. Does that prove one caused the other? Is there another reason the fish could have decreased?

steps.explain: Melanie observes two changes in the same year: pollution increased and fish numbers decreased. This timing alone does not prove one caused the other.
steps.work: Correlation does not by itself establish cause.

steps.explain: More people fishing is another possible cause of fewer fish. If fishing increased, it could explain the decline even while pollution also rose.
steps.work: Alternative cause: increased fishing.

steps.explain: So the clue that more people may have fished from the lake identifies the flaw in Melanie’s answer.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{More people may have fished from the lake over the past year.}}\)

keyPoints.note: “Must” — could something else explain fewer fish?

One of the plants bloomed a day before any of the others. Which one was it?
questions.hint: The plant in the school hall is the wax plant. Put the bromeliad, wax plant and guppy plant in order, then add the geranium.

steps.work: bromeliad → wax plant → guppy plant

steps.explain: The geranium bloomed on the same day as the wax plant.
steps.work: bromeliad → wax plant + geranium → guppy plant

steps.explain: The bromeliad bloomed first.
steps.work: Answer: the bromeliad

questions.stem:
A gardener is giving advice about taking care of plants. He says: “Some people think talking to plants is strange, but it’s actually a really good idea. After all, you’re more likely to remember to water them if you treat them like friends!”

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the gardener’s claim?
options: People often notice details about a plant’s health when they are talking to it.
Some people believe that plants can understand what people say to them.
Talking to plants won’t help people avoid overwatering them.
Talking to plants is a very old tradition.
questions.hint: Look for a real BENEFIT of talking to plants.

steps.explain: The gardener says treating plants like friends makes people more likely to remember to water them. Strong support should connect talking to the plant with a practical benefit in caring for it.
steps.work: find the claim: talking to plants helps people care for them.

steps.explain: Talking to a plant may help someone notice when it looks unhealthy and needs care. That is a benefit. The other choices do not explain a benefit of talking to plants.
steps.work: Talking → noticing plant health → better care.

steps.explain: so option A is the best support among the choices because it gives a real plant-care benefit.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{People often notice details about a plant’s health when they are talking to it.}}\)

questions.stem:
Four friends are in a car together. There are two seats in the front and two in the back.

Katelyn is either driving or sitting beside Talia. Talia is sitting behind the driver. Jimmy is not sitting in the back, and he is not sitting beside Andrea.

Who is driving the car?
questions.hint: Talia is in the back. Try Katelyn NOT driving — where would everyone sit, and does it break a rule?

steps.explain: Talia sits behind the driver, so Talia is in the back. Jimmy is in the front.
Suppose Katelyn is not driving. Then she must sit beside Talia in the back, leaving Jimmy and Andrea side by side in the front — but Jimmy is not beside Andrea.
steps.work: That is impossible.

steps.explain: So Katelyn must be driving.
steps.work: Answer: Katelyn

keyPoints.text: Katelyn is either driving or sitting beside Talia
keyPoints.note: Test each possibility and see which one breaks a rule.

questions.stem:
In a word game, players make words out of letters. Each letter has a value that is a whole number that is at least 1. The score for the word is the total of the values of all the letters in the word.

For example: The word TOO scores 4.
The word TWO scores 6.
The word HOOT also scores 6.
The word THAT scores 7.

What is the score for the word THAW?
questions.hint: Compare TOO and HOOT — they differ by one letter. Then use the fact that every letter is worth at least 1.

steps.explain: HOOT = TOO + H, so H = 6 − 4 = 2.
TOO = T + O + O = 4. Every letter is at least 1, so O cannot be 2 or more (that would make TOO at least 5). So O = 1 and T = 2.
THAW = T + H + A + W.
steps.work: 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 8

keyPoints.note: This rule helps pin down the value of O.

questions.stem:
Iluka wants to buy a sandwich. He is currently waiting in the queue at Sliced Bread Sangers.

**Iluka:** “Sliced Bread Sangers always take 15 minutes to make my favourite sandwich. But the Loafing Around bakery down the road always take 10 minutes. It takes less than five minutes to walk there – so I should head to Loafing Around and then I’ll get my sandwich sooner.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Iluka has made a mistake?
options: Sliced Bread Sangers may make better sandwiches than Loafing Around.
Sliced Bread Sangers may have a wider range of sandwiches than Loafing Around.
The sandwiches at Loafing Around may be more expensive than those at Sliced Bread Sangers.
The queue at Loafing Around may be longer than the one at Sliced Bread Sangers.
questions.hint: Iluka counted making time and walking time. What other waiting has he forgotten?

steps.explain: Iluka compares sandwich-making times, but he is already waiting in a queue at the first bakery. The total waiting time includes both the queue and preparation.
steps.work: Total time = walk + queue wait + sandwich preparation.

steps.explain: The walk takes less than 5 minutes and getting ready takes 10 minutes, so those parts take under 15 minutes. A long queue can still make the whole trip too long.
steps.work: Loafing Around total: <5 + queue + 10 minutes.

steps.explain: The queue length is the missing factor that could reverse his answer.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{The queue at Loafing Around may be longer than the one at Sliced Bread Sangers.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Have all the waiting times been counted?

steps.work: Robyn ✔

steps.explain: Both are correct.
steps.work: Answer: both Maliyan and Robyn

questions.stem:
To win a soccer match you have to score more goals than the other team.

Grant Valley High School plays soccer in a competition with a group of other schools. They are awarded points for winning and drawing matches but no points for losing. The team with the most points at the end of the season comes top of the competition.

At the end of the season, Grant Valley High School had sadly failed to score a single goal.

Which one of the following must also be true?
options: Grant Valley High School came bottom of the competition.
Grant Valley High School lost more matches than any of the other teams.
Grant Valley High School won fewer matches than any of the other teams.
Grant Valley High School failed to win any matches.
questions.hint: Could a team that scored no goals ever win a match?

steps.explain: To win a match, a team must score more goals than its opponent. Grant Valley scored zero goals in the whole season.
steps.work: Goals scored across all games = 0.

steps.explain: If Grant Valley scores 0, the other team scores at least 0 too. If they also score 0, the game is a draw. If they score more than 0, Grant Valley loses. So Grant Valley cannot win.
steps.work: Against an opponent: 0 ≤ opponent goals, so never 0 > opponent goals.

steps.explain: so Grant Valley could draw or lose, but it could not win any match.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Grant Valley High School failed to win any matches.}}\)

keyPoints.text: failed to score a single goal
keyPoints.note: No goals means no wins — but draws are still possible.

questions.stem:
The students in Tahnee’s class must choose either Jacob or Nicole to represent their class in the school chess competition.

Jacob won 3 of his last 14 games in the chess club.
Nicole won 11 of her last 12 games in the chess club.

**Tahnee:** “Nicole has won a higher fraction of her recent games at the club, so she must be the better player. She should represent our class.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Tahnee has made a mistake?
options: There may be another player in the class who is better than Nicole.
Jacob might have played against better opponents in his games.
Nicole has not played as many games as Jacob.
They may have played lots of other games outside of the chess club.
questions.hint: Tahnee only compares how many games each player won. What about who they were playing against?

steps.explain: Compare the fractions won, not just the number of wins. Jacob won \(3/14\); Nicole won \(11/12\), which is much larger.
Those fractions describe results against the opponents each player faced. If Jacob played much stronger opponents, his lower win fraction may not mean he is the weaker player.
steps.work: The comparison lacks information about opponent strength.

steps.explain: So Tahnee’s mistake is treating different win records as a fair direct measure without checking the difficulty of the games.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Jacob might have played against better opponents in his games.}}\)

keyPoints.text: she must be the better player
keyPoints.note: Is the win fraction a fair comparison?

questions.stem:
In a school for young magicians, the weekly timetable is the following:

| | Monday | Tuesday | Wednesday | Thursday |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9:00–10:00 | stars & sky | potions & poisons | spells | herbs |
| 10:00–11:00 | farsight | herbs | broom flight | stars & sky |
| 11:00–12:00 | spells | charms | farsight | broom flight |

The young magicians need their magic wand for three classes: spells, charms, and herbs. There are no classes on Fridays.

This week, the classes on Wednesday are cancelled due to a competition.

For how many classes do the young magicians need their wands this week?
questions.hint: Count the spells, charms and herbs classes for each day, but skip Wednesday.

steps.explain: Wands are needed for spells, charms and herbs. Remove Wednesday classes first: spells and broom flight are cancelled; farsight needs no wand.
steps.work: Cancelled Wednesday spells means that class no longer requires the wand.

steps.explain: Count the remaining wand-using classes in the timetable: Monday spells (1), Tuesday herbs (2) and charms (3), Thursday herbs (4). Wednesday charms? Wednesday has no charms.
steps.work: Monday: spells; Tuesday: herbs, charms; Thursday: herbs. Total \(1+2+1=4\).

steps.explain: So the students need their wands for four classes this week.

keyPoints.text: the classes on Wednesday are cancelled
keyPoints.note: Do not count Wednesday’s classes.

If Chris makes the sandwich following Sally’s rules, which ingredient will be on top?

The lettuce cannot touch the mayonnaise, so the cheese goes on top and the lettuce at the bottom.

cheese / mayonnaise / chicken / lettuce

Handling puppies and kittens often helps them to be less afraid of people.
Many people help wild animals by putting out food and water for them.
Handling puppies and kittens is something many people enjoy doing.

steps.work: Check which statement connects handling to a useful outcome.

steps.explain: If regular handling helps puppies and kittens become less afraid of people, then handling supports their social development.
steps.work: Careful handling → less fear of people.

questions.stem:
Peter needs to return a book to Fiona, but he will not see her today. However, he knows that the following meetings will happen:

Sam will meet Tim at 10:00.
Tim will meet Ursula at 11:00.
Ursula will meet Fiona at 12:00.

Which one of the following additional meetings would enable Fiona to receive the book today?
questions.hint: Follow the book: Peter can only hand it to Zhang. Who must Zhang meet, and before what time?

steps.explain: Peter can only pass the book to Zhang at 09:00.
Tim → Ursula (11:00) → Fiona (12:00) already gets a book to Fiona. So Zhang must reach Tim before 11:00 or Ursula before 12:00.
Zhang meeting Tim at 10:30 works: Zhang → Tim (10:30) → Ursula (11:00) → Fiona (12:00).

D is too late (12:30). A and B do not involve Zhang or Peter.

Answer: C

questions.stem:
Last winter, Mr Murray planted twenty crocus plants but only five of them grew. After some research, Mr Murray found that there were two possible reasons for this:

• The winter may have been too warm, as crocuses need cold weather to grow.
• Possums may have dug up the crocus plants for food before they could fully grow.

**Mr Murray:** “I checked the weather reports and the average temperature during the winter was indeed higher than normal. That must be the reason why so many of the crocuses didn’t grow, so I shouldn’t blame the possums.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Mr Murray has made a mistake?
options: The crocuses may have been affected both by warm weather and by possums.
The warmer winter may have allowed possums to find other food sources.
Possums may also like to eat other flowering plants such as tulips.
Possums may only dig up crocus plants to eat if they cannot find anything else.
questions.hint: Mr Murray found one possible cause. Does that rule out the other cause?

steps.explain: Mr Murray knows that warm weather is one possible reason for poor growth. But he has not checked whether possums also dug up the plants.
steps.work: clue for one possible cause does not rule out another cause.

steps.explain: Both causes can happen in the same winter: warmer conditions may harm some crocuses, while possums may dig up others. The facts do not require choosing only one cause.
steps.work: Warm weather AND possums can both contribute.

steps.explain: so he is wrong to conclude that warm weather must be the only reason and that possums are not responsible.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{The crocuses may have been affected both by warm weather and by possums.}}\)

keyPoints.note: Finding one cause does not rule out another.

The tree is about 4 times the height of the swing: 4 × 2.5 m ≈ 10 m. The truck is less than 3 times the shed: less than 3 × 3 m = 9 m.
The house (next to the 1.5 m car) and the dinosaur (next to the 2 m person) are also smaller than 10 m. The tree is tallest.

questions.stem:
During a science lesson, the teacher says that the most effective way to reduce water waste at home is to make sure that your taps are not leaking.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the teacher’s claim?

It is very easy to fix taps that are leaking.
Leaking taps are the biggest source of water waste in households.
There are many different ways to reduce water waste at home.
questions.hint: The claim says fixing taps is the MOST effective way. Which statement shows leaking taps matter more than anything else?

steps.work: A large amount of waste alone would not show leaks are the largest source.

steps.explain: If leaking taps are the biggest source of household water waste, fixing them targets more waste than any other single source.
steps.work: Largest source → fixing it has the greatest potential reduction.

steps.explain: That comparison directly supports the claim.

questions.stem:

**Clue 3:** Box W contains more treasure than box X.

After reading all four clues, Idris is able to put the chests in order of how much treasure they contain.

Which one of the following could be the fourth clue?

Box X contains more treasure than box Y.
Box W contains more treasure than box Z.
Box Y contains more treasure than box Z.

steps.explain: Clues 2 and 3: W is more than X and Y. Clue 1: X is more than Z. So W has the most.
steps.work: W > X > Z, and W > Y

steps.explain: The fourth clue must place Y exactly among X and Z. “Y is more than X” gives one clear order.
steps.work: W > Y > X > Z

steps.explain: B and D each leave two possible orders, and C tells us nothing new.
steps.work: Answer: A

questions.stem:
ADVERTISEMENT: Anyone who loves musicals will love the new animated musical Carimba!

**Tina:** “Connor adores Carimba! So that tells me he is a big fan of musicals.”

Which one of the following sentences shows that Tina has made a mistake?
options: Carimba! may have won the award for best musical.
Carimba! may appeal to people who do not normally like musicals.
Carimba! may be Connor’s favourite movie.
Carimba! may have changed the kind of things Connor likes to watch.
questions.hint: The advert says musical-lovers will love Carimba!. Does that mean everyone who loves Carimba! loves musicals?

steps.explain: Tina uses the advertisement’s claim that musical fans will like Carimba. Connor likes the film, but Tina has no clue that he likes musicals.
steps.work: The advert only says: musical fans will probably like Carimba.

steps.explain: That if-then rule cannot automatically be reversed. Someone who is not usually a musical fan might still enjoy this particular film.
steps.work: Liking Carimba does not prove he likes musicals generally.

steps.explain: So the possible exception that Carimba appeals to people who do not normally like musicals shows Tina’s idea from the clues may be wrong.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Carimba! may appeal to people who do not normally like musicals.}}\)

questions.stem: If the order of these solids was reversed, then the second and third (from the top) shapes were swapped around, and then the whole stack was turned upside down, what shape would be second from the top?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" width="50%" viewBox="0 0 300 250" role="img"><image x="0" y="0" width="300" height="250" preserveAspectRatio="none" href="data:image/png;base64," xlink:href="data:image/png;base64,"/></svg>

questions.hint: Write the blocks from top to bottom after each instruction. Reversing flips the order; swapping positions 2 and 3 changes only those two middle entries.

steps.explain: Read the stack from top to bottom: N, E, I, L.
steps.work: Top → bottom: N, E, I, L.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" width="90%" viewBox="0 0 320 340" role="img"><rect width="320" height="340" fill="#fff"/><image x="10" y="0" width="300" height="250" preserveAspectRatio="none" href="data:image/png;base64," xlink:href="data:image/png;base64,"/><text x="160" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Starting order</text><text x="160" y="282" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#64748b">Read left to right: top → bottom</text><rect x="13" y="294" width="62" height="39" rx="7" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="3"/><text x="44" y="320" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">N</text><rect x="87" y="294" width="62" height="39" rx="7" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="118" y="320" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">E</text><rect x="161" y="294" width="62" height="39" rx="7" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="192" y="320" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">I</text><rect x="235" y="294" width="62" height="39" rx="7" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="266" y="320" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">L</text></svg>

steps.explain: Reverse the order, so the bottom goes to the top: L, I, E, N.
steps.work: N, E, I, L → L, I, E, N.

steps.explain: Swap the second and third shapes only: L, E, I, N.
steps.work: L, I, E, N → L, E, I, N.

steps.explain: Turn the stack upside down, which reverses the order again: N, I, E, L. The second shape is I, so the answer is C.
steps.work: L, E, I, N → N, I, E, L; second = I (C).

questions.stem:
Luke, Jayden, Rohan, and Max are seated around a table on a train. Two of them are facing forwards (in the direction of travel), while the other two facing backwards. Two of them have window seats while the other two have aisle seats.

I know that:
- Luke is sitting diagonally opposite Rohan
- Max is facing forwards
- Jayden is next to Luke

Which one of the following do I also know?
questions.hint: Draw two forward-facing and two backward-facing seats. Then place Luke and Rohan diagonally opposite.

steps.explain: Draw four seats: two facing forwards and two facing backwards. Put window seats in one column and aisle seats in the other. “Diagonally opposite” means across a corner; “opposite” means facing across the table in the same column.
steps.work: Make a 2-by-2 seat map: 2 directions × 2 seat types.

steps.work: This order leaves Max facing backwards, so cross it out.

questions.stem:
Jason folded a square piece of paper in half. He opened the paper out and then folded it in half again, but this time in a different way.

What did the paper look like when he opened it out again?

questions.hint: A fold in half leaves a crease that bisects the square. Look for exactly two different crease lines, each passing through the centre and splitting the paper into equal areas.

steps.explain: Each fold in half makes one crease that cuts the square into two equal parts. Two different half-folds make two different centre-crossing creases.
steps.work: One half-fold $\longrightarrow$ one crease that bisects the square. Two different half-folds $\longrightarrow$ two distinct bisecting creases.

questions.stem:
Alexis: “To even have a chance to be in the basketball team, you need to be at the team practice at least 4 times a week”.

Mae: “I practice at home 5 times a week so I will definitely make the basketball team”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mae made?
options: Mae may not learn the teamwork skills needed to make the team
Training for basketball alone is just as effective as team training
Practicing more alone does not guarantee Mae a spot on the team
The basketball team may already have enough players
questions.hint: Alexis specifies team practice, not just any practice. Check whether Mae meets that exact requirement and whether it guarantees selection.

steps.explain: Alexis’s condition is about attending team practice at least four times each week.
Mae says she practices at home. Home practice is not the same as team practice, so it does not establish that she has met Alexis’s condition.
Even attending the required team practices would only give Mae a chance; it would not promise a place.
Option A identifies the missing teamwork practice. Mae wrongly treats solo practice as satisfying the stated condition and as a promise.

keyPoints.text: at the team practice at least 4 times a week
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

keyPoints.text: practice at home 5 times a week
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
There is a library, post office, gym, shopping centre, hospital and bank in the suburb of Candyland.

The post office is north of the gym and northeast of the library. The gym is north of the shopping centre and west of the hospital. The bank is east of the hospital.

What building is northwest of the shopping centre?
questions.hint: Start at the shopping centre and place the gym directly north of it. Then use the “northeast of” clue to place the library relative to the post office.

steps.explain: Place the shopping centre as a reference point. The gym is north of it, and the hospital is east of the gym.

questions.stem:
Kelly believes that, in light of the global pandemic, it has been more important to support local businesses now than ever.

Which one of the following statements, if true, best supports Kelly’s belief?
options: It is important to support all businesses including international
Smaller, local businesses are struggling much more and need the support
International shipping for products can be expensive
Some products you can only get from overseas
questions.hint: Look for a statement that explains why local businesses especially need support during the pandemic.

steps.explain: Kelly’s claim is specifically that local businesses need support more than ever.
A strong supporting reason should describe a greater need among local businesses, rather than a general fact about international trade.
Option B says smaller local businesses are struggling more and need support, which directly explains why supporting them matters now.
The other statements do not establish a special need to support local businesses. Choose B.

keyPoints.text: support local businesses now than ever
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Whenever Mr Hansen’s chocolate is not delivered by Saturday, he gets angry. And when he gets angry, he cleans the classroom.

Jacob: “Mr Hansen cleaned the classroom this morning so he must have not gotten his chocolate on Saturday”.

Ben: “He may have just needed to clean the classroom because it was dirty”.

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The rules run from missing chocolate to anger to cleaning. Do not run that chain backwards unless the information guarantees it.

steps.explain: Given chain: chocolate not delivered $\Rightarrow$ angry $\Rightarrow$ cleans.
Jacob observes the last event (cleaning) and concludes the first event (no chocolate). That reverses the if-then rule; Mr Hansen could clean for another reason.
Ben says the room may have been dirty. The information does not rule out this other reason for cleaning, so his explanation is possible.
Only Ben’s reasoning is supported: option B.

keyPoints.text: Whenever Mr Hansen’s chocolate is not delivered by Saturday
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

keyPoints.text: he cleans the classroom this morning
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

Abba has two jigsaw puzzles.

Which one of these pieces can be found in one puzzle but NOT in the other?

questions.stem:
Three handballs are lined up in the middle of the court, all of which are either green or blue. Jason picks up the green ball and throws it. That ball hits the ball in the middle which rolls and hits the last ball which is blue.

On the basis of this information, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: There is only one green ball
There is only one blue ball
A green ball hit a blue ball
A blue ball hit a green ball
questions.hint: The first ball is green and the last is blue. Consider both possible colours for the middle ball.

steps.explain: The first ball is green and hits the middle ball; the middle ball then hits the last ball, which is blue.
If the middle ball is blue, the first green ball hits a blue ball.
If the middle ball is green, that green middle ball hits the last blue ball.
Either way, a green ball hits a blue ball. The numbers of green or blue balls are not fixed, so choose C.

keyPoints.text: the first ball, which is green
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

keyPoints.text: the last ball which is blue
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Jason is in a room with 5 jars. One of them has a love potion and the rest are laced with poison. He must bring back the jar with the love potion but he can only choose one jar. The scroll unravels and gives him 5 clues to help him choose a jar.

- The blue jar is not next to the yellow or green jar.
- The red jar is to the left of the green one
- The orange jar is not next to the jar with the love potion
- The yellow jar is at the far right and 2 places away from the green jar
- The green jar is 2 places away from the jar with the love potion

Which jar should Jason choose to bring home?
questions.hint: Place the yellow jar at position 5. The green jar is two positions away, and the red jar must be to its left. Then use the potion-distance clue.

steps.explain: Number the five places from left to right: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Yellow is at position 5.
Green is two places away from yellow, so green is at position 3. Red must be left of green.
The potion is two places away from green, so it could initially be at position 1 or 5. It cannot be position 5 because orange would then be next to it and the clue forbids that.
Thus the potion is at position 1. The jar order is Blue, Red, Green, Orange, Yellow, so choose Blue (A).

questions.stem:
The table shows statistics for the different amounts and types of books that have been sold in the first quarter of 2017.

| Month | Adventure stories | Classics | Fairy tales | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| January | 250 | 180 | 370 | 800 |
| February | 150 | 200 | 350 | 700 |
| March | 500 | 480 | X | 1300 |
| Total | 900 | 700 | 1200 | 2800 |

What number best replaces the X?
questions.hint: Use a total that includes the missing value. For example, the Classics column total is 700, and January and February already contribute 180 and 200.

steps.explain: The missing entry X is in the March row and Classics column. The Classics column total is 700.

steps.explain: Subtract the two known monthly amounts from the total. First add them: 180 + 200 = 380. Then subtract: 700 − 380 = 320.

questions.stem:
When Jason was learning how to master the backflip, his gym teacher told him “To have a chance at mastering that skill, you must practice on the mats for at least 30 minutes a day”.

If Jason’s teacher is right, which one of the following statements will be true?
options: Everyone that practices every day for 30 minutes will master the backflip
None of the students that practiced less than 30 minutes a day will master the backflip
Some of the gymnasts with less practice can master the backflip
Only students that practiced less than 30 minutes a day will master the backflip
questions.hint: The teacher gives 30 minutes as a necessary condition for having a chance. Use the contrapositive: less than 30 minutes means no chance under this rule.

steps.explain: Teacher’s rule: chance of mastering $\Rightarrow$ practice on mats for at least 30 minutes a day.
Read the rule this way: if a student practices less than 30 minutes a day, that student does not have a chance to master the skill under the stated rule.
This does not mean that 30 minutes guarantees mastery; so option A overstates the rule.
so B follows from the teacher’s condition.

keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Jim’s jumper is dark blue with white stripes. He wears a size medium and only Patrick has a bigger jumper than him.

Natasha: “This jumper is dark blue and is a size medium so it must be Jim’s jumper”.

Phillip: “But it does not have any white stripes, so it can’t be!”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Jim’s jumper has three stated features. A proposed match must satisfy all of them.

steps.explain: Jim’s jumper is dark blue, medium, and has white stripes.
Natasha checks only the colour and size. Those two matching features do not prove the jumper is Jim’s.
Phillip notices that the jumper has no white stripes. That does not match a required feature, so it cannot be Jim’s.
Phillip only is correct: option B.

keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Mr Jenkins: “I know that sixteen of my students are left-handed, but I only saw 11 students using the left-handed scissors in class today, the rest must be able to use their right hands as well”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mr Jenkins has made?
options: He did not count the children using the scissors accurately
There may not be enough scissors in the classroom
Some students can use both types of scissors
Some students may not have needed to use scissors today
questions.hint: Not seeing a left-handed student use the scissors does not prove that the student can use right-handed scissors. Consider whether every student needed scissors today.

steps.explain: There are 16 left-handed students, but Mr Jenkins observed only 11 using left-handed scissors today.
He assumes the other 5 students must have used right-handed scissors. That answer requires them to have used scissors at all.
Some students may not have needed to cut anything during that class, so they would not appear in either group.
Option D identifies the missing choice and the mistake in his answer.

keyPoints.text: sixteen of my students are left-handed
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

keyPoints.text: only saw 11 students using the left-handed scissors
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Kim, Becky, Adam and Levi are seated on the light rail. In this carriage, two of them are facing forwards and two are facing backwards. Two have aisle seats and the other two have window seats.

I know that:
- Becky is next to Kim
- Kim is sitting diagonally opposite Adam
- Levi is facing forwards

Which one of the following do I also know?
questions.hint: Draw a 2 by 2 seat layout. “Diagonally opposite” means opposite corners. Put Kim and Adam on opposite corners, then place Becky next to Kim and Levi in the remaining seat.

steps.explain: A 2 by 2 seating layout has two diagonal pairs. Place Kim at one corner and Adam at the diagonally opposite corner, as required.

questions.stem:
Here are the first six shapes in a pattern.

What are the next two shapes in the pattern?

questions.hint: Compare the projecting cube’s position and facing direction. Find which earlier shape each of shapes 5 and 6 repeats, then continue the same cycle.

steps.explain: Track the projecting cube while the three-cube column stays in the same place. The first direction returns at position 5, so shape 5 repeats shape 1.
steps.work: Shape 1 = shape 5.

questions.stem:
Kelly believes that: “The local council should invest money into putting more recycling bins in the park so more rubbish can be recycled”.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports Kelly’s argument?
options: With more recycling bins, more people can choose to recycle
People will throw any rubbish into the recycling bins
Many people will litter around the park and ignore the bins
Placing more bins in the park will be expensive
questions.hint: Choose the statement that connects adding bins with the intended result: more rubbish being recycled.

steps.explain: Kelly’s reason for adding bins is to increase recycling in the park.
Option A explains the link: extra bins give more people an opportunity to recycle.
Options B and C suggest the bins may be misused or ignored. Option D adds a cost, not a benefit.
so option A best supports Kelly’s argument.

keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
When the ambulance siren goes off, there could be an accident that the ambulance must get to or a police matter.

Nelly: “If you hear a siren there must be an accident that the ambulance must get to”.

Fanny: “No, it may be a police matter and not necessarily an accident”.

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is true?
questions.hint: The siren can have either of two causes. A statement saying “must be an accident” ignores the other possibility.

steps.explain: The prompt allows two choices: an accident or a police matter.
Nelly says every siren must mean an accident, which rules out the police-matter choice and is too strong.
Fanny correctly notes that it may be a police matter instead of an accident.
Only Fanny’s reasoning is true: option B.

keyPoints.text: an accident that the ambulance must get to
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Emma, Felix, Gary and Hannah are on the school dance team. The dance coach has announced that: If Emma does not dance tomorrow, then Felix will dance. If Emma does dance then Gary will take Hannah’s place.

So, if Felix does not dance tomorrow, which of the other three dancers will be at practice?
questions.hint: Use the first conditional backwards by contrapositive: if Felix does not dance, Emma cannot be absent. Then apply the second rule.

steps.explain: Rule 1: if Emma does not dance, Felix dances. Read the rule this way: if Felix does not dance, Emma dances.
We are told Felix does not dance, so Emma must dance.
Rule 2 says that if Emma dances, Gary takes Hannah’s place. So Gary dances and Hannah does not.
The dancers among the other three are Emma and Gary: option A.

keyPoints.text: If Emma does not dance tomorrow
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

keyPoints.text: if Felix does not dance tomorrow
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Alan and Alex played a game. To score points they had to throw hoops around the sticks. Throwing a hoop around stick A scores more points than throwing a hoop around stick B.

Alan scored 10 points by throwing 3 hoops around stick B and 1 hoop around stick A. Alex scored 12 points by throwing 2 hoops around each stick.

How many points are scored for throwing a hoop around stick A?
questions.hint: Let A and B be the scores for one hoop on each stick. Translate both players’ totals into equations and subtract.

steps.explain: Let $a$ be the points for stick A and $b$ for stick B. Alan’s score gives $a+3b=10$. Alex’s gives $2a+2b=12$.
Divide Alex’s equation by 2: $a+b=6$.
Subtract $a+b=6$ from $a+3b=10$: $2b=4$, so $b=2$. Then $a=6-2=4$.
One hoop around stick A scores $\boxed{4}$ points, option C.

keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.
Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
A doctor believes that learning how to ride a bicycle early in childhood is very important as it keeps kids physically active and benefits their mental health.

Which one of these statements, if true, best supports the doctor’s claim?
options: Some families can’t afford to buy bikes
Children can get hurt by falling off while riding their bikes
Riding bikes instead of using cars is good for the environment
Some children will be professional cyclists
questions.hint: The claim is that early cycling is beneficial. Among the options, choose the one that gives an additional positive effect of cycling rather than a cost or risk.

steps.explain: The doctor says learning to ride early supports children’s physical activity and mental health.
Option A is a barrier and B describes a risk, so neither supports the claim.
Option C adds a broader benefit: choosing bikes over cars reduces environmental harm, which supports cycling as a worthwhile activity.
Option D applies only to a small group and does not explain why children generally benefit. The best available support is C.

keyPoints.text: physically active and benefits their mental health
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Anna, Betty and Idris all have insect terrariums. Anna has butterflies, flies, ladybugs, and moths. Betty keeps ants, moths and ladybugs. Idris keeps mosquitoes, bees, ladybugs, beetles, and moths.

Which insects does Anna keep that neither Betty nor Idris keep?
questions.hint: Start with Anna’s list, then cross off every insect that appears on either Betty’s or Idris’s list.

steps.explain: Anna has butterflies, flies, ladybugs, and moths.
Ladybugs and moths are also kept by Betty and Idris, so remove them.
Neither Betty nor Idris has butterflies or flies.
Anna is the only person whose list has both butterflies and flies: option A.

keyPoints.text: Anna has butterflies, flies, ladybugs, and moths

questions.stem:
At lunch time, I have to choose what food I want for my lunch meal.

I have to choose one food or drink item from each of the following lists:

List 1:
Sandwich
Meat Pie
Sausage Roll
Ravioli

List 2:
Spaghetti
Apple
Orange
Juice

List 3:
Spaghetti
Meat Pie
Chocolate
Water

List 4:
Apple
Chocolate
Ravioli
Water

I know I want to have spaghetti, a sausage roll and a chocolate.

Which of the following can I NOT choose as my final food or drink item?
questions.hint: Choose the three named foods from lists where they appear. The final item must come from the one remaining list, and it must be different from items already chosen.

steps.explain: Spaghetti appears in Lists 2 and 3; chocolate appears in Lists 3 and 4; sausage roll appears only in List 1.
To choose one item from every list without repeating a list, sausage roll must represent List 1. Spaghetti can be chosen from List 2 and chocolate from List 3 or 4.
The remaining choice must come from the other list. Sandwich appears only in List 1, which is already used by sausage roll.
so Sandwich cannot be chosen as the last item: option A.

keyPoints.text: one food or drink item from each
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem:
Only people that wear masks on public transport and have been covid-tested are allowed onto the rides at Luna Park.

Sally: “Mitchell wears a mask but only when there are teachers on the school bus so he’ll be able to go on the rides at Luna Park”.

Mitchell: “Sally always wears her mask and has tested negative for Covid-19 so she will be able to go on the rides at Luna Park”.

If the information in the box above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Entry requires both conditions: wearing a mask on public transport and having a Covid test. Check which person is known to meet both.

steps.explain: The rule requires a mask on public transport AND a Covid test. Both conditions are needed.
Mitchell’s mask use depends on whether teachers are on the bus, and we are not told that he has been tested, so Sally cannot conclude he qualifies.
Sally always wears a mask and has tested negative, so she meets both conditions stated in the rule.
Only Mitchell’s reasoning about Sally is correct: option B.

keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition as one of the clues in your reasoning.

questions.stem: Ben, Jerry and Tom are standing in a row. If Ben is to the right of Jerry and Tom is to the left of Ben, which one of the following statements must be true?
options: Jerry is furthest to the right
Ben is the furthest to the right
Tom is furthest to the left
questions.hint: Both clues place another person to Ben’s left. Work out which position is forced and which relative order is not known.

steps.explain: Ben is to the right of Jerry, so Jerry is left of Ben.
Tom is also to the left of Ben. The clues do not say which of Tom or Jerry is further left.
Since both Jerry and Tom are left of Ben, Ben must be the furthest to the right.
The guaranteed statement is option C.

questions.stem:
In a school of 600 students, 320 study Korean, 270 study Thai and 110 study German. There are 150 students who study only two languages: 60 students study Korean and Thai, 50 students study Thai and German, and 40 students study German and Korean.

At most how many students study all three languages?
questions.hint: Use the German total. Of the 110 German students, 50 study only Thai and German and 40 study only German and Korean, leaving at most the remainder for all three.

steps.explain: The 50 Thai-German students and 40 German-Korean students are specified as students who study only two languages.
These use $50+40=90$ of the 110 German students.
At most $110-90=20$ German students remain available to study all three languages. Other totals do not increase this German limit.
So the maximum possible number studying all three is $\boxed{20}$, option A.

questions.stem:
Vanessa and George are sitting in the park.

George: “My mum told me my little sister dropped her light pink teddy bear somewhere on the play equipment, so I need to find it”.

Vanessa: “Oh I saw a pink bear on the ground near the swings! It must be hers”.

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Vanessa made?
options: His sister might not like that bear.
Even though the bear is pink, it may not be the right pink
There may be more than one light pink bear.
George may be looking for someone else’s bear
questions.hint: A general colour description does not uniquely identify one teddy bear. Consider whether several bears could match it.

steps.explain: George is searching for his sister’s light pink teddy bear.
Vanessa sees a pink bear, but “pink” alone does not tell us who owns the bear. There may be multiple bears with that colour, including more than one light pink bear.
The other choices speculate about what the sister likes or who George is searching for; the key reasoning error is treating one matching feature as proof that it is the same object.
Option C best identifies Vanessa’s mistake.

questions.stem:
A firefighter says: “everyone should check where the emergency exits are in a building that they are staying in”

Which one of the following statements, if true, best supports the firefighter’s claim?
options: Emergency exits are rarely ever used in buildings
You are able to escape faster and easier in cases of emergency
Fires do not spread as fast in buildings as in nature
People in buildings usually have access to water to put out fires
questions.hint: The advice is about knowing where exits are before an emergency. Choose the option that explains how this knowledge helps during an emergency.

steps.explain: The claim is to check exit locations in advance.
If people already know where the exits are, they can find a way out faster and more easily when an emergency happens.
The other options do not show a benefit of knowing the exit location; some even reduce the reason to prepare.
Option B directly supports the firefighter’s advice.
